item.definition_in_origin_frame: Patel's term for the layered way a poster is read: certain elements are immediately and universally understood while other elements require specific cultural knowledge to be understood.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy, diagram captions (spine 6)
item.question: A poster has one element far more distinct than everything else, and the secondary material now reads as an undifferentiated mass. What does Samara say is happening?
item.answer: He describes exactly this. An element that distinguishes itself from the others becomes a focal point and therefore assumes the greatest level of importance — but where the primary element disconnects visually to an extreme degree, that extremity diminishes the effect of the other contrasts evident in the secondary material. The contrasts among the secondary elements have not changed; they are being read against a much larger difference and so register less. The general controls he names are contrast in relative size and in relative spacing, meaning density against openness, which he says account for the most effective ways to establish a clear hierarchy, enhanced by hue or value change.
item.support: Diagram captions in "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": a distinguished element becoming a focal point of greatest importance; the extreme degree of disconnection diminishing the effect of other contrasts; size and spacing contrast as the most effective hierarchy controls.
confounders: assuming the secondary contrasts were poorly designed, when the stated cause is the primary element's extremity
assuming the remedy is more contrast everywhere; that is the change that produced the problem
confusing this with the source's general advice to push differences to greater extremes, which he gives for a complicated field

source_terms: Within the format, alignments between elements create structure.
space is divided based on content: like information is grouped together, disparate information is separated; their resulting widths and heights subdivide the surrounding field
item.claim: Structure arises from the content, not the other way round. Like information is grouped and disparate information separated; the widths and heights those groups occupy are what subdivide the surrounding field. A grouping may yield a single axis dividing the space into two fields, or many axes and correspondingly complex subdivisions. Changes in weight and scale introduce hierarchy — the source's word for visual ordering — to the information.

mechanism.text: Grouping and separating produce edges; the edges are alignments; the alignments are the structure. The demonstration holds content constant and varies only the grouping.

scope.conditions: any composition of mixed information within a format

caveats.text: the source notes both demonstrated compositions use the same type family and only a selection of possible sizes, so an enormous variety of layouts is reachable within strict limitations
this is the section's clearest controlled comparison, but it is a designed illustration rather than a test — no claim is made about what a viewer does with either version

positive.description: same event poster set two ways, each shown beside the alignment structure it implies: a two-field division and a multi-field grid

intra_source_relations.note: the reciprocity of content and structure is argued at length later
same page spread

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
item.question: A key label in a dense, structureless poster is partly obscured. A colleague proposes repeating it in a clear area of the page. What does Samara say about that move, and what does he prefer?
item.answer: He allows it and then withdraws most of the allowance. Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help, he says, but it may also confuse a viewer with its redundancy — better to give the information a little extra room where it appears in sequence. So his preference is to fix the element in place rather than duplicate it. He pairs this with a general fallback: when in doubt, simplify, because if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, the element will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.
item.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": repetition of obscured information may help or may confuse through redundancy, with extra room in sequence preferred; and the when-in-doubt-simplify rule with its reason.
confounders: treating repetition as a straightforwardly safe redundancy strategy
assuming the fix is to increase the label's size, which is a different lever in his account
confusing this repetition with the repetition he recommends elsewhere, which marks which elements are alike in meaning

source_terms:
Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy
All of the means of constructing a clear hierarchy in a grid-based layout remain the same when trying to do so in a layout based on some alternative approach; there's no reason why an unsual composition can't also be a friendly one.
The two aspects of hierarchic control that deserve the most attention—and which tend, most often, to be the root of viewers' navigation trouble in unusual circumstances—are those of optical differentiation and "eye path," or compositional flow.
item.claim: Every means of constructing a clear hierarchy in a grid-based layout remains available and unchanged in a layout built on an alternative approach; there is no reason an unusual composition cannot also be a friendly one. Two aspects of hierarchic control deserve the most attention because they are, most often, the root of viewers' navigation trouble in unusual circumstances: optical differentiation, and eye path — also called compositional flow.

scope.conditions: layouts organised by any alternative to the grid

caveats.text: This is the chapter's diagnostic proposition: when an unconventional layout fails for a reader, the source locates the fault in one of exactly two places rather than in the decision to depart from the grid. It is stated as experience, not measured.

The claim that hierarchy methods carry over unchanged is asserted rather than demonstrated, and it sits against the same chapter's admission elsewhere that visual clarity is decreased by some of these operations.

source_stated_problems: viewers' navigation trouble in unusual circumstances

intra_source_relations.note: where the objective diagnosis should look
the optical differentiation half
the eye path half

source_terms:
Contrast in relative size (large versus small) and relative spacing (or density and openness) account for the most effective ways to establish a clear hierarchy.
When an element in a visual field distinguishes itself from others... it becomes a focal point and, therefore, assumes the greatest level of importance.
Repetition assigns relative meaning to elements that will be understood as related no matter where they occur within the visual field
item.claim: Contrast in relative size — large against small — and in relative spacing, meaning density against openness, account for the most effective ways to establish a clear hierarchy. As expressions of purely positive/negative interaction, these two contrasts change the sense of the format being divided into darker and lighter areas, an effect that is enhanced by altering hue or value. An element that distinguishes itself sufficiently from the others becomes a focal point and therefore assumes the greatest level of importance; where that disconnection is extreme, it diminishes the effect of other contrasts present in the secondary material. Repetition performs the complementary function: it assigns relative meaning to elements that will be understood as related wherever they occur in the field, even when separated by clearly different material. Hierarchy, the source states, is not only about level of importance but also about relation — establishing which elements are alike in meaning, whether or not they are important.

mechanism.text: Size and spacing act on the same underlying variable — how much of the format reads dark and how much light — which is why they dominate over other contrasts, and why an extreme focal point flattens the differences among everything else.

scope.conditions: any composition, grid-based or alternative

caveats.text: The redefinition of hierarchy to include relation as well as rank is the load-bearing part of this object and is easily lost: it is what lets a layout without a reading order still be hierarchically organised.

The claim is illustrated by diagrams — a vivid red dot among neutral elements, and repeated forms across a field — which this lane could not inspect. The words are recorded; the demonstrated magnitudes are not.

source_stated_problems: an extremely disconnected primary element diminishes the effect of the other contrasts present
source_stated_remedies: establish hierarchy through contrast in relative size and in relative density or openness
enhance the effect with hue or value change
use repetition to mark which elements are alike in meaning

item.label: how_a_still_image_carries_a_narrative_to_a_viewer_who_holds_the_code
item.description: Patel's chapter-4 account of poster meaning, assembled: the face opens attention before recognition; recognition of the star brings forward a persona that was built cumulatively by star, artist and public and is carried by a few fixed features; character types compress whole sets of relations into single figures so that the relations BETWEEN them are inferred rather than depicted; and because the code does the work, text can be minimised, which is what Indian posters in fact do.

whole_system_claim.text: A poster can carry a narrative structure it never depicts, provided the viewer holds the code. Attention is won by the face without recognition; meaning is then supplied by the viewer out of an accumulated persona and a familiar typology, not out of the poster. The poster's job is therefore indexing, not describing — which is why minimal text suffices and why the same design fails outside the code.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Patel connects the first three members explicitly through her "hierarchy of responses" and her worked reading of the Deewaar poster. She does not present them as a model, does not draw the consequence for text as following from the type code, and never cites Dwyer's chapter-1 account of personification as the precondition. Assembling them into a causal chain, and adding those two members, is the extractor's. What the grouping ADDS, and what must be attributed to CANON-014, is the observation that all four devices fail together at the same boundary - the viewer who does not hold the code - which is visible across the set and not within any member.

dependencies.nature: the persona can only be indexed by a few features if personification, not impersonation, is the prevailing mode; Dwyer establishes that in chapter 1 and Patel relies on it in chapter 4 without restating it
text can be dropped only because the type code already carries the information text would have carried

tradeoffs.nature: Patel states the trade-off herself: designs that focus on one element are more universally understood but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. Reach and specificity are exchanged

item.source_warning_ref: Patel states that character types 'are not universally recognized' and are 'only fully understood by those with a knowledge of that culture' (printed p. 194); she draws the same boundary for star recognition at p. 183

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. The members are all Patel's, all from one chapter, and she does connect the first three explicitly through the "hierarchy of responses". What is the EXTRACTOR'S and must be attributed to CANON-014 is the addition of sk_dpci_0130 (minimal text) as a consequence of the code rather than as a separate observation, and the addition of sk_dpci_0080 (personification) from Dwyer's chapter as the precondition — Patel never cites Dwyer's chapter for this. The causal ordering is likewise the extractor's. The system is recorded as a reading of Patel's argument, not as a structure she sets out.

provenance.chapter: 4, Advertising and the Communication of Meaning (with one member from Ch. 1)
provenance.section: The Star Image; The Cultural Construction of Meaning; Character Types

extractor_notes.text: Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Every member is argued and illustrated by readings of specific posters; none is measured. No audience study exists anywhere in this book.

source_terms: triggering a hierarchy of responses
the primary field of expressive action
item.claim: Patel argues that the star portrait is the natural opening component of a poster because it activates a "hierarchy of responses" in two distinct stages that she separates explicitly. First, an image of a human face is "instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all" — of any mix of images, the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a star, which arouses expectations built up over time. She states the boundary in the same breath: "an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response."

mechanism.text: Patel grounds the first stage in the claim that the structuring of human relationships from the earliest stages of life is based on physical appearance and facial recognition, and that the face is "the primary field of expressive action" where all forms of emotion can be made visible, so it holds attention at a deeper level than other visual images. The second stage is not perceptual but cultural: it depends on the viewer holding the star's accumulated text.

scope.conditions: Stated for film posters, Indian and Western alike ("the majority of film posters (both Indian and Western) use portraits"). Stage one is offered as general; stage two is expressly bounded to viewers inside the culture.

caveats.text: THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ABOUT THIS OBJECT IS THE SEPARATION IT MAKES. The source itself divides a putatively universal attentional effect from a culturally-specific recognition effect, and states that the second does not travel. Collapsing the two would be the error the source is guarding against

the first stage is asserted from developmental and expressive premises with no measurement; Patel reports no eye-tracking, no attention study and no test of any kind. It is a plausible mechanism, not a demonstrated one
the source is a 2002 art-historical book, not a perception study, and should not be cited as evidence for a face-attention effect

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: The universal half of the claim rests on assertion. The source's real contribution is the boundary it draws, not the effect it posits.

positive: Muqaddar ka Sikandar (1978), Bachchan on a motorbike against a background of four large portraits, differentiated by contrasting colours

source_terms:
Imagery as a Source
what happens if the visual aspects of imagery are allowed to rule, so to speak—to determine not only the compositional structure of a project overall, but the compositional and stylistic attributes of the type?
Typography is always a pattern of lines, but images present a radically greater range of form languages
item.claim: Bringing type and image together is described as notoriously difficult because each has formal characteristics most often at odds with the other, and because the two are usually assumed to be mutually dominant and referential. The source proposes inverting that assumption and letting the imagery rule — determining not only the project's overall compositional structure but the compositional and stylistic attributes of the type. Its reason is that typography is always a pattern of lines whereas images present a radically greater range of form languages, so applying an image's language to text quickly relieves a designer of presumptions about how text should behave and how layouts ought to be organised. Two directions are named: one in which typographic elements become in essence part of the imagery, and one in which the imagery sets up the logic for how type responds to it pictorially while the type retains its identity as a separate entity alongside the images.

mechanism.text: Type's form language is narrow — lines — so it cannot supply the variety a layout needs; imagery can, and letting it lead breaks the designer's default assumptions about text behaviour rather than arguing with them.

scope.conditions: projects that carry substantial image material

caveats.text: The source is explicit that the correspondence need not be literal: in one study the sizes, positions and radii of type arcs are not direct repetitions of any attribute in the image, and the mere fact of them is enough to create the visual connection. That weakens the method into a judgement call with no test.
Every instance is a layout this lane could not see. The two named directions are recorded because they are stated in words; the visual result of either is not inferred.

source_stated_problems: type and image are notoriously challenging to bring together; each has its own formal characteristics most often at odds with the other
source_stated_remedies: let the imagery determine the compositional structure and the type's compositional and stylistic attributes
either absorb the typographic elements into the imagery, or let the imagery set the logic to which separate type responds

positive.description: an exhibition poster whose titling and text typography are composed and styled to become one with a field of forensic bone images, with transparency, overlapped edges and misaligned grids inside the imagery informing font choices and forcing text into cut-out areas that look grid-based but are not
a promotional calendar in which each month's date matrix changes in width, depth and weekday-list orientation in response to the formal conditions of that month's photograph
running text set flush right so that the difference between its aligned edge and its irregular rag echoes the hard, soft, dark and light stems of a bamboo image

intra_source_relations.note: one of the alternative systems context may select
the inverse operation — bending the image toward the environment rather than the environment toward the image

provenance.section: Alternative Architectures — Intuitive, Relational, and Conceptual: 'Imagery as a Source' (spine 6)

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 83-84 (Ch. 16, 'The Law of Shape', the typography passage)
item.question: Why do the authors put legibility above expressive character in a logotype? Give the cycle they describe, and say what they concede about typographic mood.
item.answer: Because they hold the trade is not worth making. The cycle: to get an average prospect to notice the mood of a logotype you have to exaggerate the characteristics of the typography, and when you do that you lose the logotype's legibility — and an illegible logotype has little or no meaning in the consumer's mind, not because of the face but because the prospect cannot read the words and therefore cannot remember the name. Hence legibility is the most important consideration in selecting a typeface. What they concede is that perceptual differences are real: sans serif faces look modern and serif faces old-fashioned, bold looks masculine and light feminine. Their point is that these differences only become obvious through exaggeration — they ask whether you would really set a brand name in black-letter Gothic to look established, and answer that few prospects could then read it. They also say customers are only dimly aware of typeface differences, paraphrasing David Ogilvy to the effect that no one ever declined to buy a detergent over the choice of Futura Demibold.
item.support: Printed pp. 83-84. The argument is the authors' own with a stated cycle; no legibility measurement is cited, and the chapter's only external authority is a paraphrase of Ogilvy.
confounders: assuming they say typography carries no meaning; they concede specific perceptual associations and rank them below readability
reading this as an accessibility argument; the concern here is recall of a name, not readability for readers with impairments, and no criterion or threshold is given
the brand-expression default of choosing a face to express brand attributes, which is the practice the chapter is arguing against

item.source_locator: Ch. 'No Squeeze…', KamaSutra passage
item.question: A brand must enter a category whose only mass public framing is a government health programme, and wants to be premium. What three requirements does this source report a name having had to satisfy at once, whose finding is it, and how was it arrived at?
item.answer: Maximum reach and intelligibility, an erotic connotation, and cultural legitimacy — satisfied simultaneously by naming the condom brand 'KamaSutra', positioned against the state's Nirodh family-planning framing as an enabler of better lovemaking and priced at a premium to both Nirodh and imported brands. The finding is the anthropologist William Mazzarella's, not the author's, and Mazzarella reached it by speaking with the campaign's creators after the fact — so it is a reconstruction of a naming decision rather than a record made at the time. The source presents the three requirements for this case and does not claim they generalise.
item.support: 'it instantly satisfied three crucial requirements: maximum reach/intelligibility, an erotic connotation, and cultural legitimacy'
item.confounders: The campaign's outcome was contested — ASCI ordered modifications, a Rajya Sabha member sought a ban, Doordarshan withdrew its storyboard approval, and the company fell back to shop displays. Commercial success is not established.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction, closing (spine 6)
item.question: Samara suggests deconstruction "might even improve readability." What does he mean by readability there, and how confident is the claim?
item.answer: He redefines the word. Readability in that sentence means the quality of, and the degree to which, the type engages its readers with the content — not the ease of decoding it. The claim is hedged: "might even", and it arrives immediately after his statement that these qualities should be made visual not merely as a tool for clarifying hierarchy and not just as intriguing eye candy, but to lay bare an author's methods and intent. It carries no reader evidence of any kind. Read as a claim about decoding ease it would flatly contradict his own admission that fragmenting text interferes with reading; read as a claim about engagement it does not.
item.support: Closing of "Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction": the hedged suggestion about readability, with the source's own parenthetical definition of readability as engagement with the content.
confounders: reading 'readability' in the standard legibility sense, which makes the sentence contradict the same section
treating a hedged aside as one of the chapter's supported claims
confusing it with the accessibility sense of readability, which this book does not discuss

item.visible_content: Four panels in two rows. Left of each row, a poster for the same event — a Hear-Say reading by Henry Magaziner at a Philadelphia bookshop, with the same date, time and address. Right of each row, the alignment structure that composition implies, drawn as teal rules. Top row: the information is set as one flush-right stack, and the derived structure is two fields divided by a single vertical axis. Bottom row: the same information is broken into several differently-weighted groups scattered across the format, and the derived structure is a multi-field grid of roughly five vertical and five horizontal divisions.
item.what_the_visual_supports: That a grid is READ OFF a composition rather than imposed on it. The content is held constant and only the grouping changes, and the structure changes with it. It also supports the source's narrower claim that a large variety of layouts is reachable inside strict limits: both posters use one type family and a small set of sizes.
item.requires_prose: That like information is grouped and disparate information separated, and that changes in weight and scale are what introduce hierarchy. The picture shows the outcome; the caption supplies the rule that produced it.
item.extractor_note: This is the clearest minimal pair in the section — same content, one variable (grouping) changed, both results shown with their derived structures. The caption states the claim, so a text-only extraction keeps the claim and loses the proof.

item.claim: Sullivan holds that visual clichés are category-specific rather than general, and that the working procedure is therefore to go and learn which ones your category is using — visit the competitors' sites, watch their videos, study their social posts — and then not use those. He gives examples by category: grandfathers flying kites with grandchildren in insurance, earnest bespectacled people with a screen reflected in their glasses in technology. He calls the tired visual the picture version of low-hanging fruit, and prescribes the same clearing move: get them out of your system right away.

item.question: A car company argues that its parent name is a megabrand and its model names are the brands beneath it. What is the authors' specific objection to that structure, and what image do they use to make it?
item.answer: Their objection is that people assign exactly one name to each product, and they choose the name that best captures its essence — sometimes the parent name, sometimes the model name, sometimes a nickname — and are not consistent about which. The hierarchy therefore does not survive contact with a customer. Their image is a teeter-totter: thousands of tiny ones in the consumer's mind, and like real ones both sides cannot be up at once. On the Chevrolet/Lumina teeter-totter the Chevrolet side is up, so the owner says "I drive a Chevrolet"; on the Chevrolet/Corvette one the Corvette side is up, so the owner says "I drive a Vette". Which end rises is not the marketer's choice. They add that customers want brands that are narrow in scope and distinguishable by a single word, the shorter the better.

source_terms: The Law of Subbrands

item.claim: Law 14. The authors treat subbranding, masterbranding and megabranding as terminology invented to legitimise moves management already wanted to make, and say the concepts have no meaning in the minds of most consumers. Their diagnostic is a demand test framed as a question nobody asks: did anyone ever ask a Holiday Inn clerk for a more expensive hotel, or a Cadillac dealer for a smaller Cadillac? Where the question is absurd, the subbrand answers a demand that does not exist. They add a naming-authority point: what the manufacturer calls a brand the customer calls a model, and what the manufacturer calls a megabrand the customer calls a brand — a company cannot impose its own branding system on a market that sees things differently.

Subbranding pushes the core brand outward from inside the company rather than answering anything the customer wanted, and it captures management attention because of what it promises rather than what it delivers. The core brand's established meaning then works against the extension: a customer paying a premium wants a premium brand, so paying more to stay at a Holiday Inn is the objection the strategy cannot answer.

item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', sections 'Posters' and 'Subway cards' (spine 13)
item.question: You are handed one brief covering a roadside poster and a transit card inside a train carriage, and asked to run the same execution on both. Using only what Ogilvy states, say what you would do and how confident you could be in each half.
item.answer: You would not run the same execution. For the poster he prescribes a visual scandal, the promise delivered pictorially as well as in words, the largest possible type, a brand name visible at a distance and no more than three elements. For the transit card he prescribes the opposite of that compression: he warns explicitly against designing a subway card like a billboard with five or six words, because the average rider was exposed to the card for twenty-one minutes and eighty-five per cent of passengers carried nothing else to read, so a long message can be read — he reports writing seventy-six words for one. Confidence differs sharply. The transit prescription follows from two reported audience measurements; the poster prescription he marks himself as resting on little or no research, closing the section by asking the reader to tell him if they know more. Both figures describe one transit system in one era.

item.question: Samara says hierarchy is not only about importance. What else does he say it is about, and which device carries that second job?
item.answer: It is also about relation — establishing which elements are alike in meaning, whether or not they are important. The device that carries it is repetition: repetition assigns relative meaning to elements that will be understood as related no matter where they occur within the visual field, even when separated by material that is clearly different. This matters more in an unstructured layout than in a grid, because a grid encodes relatedness by position and a structureless layout has no position to encode it with.

source_terms: The Law of Shape
A brand's logotype should be designed to fit the eyes. Both eyes.
Legibility is the most important consideration in selecting a typeface used in a logotype.
The meaning lies in the word, or words, not in the visual symbol.
item.claim: Law 16. Three connected claims about visual identity. First shape: because human eyes are mounted side by side, the ideal logotype is horizontal, roughly two and a quarter units wide to one high, and a vertical logotype is at a severe disadvantage, especially on a retail frontage. Second typography: legibility is the most important consideration, over any expressive quality, because a typeface's mood only becomes noticeable through exaggeration and exaggeration costs legibility — a trade the authors say is not worth making. Third symbol: the trademark is overrated, the meaning lies in the word, and it is the name that gives the symbol meaning rather than the reverse. A symbol may come to stand for a name through long association, but the authors say the advantages of using it alone are slim, and that if history has not already given a brand one of the few simple effective symbols it is probably too late to create one.

mechanism.text: For shape, binocular geometry: two eyes side by side make a horizontal field, so a horizontal mark takes maximum advantage of it. For typography, a stated vicious cycle: to make the mood of a face noticeable to an average prospect you must exaggerate it, and exaggeration destroys readability, so the name cannot be read and therefore cannot be remembered. For the symbol, a "rebus" effect: the mark can stand for the name only after the name has given it meaning.

scope.conditions: the horizontal claim is said to hold wherever a logotype is used and to matter most on retail premises

caveats.text: the 2.25:1 proportion is given with no derivation and no evidence; the binocular argument is stated as though it settled the ratio, which it does not
the typography claim rests on a paraphrase of David Ogilvy and on the authors' own rhetorical questions about which typeface Rolex or Rolls-Royce uses; no legibility measurement is cited

item.question: When an unconventional layout gives readers trouble, Samara says the fault is almost always in one of two places. Which two, and what does he claim about the tools available to fix them?
item.answer: The two are optical differentiation — whether the reader can identify the most important elements, or the ones a sequence starts from — and eye path, also called compositional flow, meaning how the first element optically connects the reader to what comes next. His claim about the tools is that nothing new is required: every means of constructing a clear hierarchy in a grid-based layout remains the same in a layout built on an alternative approach, and there is no reason an unusual composition cannot also be a friendly one. The difference is one of degree, not of kind — he recommends applying the familiar size and weight differences to greater extremes than usual.

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. xi-xii (Introduction, the passage beginning 'Some managers believe that brands possess unique identities')
item.question: Ries and Ries reject the whole vocabulary of brand architecture — flanker brands, megabrands, subbrands, model names. What test do they apply to reach that conclusion, and what definition of a brand do they put in its place?
item.answer: Their test is conversational: they ask the reader to imagine a customer saying to a friend "what do you think of this new flanker brand?" and answering "not much, I stick with megabrands or subbrands". Since nobody talks or thinks that way, they conclude the distinctions have no existence in the only place they regard as real — the prospect's mind — and that on paper there is no difference between a company name, a product name and a brand name. In their place they put a definition with no hierarchy in it at all: a brand name is a word in the mind, specifically a proper noun, and any and every proper noun is a brand. That deliberately extends beyond registered trademarks to places (Philadelphia the cheese and the city, Patagonia the clothing and the region) and to people. They separately insist a brand name on a package is not the same thing as a brand name in a mind, since the same shopper may buy milk and bread as commodities and beer and cigarettes by brand on one trip.

item.question: Marketers observed richer consumers buying popular-segment products and called it down-trading. What does this source say was actually happening, and what is the general shape of the error?
item.answer: That the direction of the inference was wrong. The observation was read as a consumer trait — 'many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy' — and her correction is that 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', so the popular and discount segments in many cases now offered equivalent or better benefits at a lower price. Her instances are automotive — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B-segment car with premium features — and her conclusion is that 'the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant'. item.question: Ogilvy's typography advice runs off one organising principle. Name it, derive two of his specific rules from it, and state the limit he himself places on the whole subject.
item.answer: The principle is that the eye is a creature of habit: what is easy to read is what people are accustomed to reading. From it he derives that capitals retard reading, since they have no ascenders or descenders to help word recognition and tend to be read letter by letter, and that copy should be set about forty characters wide, the measure people are used to in newspapers; the same principle gives him familiar faces such as Century, Caslon, Baskerville and Jenson, and his line that the drama belongs in what you say, not in the typeface. The limit he states himself is that no reader ever bought a product because of the typeface, but an advertisement nobody can read cannot sell — you cannot save souls in an empty church. item.question: A magazine spread is proposed with a full-bleed photograph, a sans-serif headline reversed out of it, one column of copy running the full page width and no captions. Working only from what Ogilvy states in the layout and typography sections, list what he would change and give his reason for each.
item.answer: Five changes, each with its own stated reason. Move the headline off the illustration and beneath it: readers look first at the illustration, then the headline, then the copy, and he reports headlines below the illustration read by ten per cent more people. Set the headline in lower case rather than reversed out: reverse is almost impossible to read and capitals retard reading because they lack ascenders and descenders. Set the copy in a serif face: readers are accustomed to serifs in books, magazines and newspapers, and the eye is a creature of habit. Break the single full-width column into columns of roughly thirty-five to forty-five characters: people are used to about forty characters in newspapers, and a measure too wide is illegible. Add a caption under the photograph carrying the brand name and the promise: more people read captions than read body copy, so an uncaptioned illustration wastes the best-read position on the page. Every reason turns on what readers of his period had been trained by editorial print to expect.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
item.question: How does Samara account for the order in which a reader moves through a layout that has no reading structure, and what does that account let a designer do?
item.answer: He accounts for it as a gradient. Compositional flow, or eye path, occurs as the viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast against the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance — contrast restated as resistance — so the eye moves from the area of greatest overall contrast to the least. Because the order is produced by a gradient rather than by position in a structure, a layout with no grid can still have a reading order, and the designer can support the direction by positioning axes or by using graphical forms to point. Practically, he adds that each element to be encountered next must either differentiate from its context to a similar degree, since like things attract attention, or be positioned near where the eye is likely to leave the previous element; and that graphical markers or anchoring points inserted at strategic locations help focus attention and direct the flow.
item.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": compositional flow as decreasing optical resistance; the eye moving from greatest to least contrast; supporting the direction with axes and pointing forms; like things attracting attention; markers and anchoring points.
confounders: assuming reading order in an unstructured layout is arbitrary

item.label: the_print_readership_cascade
item.description: A single quantity — how far into a print advertisement a reader gets — from which the source derives almost every rule in his print chapter. Readership falls off in a known order across illustration, headline, caption and body copy; each craft rule is an intervention at one step of that fall, and the value of each rule is set by how many readers survive to that step.

whole_system_claim.text: The print chapter is not a list of independent findings but one model applied repeatedly. Every rule in it is a decision about what to put where the readers still are: the brand name goes in the headline because eighty per cent never reach the body copy; the caption must carry the brand name and the promise because more people read captions than body copy; the layout runs illustration, headline, copy because that is the order the eye moves; editorial graphics are adopted because advertising graphics cause readers to leave before step one; and the typographic devices exist to keep the survivors moving. Retrieved separately, each rule reads as an arbitrary preference; retrieved together, they are one argument about a falling curve.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source never states this as a model. It is synthesised from three things he does state: that five times as many read the headline as the body copy and that it follows the headline must sell; that readers look first at the illustration, then the headline, then the copy, and that the layout should therefore run in that order; and that captions outdraw body copy and must therefore carry the brand name and the promise. Each of the three moves from a readership fact to a placement rule by the same step. Extending that step to the editorial- graphics and typography sections is ours.

dependencies.nature: the layout order is derived from the readership order
devices for continuation only matter for readers the advertisement has already entered

conflicts.nature: The cascade is presented as a property of advertisements, but one of its two determinants — category interest — is stated by the source to lie outside the advertisement entirely. A low readership figure is therefore not by itself a verdict on the craft.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The members are individually well supported by reported readership figures whose sources are not given. The claim that they constitute one causal model is OURS. The source states the derivation for two of the six members and we have extended it to the rest. The whole model is also bound to the print of 1983 — the readership proportions, the graphic conventions and the reader habits it rests on are all of that period, and none is carried forward here.

item.question: A client asks for "a campaign that will last". Using Sullivan's own definitions, what is the difference between a campaign and a platform, and what property decides how long the thing keeps producing?
item.answer: A campaign, in his working definition, is a series of executions held together by similar messaging, typography, art direction, tone and architecture. A platform is a world with its own internal rules, and those rules can be used again and again to spin further stories — prequels, sequels, spin-offs. The property that decides longevity is the richness of the rule set: the more rules to your world, the more stories can be pulled out of it, which is why he says platforms outlast campaigns. He applies this to his own examples rather than exempting them: a One Show-winning parking-assistance campaign is excellent and is a world with essentially one rule — change what is on either side of the space — whereas a soft-drink platform that imported the entire rule set of the legal world kept generating spin-offs, a web mechanic and billboards.
item.support: Stated definitions, explicitly offered "for the purposes of discussion" rather than as industry standard terms, with two named campaigns compared by inspection. Rule count is never defined or counted.
confounders: answering in terms of duration or budget rather than in terms of a generative rule set
assuming a platform must be bigger or more expensive; his distinction is structural
treating Ogilvy's thirty-year durability test as the same idea — that is a criterion for a big idea, not an account of why a rule set keeps producing

item.claim: Bijapurkar states a specific and repeated failure in designing for low-income consumers: firms "reduced the price by reducing performance and assumed that this combination would work," offering reduced functionality, reduced styling and old or obsolete products, and "the consumer, as always the wiser, rejected all of it. Marketers then blamed the consumer and the country for not being evolved, whereas, in reality, the consumer was way ahead in sophistication." Her diagnosis is a single line: "What suppliers consider to be a frill, consumers consider to be a necessity." She supports it with the constraint that produces it — these consumers are "aware of what is happening in the rest of the world — as it happens, in real time," so "a better wood stove is not good enough in the world of LPG, nor is a black-and-white television or even a colour one without a remote" — and with the observation that they will "rather defer a purchase and get a better product than settle for something of a far lower standard today."

mechanism.text: The supplier decides which attributes are inessential by reference to its own product hierarchy; the buyer decides by reference to what they have seen to exist. Where the buyer's reference set is the same global one as the supplier's premium customers, the attributes the supplier treats as removable are the ones the buyer treats as defining, and the stripped offer fails not on price but on relevance.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, sections 'Character Types' and 'Female Character Types', printed pp. 194-204
item.question: How does a poster carrying three portraits and no text convey a plot, on this account?
item.answer: Through a compression code the viewer already holds. Indian film is understood through the familiarity of its characters, depicted as social types defined by their differences from each other — good against bad, rich against poor, weak against strong, traditional against modern — yielding recurring roles: the long-suffering mother, the wife, the vamp, the good brother, the bad brother, the villain. Because the same actor is repeatedly cast in the same type, the public is familiar with both actor and type and transfers meaning between them, so posters 'use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film'. Patel works one through: in a Deewaar poster Bachchan's persona is recognised, the older woman reads as the long-suffering mother, her presence implies a filial relation between the two male portraits, and the theme of brothers divided is delivered without a word of text. THE CODE IS THE VIEWER'S, NOT THE POSTER'S — a viewer without it sees three faces.
item.support: posters 'use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film.'
item.confounders: The compression looks like an economical design decision and is actually a dependency: it works only where the casting convention that built the types has been running long enough for the audience to hold them.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Advertising and the Communication of Meaning', opening of 'The Star Image', printed p. 183
item.question: Patel's account of why a poster opens with a face has two stages. Separate them, and say which one survives outside the culture.
item.answer: Stage one is pre-cultural and stage two is not, and she separates them explicitly. First, an image of a human face is 'instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all': of any mix of images the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a particular star, which arouses expectations built up over that star's career. Only the first survives outside the culture, and she states the boundary in the same breath — 'an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response'. The practical consequence is that a face still buys the glance anywhere; what the glance then delivers is entirely dependent on the viewer holding the star's history.
item.support: 'an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response.'
item.confounders: Collapsing the two stages produces the false generalisation that 'putting a face on it works' — which is true only of the attention effect, not of anything the face is supposed to mean.

source_terms: a platform is a world with its own rules
platforms are ideas that create ideas
world building
item.claim: Sullivan draws a hard line between a campaign and a platform. A campaign he defines as a series of executions held together by similar messaging, typography, art direction, tone and architecture. A platform is a world with its own internal rules, and those rules can be used again and again to generate further stories — prequels, sequels, spin-offs. His governing claim is that the richer the set of rules in the world, the more stories can be pulled out of it, and that this is why platforms outlast campaigns. He applies the test to his own example: VW's computer-assisted parallel-parking campaign is excellent but is a world with essentially one rule — you change what is on either side of the parking space — whereas Coke Zero's "taste infringement" imports the whole rule set of the legal world and therefore keeps producing.

A shared, internally consistent set of conventions gives a team a combinatorial space to recombine rather than a single idea to repeat, so the number of distinct further executions available is a function of the rule count rather than of further invention from scratch.

item.question: What is Hopkins's verdict on colour, what exception does he state, and what makes the exception work?
item.answer: His verdict is that colour does not generally pay better than black and white, "according to the evidence we have gathered to date" — one of the few explicit provisionality hedges in the book. His exception is lines whose appeal is the appearance of the product itself: certain food dishes look far better in colours, and tests on lines like oranges and desserts are said to show colour paying. What makes it work is that colour "comes close to placing the products on actual exhibition" — it does selling work no other treatment can do. Colour used to amuse or to gain attention falls back under his general rule: it may attract many times as many people yet secure a hearing from no more of the people wanted. source_terms: If the proportions of images to be included all conform to the same aspect ratio... one might use this aspect ratio to define the proportions of a module, and then build columns and rows based on that proportion.

item.claim: Where imagery rather than text is the focus — a poster, a coffee-table book — the structure may be defined from the proportions of the images, though typesetting attributes should still be considered. If all the images share an aspect ratio, that ratio can define the module's proportions, and columns and rows are built from it. Images then scale to sizes defined by fields of modules, and typographic elements inherit the same logic and appear intrinsically related to the pictures. The resulting grid transposes across formats: margins may stay the same or change around the module group; columns or rows of modules may be added or removed to suit a format's proportion; and the whole module group may be scaled down as a unit for a more detailed grid or up for a simplified, bolder one.

mechanism.text: When one proportion generates the module, everything sized by the module shares that proportion, so the relationship between type and image is structural rather than judged.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 191-192 (Chapter Eighteen, why he specialised on repeat-purchase goods)
item.question: Hopkins states the rule that governed which products he took on at all. State it, and explain what it does to the reported success rate in this book.
item.answer: He specialised on proprietaries and foods — products people buy over and over — because the whole profit on a one-sale article must be made on that sale, which caps what may be spent to obtain it, whereas a product in daily consumption permits almost unlimited acquisition spending. His stated ideal is products that appeal to nearly every home and must be advertised forever, giving the example of foods mothers teach their children to use. He reports accepting a premium costing more than the profit on the six purchases required to earn it, because those six purchases made the brand familiar and the user then asked for it by name. What it does to the book is create a survivorship effect he built deliberately: his reported success rate is conditioned on a selection rule that excluded the hardest cases in advance. He also concedes the counter-case — a carpet sweeper lasting ten years at about a dollar of profit, which he says nobody has found an ordinary way to advertise profitably.

item.label: logo_identity_brand_nesting
item.description: Three terms the source distinguishes and keeps distinguishing: the logo (one mark), the brand identity or visual identity (the applied system — stationery, vehicle graphics, signage, packaging, website), and the brand (mission, history, and people's perception). The source uses the distinction to do two opposite jobs, and that is what makes it a system rather than three definitions. Upward, it limits the designer's claim: an effective logo will not save a poor product or a weak mission. Downward, it expands the designer's engagement: a client asking for a logo in isolation should be advised that the value lies in applying it across the whole range of corporate literature, stationery and advertising.

whole_system_claim.text: The three levels are not a hierarchy of importance but of controllability, and the source uses them in both directions at once. Everything the designer controls sits at the bottom two levels; everything that decides whether the work succeeds commercially sits at the top one. This is why the same distinction can be honest ("a logo is not a brand") and self-interested ("so hire me for the whole identity") in the same book without contradiction — and the source makes both moves within two pages of each other.

The textual basis is that both moves are present and adjacent: the limiting claim at 190 ("will not save a poor product or service, or a company with a weak mission") and the expanding claim at 162 (advise a client who wants a logo alone that they should take the expert guidance on applying it across the full range). item.claim: A further allusive strategy is to appropriate the visual language of common, everyday experience or the stylistic gestures associated with a particular context — the vernacular. Using vernacular imagery or a vernacular compositional conceit imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated; the source's example is an invitation to an exclusive art auction designed with the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. item.source_locator: Ch. 4, 'Premium, Popular and Discount'; Ch. 10, 'Women'
item.question: A product's usage among 25-34 year-olds has fallen for three quarters and the team concludes that this cohort is becoming less brand-loyal. Apply this source, and say what it cannot settle.
item.answer: The source's response is that a change in a measured series has been attributed to a change in the PEOPLE without testing whether what changed was the OPTIONS, and it supplies two worked cases of exactly that error. In the down-trading case the observation was read as 'the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy', and the actual cause was supply-side: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', after tax and duty changes forced small manufacturers into open competition and produced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. In the working-women case a plausible driver was adopted and never checked, and the data ran the other way through the affluent segment. The rule to apply here: BEFORE ACCEPTING A DEMAND-SIDE EXPLANATION FOR A MOVED SERIES, ESTABLISH WHAT CHANGED ON THE SUPPLY SIDE — what entered the category, what changed price, what changed in distribution, and what a competitor did in the same three quarters. Character explanations should be the residual, not the first hypothesis, because they need no data and predict everything. What this source CANNOT settle is whether the loyalty explanation is wrong in this case. It supplies no test, no threshold and no metric — two cases in which a demand-side reading was wrong establish that the check is worth running, not what it will return.
item.support: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer'
item.confounders: Both of the source's cases are ones where the supply-side explanation won, which is a selected sample of two. The asymmetry it justifies is one of ORDER — check supply first — not a presumption about the answer.

source_terms: text is seen as a cultural barrier
a dramatic enigma

item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

caveats.text: the comparison is drawn between two practices as the author characterises them; no sample of Western posters is enumerated and no count is given on either side

item.question: Samara asks what happens if the imagery is allowed to rule a layout. What reason does he give for expecting that inversion to be productive, and what are the two directions it can take?
item.answer: His reason is an asymmetry of vocabulary: typography is always a pattern of lines, whereas images present a radically greater range of form languages. Applying an image's language to text therefore relieves the designer quickly of presumptions about how text should behave in a layout, or how layouts ought to be organised — presumptions he says are hard to dislodge because type and image are usually assumed to be mutually dominant and referential. source_terms:
symmetry is unforgiving with regard to layout flexibility
a viewer is likely to gloss over material and come to an intellectual rest quickly, rather than investigate a work more intently
Exaggerating contrasts in scale (or proportion) and spacing (density and rhythm) when working with symmetrical compositions is critical to ensuring optical vitality
item.claim: Symmetry is unforgiving with regard to layout flexibility because it demands that every element adhere to a single axis; elements that do not typically appear disunified from the whole. The restfulness and overall uniformity that follow can be problematic relative to the goals of designed communication — a viewer is likely to gloss over the material and come to an intellectual rest quickly rather than investigate the work more intently. The source's stated remedies are to exaggerate contrasts in scale or proportion and in spacing, density and rhythm; to enlarge symmetrically organised forms until they are clearly bigger than the remaining symmetrical spaces, so that their confrontation with the format becomes tense and the composition's static quality is reduced; to juxtapose dramatically different emphases in proportion among both the forms and the spaces separating them, under a defined logic of progression or alternation along the axis from beginning to end; and to make radical changes in size or in relative lightness and darkness so that lateral movement is reordered dimensionally, from near to far.

mechanism.text: A single axis and mirrored shapes remove the optical differences that hold attention, so contrast has to be reintroduced by exaggerating the dimensions symmetry does not govern — scale, density, value — rather than by moving elements off the axis.

scope.conditions: symmetrical compositions, including a desktop browser and a smartphone screen

caveats.text: The failure named here — the viewer resting too soon — is asserted, not measured. No reader evidence is offered.

The source notes that maintaining a logic of contrasting form widths and margin spaces is easy in a wide desktop browser and harder within a smartphone's narrow confines, where text must be forced into a narrower-than-optimal width and punctuating graphical forms introduced so that some lateral contrast survives.

source_stated_problems: elements that do not adhere to the single axis appear disunified from the whole
restfulness and overall uniformity
a viewer is likely to gloss over material and come to an intellectual rest quickly
source_stated_remedies: exaggerate contrasts in scale or proportion and in spacing, density and rhythm
enlarge symmetrical forms until they are clearly bigger than the remaining symmetrical spaces
define a logic of progression or alternation of shape proportions and distance intervals along the axis
make radical changes in size or in relative lightness and darkness to reorder movement from near to far

source_terms: the activation of memory was a key factor in the redesign
key signifiers of the films
item.claim: Patel documents a distinct design problem and the solution the industry converged on. When Mehboob Studios redesigned posters in the 1980s for a set of re-released classics, "the activation of memory was a key factor in the redesign": because the public was already familiar with these films, "the primary function of the new publicity was to create an image that would most effectively trigger people's memories," so the new designs highlighted scenes, images and stars that had over time become key signifiers of the films. She reports the specific moves — Anokhi Ada reduced to the three central characters of its love-triangle theme; Aan given a sword fight that did not appear on the original poster at all; Mother India reduced to the single image of Radha pulling the plough, seen from a low viewpoint. She states the general rule she draws from the set: "the new designs therefore refined the originals by either adding or subtracting images according to their perceived contemporary impact or relevance."

mechanism.text: For a work the audience has already seen, the design does not have to describe the work; it has to index it. What indexes it best is not what was salient at release but what has since become the film's remembered signifier, which may be an element the original publicity did not carry. Hence images may be added that were never on the original poster.

scope.conditions: Documented for one studio's 1980s redesign programme covering eight named Mehboob titles, all designed by Raj Tilak of Seth Studios. It is a single-studio, single-period case.

caveats.text: one studio, one designer, one decade. The mechanism is clearly stated and the cases are specific, but it is not a survey and the source does not claim it is
the claim that these particular images had 'become key signifiers' over time is asserted; no evidence of what audiences actually remembered is presented

INSPECTED: illus. 96, the 1980s Mother India poster, was opened and read directly. The outstretched arm across the diagonal, the low viewpoint, the orange-red-yellow palette and the three-dimensional lettering are all present as Patel describes them

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Single-studio case material, asserted rather than surveyed.

source_stated_problems: for a re-released film the audience already knows, describing the film is the wrong job
source_stated_remedies: identify what has become the film's remembered signifier and build the design on that, adding or subtracting relative to the original

item.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Typography', the reverse-type passage, with Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Direct response advertising in magazines and television' (spine 13 and spine 18)
item.question: Reverse type is the rule Ogilvy repeats most often. What is the one comparison he reports for it, and what two exceptions does he allow — and what do the exceptions have in common?
item.answer: The comparison is a charity that had been running advertisements in reverse — white type on black — and, on his suggestion, tested black type on white; he reports it raised twice as much money. The two exceptions, given in the direct-response chapter, are theatre programmes, which people read in the dark by holding them up against the light coming from the stage, and slides projected onto a screen. What they share is that the page is not the light source: in both, the surface is backlit or projected rather than reflecting, which reverses the legibility. These are the only boundary conditions he gives for a typography rule anywhere in the book.
item.support: A reported before-and-after comparison with a result supplied, and two exceptions stated in a later chapter. The shared property — the page not being the light source — is implicit in his own descriptions of both exceptions.
confounders: treating reverse type as a matter of taste; he reports a fund-raising difference
generalising the exceptions to any bright display without noticing that his stated reason is the direction of the light
assuming the charity comparison was controlled — it is a before-and-after on one organisation with no other cause excluded

source_terms: Professor Tinker of Stanford has established that capitals retard reading. They have no ascenders or descenders to help you recognize words , and tend to be read letter by letter.
The eye is a creature of habit.

Which typefaces are easiest to read? Those which people are accustomed to reading... The more outlandish the typeface, the harder it is to read. The drama belongs in what you say, not in the typeface.
You can't save souls in an empty church.
item.claim: The source's organising principle for typography is that the eye is a creature of habit: what is easy to read is what people are accustomed to reading. From this he derives both the failures and the settings. Failures: capitals retard reading because they have no ascenders or descenders and tend to be read letter by letter; headlines superimposed on the illustration; a full stop at the end of a headline, which he says stops the reader dead; a measure too wide or too narrow; copy used as raw material for designing shapes; and reverse type, white on black, which he calls almost impossible to read and reports counting forty-seven instances in one magazine issue. Settings: familiar faces such as the Century family, Caslon, Baskerville and Jenson, and a measure of about forty characters, the width people are used to in newspapers. He then states the limit of the whole subject himself: no housewife ever bought a detergent because the advertisement was set in Caslon, but an advertisement nobody can read cannot sell — you cannot save souls in an empty church. He notes that layouts are often pinned to a board and approved at fifteen feet, which leads to headlines set in seventy-two point that are impossible to read at the actual reading distance of twenty inches.

mechanism.text: Reading is a trained habit, so legibility is a function of familiarity rather than of design quality; and typography is a necessary condition for selling rather than a cause of it.

scope.conditions: readers trained on the books, newspapers and magazines of the period

caveats.text: the reverse-type claim is the one point in the chapter where the source reports an actual comparison with a result: a charity running advertisements in reverse was persuaded to test black on white and raised twice as much money
Tinker is cited by name and institution but without a study or a date, and the serif claim is supported by a novelist's opinion rather than by measurement
the familiarity argument is explicitly relative to what readers of that period were accustomed to; it is a claim about trained habit, not about letterforms, and its conclusions move with the habit

the direct response chapter names two exceptions to the reverse-type rule — theatre programmes read against stage light, and slides projected on a screen — both cases where the page is not the light source

item.claim: The source reports investigating a category and finding that the competition every advertiser was fighting over was six per cent of the market, while ninety-four per cent of buyers were served by an alternative nobody was arguing against — the household making the product at home. The natural rhythm of spoken language, for example, is often used as a guide for changing weight, size, color, or alignment among lines of type; louder or "faster" words may be set in larger or bolder type or in italics, corresponding to stresses and lulls in actual speech.
Giving a "voice" to visual language can help alter the structure of a text by pushing words out of paragraphs or forcing modules or columns into relationships where the natural logic of the writing creates a visual order.
treating all of the adjectives in a particular way would create a secondary structure
item.claim: Verbal or conceptual cues inside the content can be used to break a grid or to create a new one entirely. The natural rhythm of spoken language is the source's principal example: louder or faster words set larger, bolder or italic, corresponding to the stresses and lulls of actual speech. Giving a voice to visual language alters the structure of a text by pushing words out of paragraphs, or forcing modules and columns into relationships in which the natural logic of the writing creates the visual order. Grammatical categories work the same way — treating every adjective in a particular way creates a secondary structure with a rhythmic, organic quality. The source presents three graded versions of one text: size change alone produces loudness and a crescendo; changes of weight, posture, width and spacing produce a rhythmic journey of slowing and speeding; and changes applied to distinguish linguistic and conceptual relationships give the reader a snapshot of the content before they fully engage the text.

mechanism.text: The structure is read off a property the content already has, so the resulting arrangement is motivated by the writing rather than imposed on it.

scope.conditions: text whose spoken or grammatical character carries meaning worth showing

caveats.text: The source traces this to Dada and Futurist practice, in which letters and words were pictures of emotional or psychological states whose power came from aggressive visual arrangement rather than from literal meaning, and to Ruder's mixing of weight, slant and size within single lines for a semiotic representation of language. The craft rule and its historical warrant are the same claim at different dates.

The three graded versions are a figure sequence. The text names what each version does; the versions themselves are images not inspectable in this copy, so the ladder is recorded on the captions' word and not verified.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing, Note 1; Understanding SC 1.4.12, Author Responsibility
item.question: SC 1.4.12 names four spacing values — 1.5x line height, 2x paragraph spacing, 0.12x letter spacing, 0.16x word spacing — and then says content is not required to use them. What is the requirement, then, and what does failure look like?
item.answer: The requirement is resilience, not typography. The criterion is that no loss of content or functionality occurs when a user sets all four properties to those values and changes no other style property. Note 1 states it plainly: content is not required to use these values; the requirement is that when a user overrides the authored text spacing, content or functionality is not lost. The Understanding note frames the author's duty as twofold — not interfering with the user's ability to override, and ensuring the overridden content does not break. Failure is a layout failure, and the source illustrates three kinds: text cut off vertically, text cut off horizontally, and text overlapping other content. The note adds that the values are a baseline rather than a ceiling, and that ellipsised truncation can still conform provided a mechanism reveals the truncated content — if there is no such mechanism, it fails. A separate normative exception allows human languages and scripts that do not use one or more of these properties to conform using only the properties that exist for that language and script.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.12 and its Note 1, and its language-and-script exception. NON-NORMATIVE for the author/user split, the ellipsis allowance and the illustrated failures — Understanding SC 1.4.12, "Author Responsibility", "Use of ellipses" and "Effects".
confounders: reading the four values as a required type specification
confusing them with SC 1.4.8's leading provisions, which are an availability requirement for blocks of text
assuming any truncation fails — the source permits it where a mechanism reveals the content
