source_terms: because of Nike's stature, standing and visibility in the market, the potential damage to the company's identity is much greater
sometimes a complete redesign could mean going a step too far when all that is needed is a refinement
sales of the Tropicana Pure Premium line plunged 20 per cent in less than two months
item.claim: The source separates identity work into two categories with different risk profiles. Designing from scratch for a new company is the simpler case, because there is no brand equity for either party to take into account. Redesigning for an established company carries much higher risk for both, and the source makes the scaling explicit by contrast: Nike abandoning its internationally recognised swoosh for the outline of a shoe versus a new business called "Pete" commissioning a first identity — the potential damage is far greater in the first because of stature, standing and visibility. Three consequences follow in the same chapter. First, the redesign process is necessarily longer and stricter, with more thought and discussion per decision. Second, refinement is the right answer when the identity has become dated but consumer familiarity with it is high — the source's case keeps the distinctive red lettering so the equity around the old design stays intact. Third, the reasons must be sound: rebranding for its own sake or to follow trends can be a disaster, and without that guidance market leaders can throw away millions and their reputation with it.

mechanism.text: Brand equity is accumulated recognition held by the audience, not by the company, so replacing the carrier of that recognition destroys it. The Tropicana case is the source's demonstration: loyal customers could easily spot the old packaging when shopping, and the redesign removed the device they were spotting.

scope.conditions: established companies with existing recognition; explicitly not applicable to start-ups with no equity

caveats.text: OUTCOME CLAIMED WITHOUT CONTROLS. The 20 per cent sales fall and the $33 million figure are cited to trade press, not to a controlled study; no alternative explanation is examined and the source does not claim to have one. The New Coke case is reported with a similar structure and the source openly says it does not know whether that was a deliberate manoeuvre or a genuine error.

the source itself notes that most brand redesigns do not go as badly as these two, and that both companies have probably had successful redesigns as well — the cases are selected for being famous failures
the source's speculation that the dilution may have been a deliberate alignment with generic store-brand packaging is offered as an open question, not an answer

a redesign that removes the device customers use to find the product
source_stated_remedies: establish the specific reasons for the rebrand first

item.claim: Across several exhibit commentaries Samara describes the same relationship between how a layout looks and what produced it. An exhibition catalogue whose apparent simplicity looks, at a glance, not really designed is said to require almost obsessive attention to the selection, ordering, cropping, colour transitions and colour-reversal logic of its images to be credible. A poster on the theme of improvisation, with no baselines, alignments or margins and letters floating as though scattered, is described as a carefully randomised layout to which two spatial levels add further control, with precise placement given to the forms so that legibility is not impaired even where red and black letterforms of close optical colour overlap. A third project's playful structure is called accessible because each part of the information is decisively located and individual components are separated so the eye can reach them easily. In each case the randomness is in the appearance and the control is in the placement.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 101-102 (Chapter Nine, the blind tasting at the Van Camp factory) read against printed p. 103 (the evaporated-milk refusal)
item.question: A client's product cannot be told from its rivals in a blind comparison, and he concludes that advertising cannot help him. Hopkins met this literally — in the Van Camp factory a half-dozen brands were served and nobody present could pick out Van Camp's. What did he do, and where does he say this move stops working?
item.answer: He did not look for a superiority claim. He told the ordinary facts of good canning practice that no competitor had bothered to state: beans grown on particular soils, vine-ripened Livingston Stone tomatoes, every lot analysed, steam ovens baking for hours at 245 degrees, boiling in soft water so the skins would not toughen, sealing so flavour could not escape. He says plainly that this was the same story any rival could have told, and that the others thought it too commonplace to tell. The claim is not that the product is better; it is that the article first allied with those facts comes to typify them. The boundary is on the facing page. When Van Camp went into evaporated milk, Hopkins advised against advertising it, because it is a standard product made to government requirements — no advantage can be established or claimed on a natural or standard product, and he lists eggs, butter, lard and flour as the same case. So the move applies where practice varies and is untold, not where the product is standardised by specification and there is nothing left to tell.
item.support: Printed pp. 101-102 for the indistinguishable brands and the list of commonplace facts he told; printed p. 103 for the refusal on evaporated milk and the eggs/butter/lard/flour comparison. The Van Camp campaign outcome is asserted as an enormous success with a price premium; no traced figures for it are given anywhere in the chapter.
confounders: the modern positioning default of finding or manufacturing a differentiator; Hopkins is explicitly conceding parity and claiming the untold fact instead
reading it as permission to imply superiority from a parity fact; he says the story is one any rival could tell
assuming the Schlitz and Van Camp move is universal; p. 103 is his own stated exception and he acted on it against his own billings
confusing 'standard product' with 'commodity category' — his test is a specification others must also meet, not merely a crowded market

Compositional flow, sometimes called "eye path," occurs as a viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast from the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance
For Western readers, it's wise to orient top-level elements toward the left-hand area of a layout.

Elements to be encountered next must differentiate from their contexts to a similar degree (like things attract attention) or be positioned in proximity to the place where the viewer's eye is likely to leave the first element behind.
item.claim: Where the first or most important element sits, and how it optically connects the viewer to what follows, matter as much as differentiation itself. Compositional flow — eye path — occurs as the viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast against the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance; the eye moves from the area of greatest overall contrast to the least, along a direction the designer can support by positioning axes or by using graphical forms to point. For Western readers the source advises orienting top-level elements toward the left-hand area of the layout. Each subsequent element must either differentiate from its context to a similar degree, because like things attract attention, or be placed near where the eye is likely to leave the previous element. Inserting graphical markers or anchoring points at strategic locations helps focus attention and direct the flow. The same rule is applied to a specific case: when setting type on a circular path or arc, orient its entry point toward the upper left and, if possible, so that the first words are relatively horizontal.

mechanism.text: Contrast is restated as optical resistance, so a sequence of decreasing contrast reads as a path of decreasing resistance. Order is therefore produced by a gradient rather than by position in a structure, which is why a layout with no grid can still have a reading order.

scope.conditions: Western reading conventions; explicitly scoped to Western readers by the source

caveats.text: The left-hand and upper-left advice is stated by the source as specific to Western readers and must not be generalised to readers of right-to-left or vertical scripts.
The mechanism is an account of perception offered without evidence; it is a designer's model of reading, not a reading study.
The comparison that carries the type-on-a-curve rule is a paired before/after image. Only the rule is recorded; the demonstrated difference in readability was not seen.

source_stated_remedies: orient top-level elements toward the left for Western readers
differentiate the next element to a similar degree, or place it near where the eye leaves the previous one
insert graphical markers or anchoring points to focus attention and direct flow
orient the entry point of type on a curve to the upper left, with the first words relatively horizontal

source_terms:
Designers need not totally discard the notion of structure in their search for compositional options beyond the grid.
taking apart or subverting a grid to generate new spatial relationships
there are also many kinds of structure that happen to not be based on a logic of repeating, modular—or even orthogonal (90°)—geometry
The appreciation of a particular structure often instigates an association with certain physical experiences—and so non-grid-based structures, too, can impart metaphorical or narrative understanding.
item.claim: Abandoning the grid does not require abandoning structure. The source names two routes. Deconstruction is one: taking apart or subverting a grid to generate new spatial relationships. The other is the large class of structures not based on repeating, modular or even orthogonal geometry — those derived from nature, such as crystals, molecules and the branches of trees, and those derived from mathematical or formal relationships, such as nested or concentric ones. Because appreciating a particular structure instigates an association with physical experience, non-grid structures also impart metaphorical or narrative understanding, and familiarity with a variety of arrangement possibilities gives the designer greater latitude to architect a project's space and serve the content's needs.

mechanism.text: Structure is a class and the grid is a member of it. Removing the member does not remove the class, and the associations a structure carries come from what it resembles in physical experience rather than from its regularity.

scope.conditions: any project where the grid has been ruled out

caveats.text: This extends, in the same author's voice, chapter 1's claim that the structure itself can be a message; the live extraction holds that claim for grids only. Chapter 2 says the same mechanism operates for structures that are not grids at all. Same author, one work.

The source's inclusion criterion is looser than it looks: one exhibit is admitted to the no-grid section although "technically, there is a grid of sorts in use here", on the ground that the grid is inconsequential — its body-to-margin relationship is near default and its two page structures do not relate to each other.

source_terms: No other activating factor compares with curiosity.

item.claim: The source claims curiosity is the strongest device it knows for producing action, and derives a specific rule from it: an undisclosed reward outperforms a described one. Its stated mechanism is selection — a described gift splits the audience into those who want it and a larger group who decide they do not, whereas an undisclosed gift is wanted by everybody. It applies the same principle to campaign concepts, citing foods shot from guns, grains pictured at eight times normal size, and a pamphlet about convict-cut Indian wood hauled to the Ganges by elephants, all built to make the reader want to see the thing.

mechanism.text: Description gives the reader enough information to refuse. Withholding it removes the ground for refusal and leaves only the impulse to find out, which the source treats as close to universal.

No comparative figure is given for described versus undisclosed gifts anywhere in the book. The claim is asserted, and the outcomes reported are one-sided.

item.source_locator: Introduction
item.question: How does this source bound its own scope, and why does that bound matter more here than in most sources?
item.answer: It bounds itself four ways, explicitly and repeatedly: it examines urban middle-class India from INSIDE that class; it uses 'we' while stating that 'the diversity of India cannot be collapsed into a single undifferentiated "we"'; it declares 'in-built biases' from the author's own experience; and it declines both to prescribe and to judge, stating its purpose is 'to understand what is happening'. It matters more here than elsewhere because the book's most quotable material — the Imperfect Solution thesis, the reading of hierarchy, the essay on Indian traffic — is essayistic generalisation about 'the Indian mind' that reads as a claim about a population, and the Introduction is what forbids that reading.
item.support: 'I am acutely aware that there are many Indias…'; 'the book carries with it in-built biases'
item.confounders: The rhetorical force of the later essays makes it easy to forget the Introduction's disclaimers.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 64-69 (Chapter Six, 'Personal Salesmanship', the Cotosuet calls on New England bakers)
item.question: A product is identical to a cheaper rival, the price premium is essential to profit, and the sales force reports the premium cannot be held. Hopkins was sent to prove otherwise. What did he actually sell, what is the general form he draws from it, and what did he refuse to claim afterwards?
item.answer: He did not sell the product. He arrived at the largest bakery with the proof of a street-car card picturing an ideal pie, set it up fifty feet away, explained what it had cost and how it was printed, and asked the baker — a pie expert — to criticise it, which turned the man from a reluctant buyer into an adviser defending his own verdict. Then he offered a card like it for every store selling that baker's pies, carrying a line that only Swift's Cotosuet was used in the shortening, at 250 cards per carload ordered. He repeated it down the New England cities, and for a baker who could not have the card he offered signs on both sides of two railway cars announcing Mansfield's pies for nine hundred miles. He reports selling more Cotosuet in a week than six salesmen had sold in six weeks, with no complaint about price. The general form he draws is that the appeal must consist of a service useful to the buyer with the seller's own advantage covered up — the average salesman's plea, buy mine and not the other fellow's, is a selfish appeal to selfish people and meets resistance. What he refused was to teach it: asked by Mr. Swift to train the other men, he said it cannot be taught, and says in 1927 that he is still of that opinion. Two things a reader should hold onto: the week-against-six-weeks comparison is his own recollection with no records behind it, and the boxcar sign is precisely the vanity advertising — keeping your name before the people — that he condemns everywhere else, which he half-concedes on the page.
item.support: Printed pp. 64-69. The pie card and its critique, the 250-cards-per-carload offer, the boxcar signs at Springfield, the week-versus-six-weeks claim, the service-not-selfishness formulation and the "it cannot be taught" reply are all stated there. Anecdotal, with an outcome claimed and no records.
confounders: reading it as a co-operative-advertising or point-of-sale programme; on his account the card is the whole sale and the shortening goes with it
the modern value-add or partnership framing, which would state the mutual benefit openly; Hopkins requires his own advantage to be covered up
treating the six-salesmen comparison as a controlled result
missing that the Mansfield boxcar sign is name-spreading of the kind he calls folly elsewhere, sold to a customer who wanted it

source_terms: Narrative Constructs
Pictorialization and Metaphorical Allusion
the layout becomes a kind of illustration
As content progresses or pursues a different direction from page to page or screen to screen, the "subject" depicted by the layout changes, but the governing logic remains the same.
item.claim: An idea embedded in the project's content can itself be visualised as the compositional structure of the page or screen. The source names two variants. In narrative pictorialisation the layout and its parts are made to look like something discussed in the text — elements arranged to give the impression of objects swept up in a flood, or to construct a literal image of a car or other machine; in simplest terms the layout becomes a kind of illustration. As the content progresses or changes direction from page to page, the subject the layout depicts changes while the governing logic stays the same. In metaphorical allusion the layout structure and the visual language of the forms it arranges refer to some tangential idea that supports or manipulates perception of the meaning — a promotion for a film festival splicing repeated images to refer to film editing. Both variants follow the idea of visual storytelling, relying on depictive strategies to deliver narrative meaning that either describes the content or reframes and augments it.

mechanism.text: Chapter 2 has already established that a viewer reads a structure as the thing it resembles. Pictorialisation and allusion are the deliberate exploitation of that reading: the arrangement is made to resemble something so that the resemblance carries meaning.

scope.conditions: content that contains an idea capable of being depicted

caveats.text: The whole method depends on the viewer recognising the resemblance. The source offers no account of what happens when they do not.
Each example is a layout whose resemblance exists only in the image. The strategy is recorded; no judgement is made here about whether any of the cited layouts achieves it.

source_stated_remedies: visualise an idea embedded in the content as the compositional structure of the space
make the layout look like something discussed in the text, holding the governing logic constant as the depicted subject changes
or let the structure allude to a tangential idea as a metaphor

item.source_locator: Ch. 3, section 'The Studio System: Image and Memory', printed pp. 149-153; Ch. 4, printed pp. 194-204
item.question: A studio is designing the poster for a sequel to a fifteen-year-old film that has since acquired a following the original release never had. What does this source's re-release material say to do, what does it not settle, and what would you have to know that the source cannot tell you?
item.answer: What it says to do: design for retrieval, not for information. The re-release finding is that where the audience already knows the film, publicity's job is 'to create an image that would most effectively trigger people's memories', and the designs accordingly targeted whichever scenes and images had OVER TIME become the key signifiers — which is why Aan's poster acquired a sword fight that was not on the original. So the operative question is not what the original was sold on but what the audience now retains, and those can differ. What it does not settle: a sequel is not a re-release. The re-release cases carry no new film to sell, whereas a sequel must both retrieve the old and introduce the new, and the source documents no case of that mixture. Nor does it establish any effect — no attendance, sales or recognition figure is reported for any redesign, so the finding is about intent and craft, not outcome. What you would have to know independently: WHAT THE AUDIENCE ACTUALLY RETAINS, which the source cannot supply for a film it never studied and which cannot be inferred from the original campaign. Patel's designers evidently knew it for their titles; how they knew it is not documented, and that gap is the whole problem in the sequel case.
item.support: 'the primary function of the new publicity was to create an image that would most effectively trigger people's memories'
item.confounders: It is easy to take the Mother India reduction — the whole film to Radha pulling the plough — as a rule that less is more. The rule is that the retained image wins, and finding out what is retained is the part the source does not teach.

item.source_locator: Essay 'Mother Pious Lady', the thirty-year study
item.question: This book contains exactly one measurement. What did it find, and what is entirely missing from how it is reported?
item.answer: A content analysis of matrimonial advertisements across thirty years, which the author says he was involved in. It found: appearance adjectives increased sharply, with a new premium on tall and slim; fairness as an articulated quality rose sharply; boys were evaluated on income and family, girls on appearance, qualifications and family; the boy's side used more words to state expectations; and — the most valuable finding — the proportion of advertisements mentioning caste origin REMAINED CONSTANT. Missing is every methodological particular: no sample size, no sampling frame, no publication list, no coding scheme, no date range, no inter-coder check, and not a single number. Every finding is directional only. 'A study I was involved in' also does not establish authorship, publication, or that it was ever written up.
item.support: 'In a study I was involved in a few years ago, we analysed matrimonial ads across thirty years…'
item.confounders: The constant-caste result is the most trustworthy finding precisely because it is a NULL running against the book's own modernisation narrative, and nulls are least likely to be reported selectively.

It's important to watch what happens when information that would normally appear in an expected place—marking a structural juncture in the grid—is moved to another place, perhaps aligned with some other kind of information in a way that creates a new verbal connection that didn't exist before.

item.claim: The payoff of splicing and shifting is not formal but relational. When information that would normally sit in its expected place, marking a structural juncture, is moved and lands beside some other kind of information, a new verbal connection is created that did not exist before. Shifted information may also end up behind or on top of other information if a change in size or density accompanies the change in placement, and the resulting optical confusion will often make foreground and background appear to swap places. The source instructs the designer to watch for both effects rather than to plan them.

item.claim: The source states the selection rule that governed its own career choices. It specialised in products bought over and over, because the whole profit on a one-sale article must be made on that sale, which limits what may be spent to obtain it, whereas a product in daily consumption permits almost unlimited acquisition spending. It names the ideal as products appealing to nearly every home which must be advertised forever, giving the example of foods mothers teach their children to use. It states the corollary concretely for a daily-consumption product: there is hardly a limit to what one can pay to get a new user established, and it accepted a gift costing more than the profit on the six units required to earn it, because those six units made the brand familiar and the user then asked for it by name.

item.claim: Patel argues that Indian film is understood through the familiarity of its characters, which are depicted as social types defined by their differences from each other — good against bad, rich against poor, weak against strong, traditional against modern — yielding recurring roles such as the long-suffering mother, the wife, the vamp, the good brother, the bad brother and the villain. Because the same actor is cast in the same role type across films, the public is familiar with both actor and type and transfers meaning between them. Posters therefore "use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film." She works one poster through: in a Deewaar poster, Bachchan's persona is recognised, the older woman reads as the long-suffering mother, her presence implies a filial relation between the two male portraits, and the audience's familiarity with the lost-and-found theme supplies the rest.

mechanism.text: A type is a compression: one figure stands for a whole set of expected relations and moral positions. When several types are placed together, the relations BETWEEN them are inferred by the viewer rather than depicted, so a still image can carry a narrative structure it never shows. This works only for a viewer holding the code.

source_terms: Centered-Axis Structure
centering is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualization

because it assumes only one governing alignment axis; because that axis is "buried" within the area of the material, rather than marked by its contours; and because the exterior contours, widths, and depths of centered elements are mutually interdependent
a sense of immediacy, or unfussy directness
item.claim: Centred-axis, or symmetrical, composition arranges elements in response to the format's centre — halfway between left and right or top and bottom edges, and sometimes in response to each other's central axes independently of the format. Although a grid may guide the proportions or positions of centred material, centring is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualisation, for three stated reasons: it assumes only one governing alignment axis; that axis is buried inside the area of the material rather than marked by its contours; and the exterior contours, widths and depths of centred elements are mutually interdependent — driven by their fit and relative proportion as they come into central alignment, not by predetermined intervals. Elements stack sequentially top to bottom or left to right, and the shapes either side of the axis, and the negative spaces beyond them, are identical. The primary visual result is a sense of immediacy or unfussy directness, followed by an appearance of formal simplicity, as the material's quality as a unit dominates perception of its internal divisions.

mechanism.text: A grid works by predetermined intervals marked at the contours of the material; a centred axis works by mutual fit around a line that is not drawn. The two allocate space by incompatible logics, which is why one cannot simply be laid over the other.

scope.conditions: classical or traditional page architecture, print or screen

caveats.text: Samara calls this the classical or traditional page architecture, so the claim is partly a statement about a Western typographic convention rather than about perception.

item.claim: In a signed sidebar, Kim Goodwin makes two claims the authors' own text does not. The first is that documentation is not sharing: criteria are not truly shared unless everyone both understands them and believes in them, and a team that treats "written down somewhere or mentioned in a meeting" as sufficient will find the criteria used as weapons rather than as tools — in her account, a persona wielded as a "trump card" ("Trust us, we did the user research"). The second is a diagnosis of directive feedback: people fall back on dictating solutions when they lack the language to describe the problem. She adds that shared criteria are hardest to build for the emotionally expressive aspects of a design, such as visual styling, because those feel more subjective than something like workflow — and that the remedy is to attach the style discussion to the persona's emotional goals and the scenario's hierarchy needs, which converts an argument about preference into an argument about whether a treatment inspires the intended confidence.

And where a person can feel a problem but has no vocabulary for it, the only expressible form of their judgement is a substitute solution — so prescription is a symptom of a missing shared language, not necessarily of a bad attitude.

item.question: Once a mailing is profitable, Ogilvy says it becomes the control. Testing then proceeds in two directions — name both, and say which one practitioners are likelier to neglect and why it matters.

source_terms: A letter which goes to an inquirer is like a salesman going to an interested prospect. You know what created that interest. Then follow it up along that line, not on some different argument.
Complete the impression already created. Don't undertake another on a guess.
People are naturally dilatory. They postpone, and a postponed action is too often forgotten.

item.claim: A follow-up must continue the specific argument that produced the inquiry rather than start a new one: the advertiser knows what created the interest, so he should follow it up along that line and complete the impression already created rather than undertake another on a guess. The second rule is about timing rather than content. People are naturally dilatory, they postpone, and a postponed action is too often forgotten — so something should be done to secure immediate action, either by offering an inducement for it or by telling what delay may cost, and the source points to the number of successful selling letters that place a limit on an offer expiring on a certain date purely to force a prompt decision. Its stated position is that one can afford to pay for prompt action rather than lose by delay, and the principles are universal even though the specific device can rarely be reused across two lines.

mechanism.text: An inquiry is evidence of which argument worked on that person, so switching arguments discards the only information the inquiry supplied. And an intention decays unless something converts it into an act while it is still held; a dated expiry supplies the reason to act now.

item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", section "The marketing of dog food" (spine 12)
item.question: Why does Godin use dog food rather than a human product to make his point about performance and appeal, and what is the general claim it is there to support?
item.answer: Because it separates the two parties cleanly and unarguably: he has never seen a dog buy dog food. The premium ingredients and rising prices are for the owners — for how buying it makes them feel, the satisfaction of caring for an animal, the status of a luxury purchase — and we have no idea whether dogs enjoy the expensive kind, because we are not dogs. The general claim is that there is almost always a disconnect between performance and appeal, and that the engineer's choice of the best price-performance combination is rarely the market's choice. So a marketer trying to sell more dog food by making food that tastes better has taken on the wrong problem; the formula is food that owners want to buy.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 5
item.question: A letterform carries an outline. WCAG says the same device can end up on either side of the contrast calculation. State the rule and the mechanism behind it.
item.answer: A border around a letter can add contrast and is used in calculating the contrast between the letter and its background. A narrow border is used as the letter — it joins the foreground. A wide border that fills in the inner details of the letters acts as a halo and is considered background. The mechanism is what the reader is actually distinguishing: once a border is heavy enough to fill the counters and interior detail of the letterform, the perceptual comparison is no longer letter against page but letter against halo, so the halo becomes the effective background. The note gives no numeric boundary between narrow and wide; the stated test is whether the border fills the inner details of the letters.
item.support: Normative — Note 5 to the glossary definition of "contrast ratio".
confounders: assuming an outline always helps, or always counts as foreground
looking for a stated pixel or point threshold separating narrow from wide — the source gives a functional test instead
assuming the underlying page colour remains the background once a heavy halo is present

item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts' and the chapter's closing footnote on spreads (spine 13)
item.question: Ogilvy tells you to swear off two-page spreads, then corrects himself in a footnote. What does the correction say, and why is the corrected version more useful than the rule it qualifies?
item.answer: The rule is that a spread costs twice a single page and seldom returns twice the readership or twice the coupons, so swearing off spreads buys twice as many insertions. The footnote, which he introduces by calling the rule one of his own over-simplifications, reports that Starch finds spreads average twenty-eight per cent higher rating than single pages, that for financial advertisers spreads average one hundred and fifty per cent more readership, and that advertisements for low-interest products benefit more from big space than those for high-interest products. The corrected version is more useful because it supplies the variable — the reader's prior interest in the category — that decides when the size premium is worth paying, instead of a blanket prohibition.
item.support: Rule in the running text; qualification in his own footnote, citing two different named sources measuring different populations. He states the low-interest generalisation but does not reconcile the two figures.
confounders: keeping the rule and discarding the footnote; he flags the rule himself as an over-simplification
reading the financial-advertiser figure as an industry quirk rather than as an instance of the low-interest generalisation
confusing readership gain with order gain — the direct-response chapter states the spread question in orders, where he again says spreads seldom double them

source_terms: Spontaneous Composition
the intuitive placement of material based on its formal aspects
This approach starts fast and loose
as an antidote to structure, which implies analytical intent
item.claim: Where structure implies analytical intent, the source offers spontaneous approaches as an antidote — working by instinct and letting purely formal instincts supersede the rational. Spontaneous composition is defined as the intuitive placement of material based on its formal aspects: seeing the visual relationships already inherent in the material and making those connections for the viewer. The method is not a single gesture but a loop. The designer starts fast and loose, working as a painter does and making quick decisions as the material is put together and the relationships are first seen; then, as the elements' optical qualities begin to interact, the designer determines which qualities those first decisions have affected and adjusts to enhance or negate them as the communication requires. Samara notes that designers often use this method as a step within the process of building a grid, and asserts that its use as an organisational idea on its own is just as valid.

mechanism.text: The method's liveliness has an affinity with collage; its immediacy and directness are described as inviting to viewers, providing a simple and gratifying experience that is very accessible.

scope.conditions: projects where a formal, experiential reading is wanted rather than an analytical one

caveats.text: The critical detail is that the placement is intuitive but not unexamined: the source's own description contains an evaluation step in which the designer reads back what the first decisions did and corrects. This is the difference the chapter relies on and it is easy to miss.
The claim that immediacy is inviting and accessible to viewers is a practitioner assertion with no audience evidence behind it.
Samara says designers often use spontaneous composition inside grid-building, which places this method upstream of the live chapter-1 procedure rather than opposed to it.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Defining the Surface of Glassware' and 'Position the Light'
item.question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
item.answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Defining the Surface of Glassware', including the two matched highlight frames and the taped diffusion sheet.
confounders: assuming brighter highlights read as more premium or more glossy
attributing the difference to the size of the source alone, ignoring the lamp-to-diffuser distance

item.question: The "everyone is equal" rule is often read as a claim that seniority should not affect decisions. That is not what this source says. What does it say, and what does it explicitly permit — and when?
item.answer: The source concedes that an organisation may legitimately make its decisions on what its leaders think. What it denies is that seniority makes an observation more accurate: "it isn't inherently true that their opinions are more accurate just because they're executives." The rule therefore governs the weight given during collection, not during decision, and the authors' instruction is to keep the two separate and sequenced — "we want to keep that separate, and hopefully after a critique." What is explicitly permitted, and when, is stated plainly: as the collected feedback is reviewed afterwards, an individual's expertise and experience may be taken into consideration rather than only their position in the hierarchy. The harm the rule guards against is suppression: participants sensing inequality either stay quiet or go along with what someone else said, and the group loses information it will not know it lost.
item.support: Printed pp. 111-112, with the later weighting permitted explicitly on p. 112 and reappearing at p. 138 as "source of the feedback" among four prioritisation considerations. The authors concede the rule is hard to implement depending on culture.

source_terms: the vision of the director could be easily transferred to posters through the use of computer technology
Advertising is therefore not about 'art' but about selling an image
item.claim: Patel documents a technology-driven change in who makes posters and what they look like. From the early 1990s, photographic stills fed into a computer could be manipulated on screen, "allowing for the smooth superimposition, juxtaposition, reduction, enlargement and colour contrasting of images and text with relative ease," and the characteristic overpainted montage of the previous two decades was replaced by images "defined by simplicity and elegance." She reports the consequence for personnel plainly: "the role of the traditional artist has been displaced by the computer specialist," naming H.R. Enterprises, run by two publicity designers who are not trained artists but have extensive computer knowledge, and Yash Raj Films' in-house Design Cell under Fayyaz Badruddin, also a computer specialist. She records the practitioners' own views on both sides: Yash Chopra prefers painted posters for their element of 'art' and greater emphasis on emotion but sees the new ones as having more modern appeal; to the new designers hand-painted posters look old-fashioned.

mechanism.text: When composition becomes cheap and non-destructive, the montage no longer has to be resolved by hand into a single painted surface, so the design constraint that produced the montage look disappears. What replaces it is not a better version of the same thing but a different object — Patel's "slick, glossy posters" that "match those produced in the West and as such they have become indicators of modernity."

scope.conditions: Indian film publicity from the early 1990s to 2002. Patel dates the first use to Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) and Yash Raj's Design Cell to 1998.

caveats.text: the source reports a loss alongside the gain and does not adjudicate it. Hoarding painters, she says, are now mimicking the computer-generated posters, 'thus displacing their own characteristic expressive interpretations ... signalling a loss of artistic freedom'. That is her judgement, not a measured outcome

the Gupt (1997) anecdote — a poster image unconnected to the film was so strong that the script was rewritten to include a scene with those outfits — is a single reported incident, attributed to one designer, with no corroboration
no commercial outcome is reported for any of this: the source does not claim the new posters sold more tickets

item.question: An expressive spread reads as a set of unrelated fragments. Samara's typographic remedy has a fallback for when the running text cannot take it. State the remedy and the fallback.
item.answer: The remedy is to apply the layout's macro-level compositional gestures to micro-scale elements such as text, at a smaller scale — which he says creates greater cohesion among disparate parts and alleviates the fractured or dissonant quality that often attends alternative compositional approaches. He notes that text at a legible point size will withstand a degree of manipulation without sacrifice. The fallback is for when that seems too challenging: treat subheadings and callouts or decks as a bridge between the macro and micro scales, so the gesture is carried by an intermediate element and the running text is left alone.

item.question: Why does WCAG allow large text a lower contrast ratio, and what second reason — a design-side one — does W3C give for the carve-out?
item.answer: The stated perceptual reason is that text which is larger and has wider character strokes is easier to read at lower contrast, so the requirement can be relaxed. The second reason is stated openly and is about authors rather than readers: the lower requirement lets authors use a wider range of colour choices for large text, which the note says is helpful for the design of pages, particularly titles. The note also marks the limit of the concession — "18 point" and "bold" can mean different things in different fonts, but should be sufficient except for very thin or unusual fonts, which is why a warning about thin strokes is attached to the definition of large scale rather than to the criterion.

source_terms: The guides in the baseline grid must land precisely where the row guides, row-gutter guides, and foot-margin guides are located.
To accomplish this, the designer will have to do some math.
item.claim: Where baselines are to align, a baseline grid is specified so text styles can be locked to it. For a column grid without rows this is simple: define the increment as the common leading number and set where the grid starts, typically just under the head margin so the smallest style can hang from the head margin and sit on the first guide. For a grid with rows it is harder, because the baseline guides must land exactly on the row guides, the row-gutter guides and the foot margin — text must be separable from images by the row gutter yet still flow down a column through that gutter and stay locked, with its last line resting on the foot margin. The source gives an eight-step arithmetic procedure: convert all measurements to points; measure the page height in points; total the depth of the rows and gutters that fit; subtract to get the remainder for head and foot margins; split that remainder, removing a row if the margins come out too tight; set the margins; create the document guides against the margins rather than the page and check the top and bottom row guides strike the head and foot margins; then set the baseline increment and start position and check the guides land on every row, row-gutter and foot-margin guide, restarting the baseline grid at a different position if they do not.

mechanism.text: Text must cross the row gutter without leaving the baseline lattice, which is only possible if the lattice is a whole-number divisor of the row and gutter depths as well as of the leading.

scope.conditions: modular grids with locked baselines, in page-layout software

caveats.text: the worked example uses a 6-point common leading, a 48-point row and a 12-point gutter on a 570-point page, giving 8 rows at 468 points and a 102-point remainder split 66 above and 36 below — specific to that example and not a general result

the remedy when the arithmetic fails is to remove a row or restart the grid at a different depth — the structure yields, not the typography

source_terms: overpainting
hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze
secular darshan
item.claim: Patel documents overpainting — applying oil or gouache over a photographic still, often with a knife in thick textured strokes — as the defining technique of Indian film poster art in the 1970s and '80s, names its principal practitioner (Diwakar Karkare, trained at the Bombay School of Art, who introduced it on Daag in 1973), and states what it was for: it "provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion." She traces its lineage to nineteenth-century Indian painted photography, where studios employed up to six artists to paint a photograph, and reports that the surviving practice — memorial photographs of the deceased — produces "hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze through the sharp reworking of the eyes."

mechanism.text: A photograph fixes what was in front of the camera; paint laid over it can select, exaggerate and intensify without discarding the photographic base. The result is not more faithful but more legible as feeling: Patel calls this "enhancing of reality" and says it is what Karkare aimed at. Combined with centrality of placement and a returned gaze, she argues it produces an image that closes the psychological gap between subject and viewer.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters of the 1970s and '80s specifically. Patel dates its displacement precisely: through much of the 1990s overpainting "was gradually almost replaced by computer-generated imagery," and Karkare closed Studio Diwakar in 1988 because he believed computer technology was displacing the artist and the new designs required no real artistic input.

caveats.text: the technique is historically closed by the source's own account; it is documentation of a superseded craft, not a current method

Patel's application of 'darshan' here is explicitly downgraded to a 'secular darshan', which is a weaker claim than the one Dwyer discusses in chapters 1-2. The two authors are not asserting the same thing

source_terms: a concurrence of self representation, artistic interpretation, and viewer expectation
symbolic biography
the mask
item.claim: Patel argues that star identity is not authored by the star alone but is "cumulatively constructed by the star, the artist and the public," so that a portrait carries "a concurrence of self representation, artistic interpretation, and viewer expectation." She then reports the pictorial consequence: the poster artist's aim is not the sitter's true identity, as in conventional portraiture, but "the 'mask' or the star's constructed identity," and a survey of the posters shows certain facial characteristics becoming the defining features that trigger recognition — for Bachchan, his heavy-hooded eyes, usually looking directly at the viewer or into the distance, and his full lips enhanced to impart a brooding air.

mechanism.text: Because identity accumulates across many artefacts and many hands, no single artefact has to carry it: a small set of features suffices to index the whole. Those features then act as symbols with which the public identifies the subject, and become the trigger that brings forward everything attached to the persona.

scope.conditions: Established for Bachchan in the 1970s and '80s and the artists of that period, principally Diwakar Karkare. Patel bounds it herself: "these images, however, relate to a specific period in Bachchan's career," and says the persona is regenerated through new modes of representation as he continues to act.

item.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'Noise Audits Reveal System Noise'; procedure in Appendix A 'How to Conduct a Noise Audit'
item.question: What, exactly, is a noise audit? Name the design requirements the book puts on it, and say what an audit does and does not tell you.
item.answer: It is an experiment in which several interchangeable professionals independently judge the same cases, real or constructed, without being told that the variability of their answers is what is being studied. The spread of the answers is the measurement. The design requirements the book names: the judges must be genuinely interchangeable — the test is that if one were unavailable another would be assigned and expected to reach a similar judgement; each judge should handle several cases, because the level-versus-pattern split is only recoverable from a multi-case design; the task should be completable from written information and answerable numerically; participants work at the same time, physically separated, and do not communicate. What it tells you is how much your people disagree, and in what proportions. What it does NOT tell you is who is right. The book is explicit that no one in its insurance audit could say how much error there was, because no one knew the right premium for any case.
item.support: The book's own audit at an insurance company, plus the procedural guide in Appendix A. The audit is the authors' own study; the numbers it produced are from one company.
confounders: assuming an audit measures accuracy — it measures disagreement, and the book keeps these strictly apart
thinking one case per judge is enough; that design cannot separate level noise from pattern noise
confusing an audit with test-retest reliability, which measures one person against themselves

item.label: the_economics_of_pictorial_space
item.description: Chapter 9's five claims about pictures are not five independent rules. They are one budget problem stated from five sides: what a picture costs (space, not artwork), what it must beat to justify that cost (the same space set in type), the one condition under which it reliably beats it (depicting the condition the buyer covets), the way a picture can win the comparison on attention and still lose the sale (eccentricity overshadowing the headline), and the source's own ranking of the whole category against the decisions that actually move results.

whole_system_claim.text: A picture is an item of purchased space competing against every other use of that space, so every pictorial decision is a comparison rather than a preference — and the same chapter that makes this comparison "of paramount importance" ends by ranking the entire class of decisions as minor economies beside the basic principles. Both positions are the source's and the source does not reconcile them.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states each claim separately and never states the system. Three things justify grouping them. First, all five arguments are conducted in the same currency — space and its cost — and each explicitly compares one use of space against another. Second, the chapter itself is bounded and self-referential: it opens with the cost premise and closes by ranking the whole chapter's subject matter. Third, the members are incoherent alone: sk_sa8_0005 read by itself makes Hopkins an opponent of pictures, which sk_sa8_0006 shows he is not, and sk_sa8_0009 read by itself makes the chapter's own subject unimportant. The contradiction recorded in `conflicts` is the source's, not ours; the decision to hold these five together so that it is visible is ours.

dependencies.nature: the colour verdict is the space-cost test applied to the colour premium
the repetition economy rests on always addressing new customers, which is a chapter 8 claim

tradeoffs.nature: A picture must be striking enough to carry an aspirational argument and not so striking that it overshadows the headline. The source gives no way to locate the line between them.
Colour raises the cost of the space without adding area, so it must clear the same bar on a worse ratio; the source's answer is that it generally does not.

conflicts.nature: Art is "a study of paramount importance" with one-third to one-half of a campaign staked on it (p.28) and art questions are "minor questions... mere economies, not largely affecting the results of a campaign" (p.30). Two pages apart, in one chapter, unresolved by the source. A reconciliation is available — the stake is in the SPACE, which is a basic decision, while execution quality is a minor one — but the source does not state it and it is not recorded here as the source's position.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Members are individually well recorded and every one is an explicit source claim. The claim that they form ONE budget problem is OURS. The internal contradiction is the SOURCE'S and is quoted rather than inferred. The whole system is technology- and cost-contingent on 1923 print economics — space sold by area, halftone reproduction, a colour premium, preparation cost small beside insertion cost — and none of it is asserted to survive a different cost structure.

item.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
item.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.
confounders: reaching for the polarizer first, which is the intuitive move and the one the source blocks here
oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass
treating this as a legibility defect rather than as a scene lit for the wrong principal subject

item.question: What does this source report about Indian brands and bazaar art, whose claim is it, and why must this material not be treated as a primary source on the subject?
item.answer: Reporting Arvind Rajagopal, it records that Indian brands borrowed totems from bazaar art — including images of gods — specifically when selling products the consumer was not yet familiar with, citing 1950s Pears advertising and Burmah Shell's distribution of calendars featuring Hindu deities. The mechanism is that an unfamiliar product cannot be argued for in its own terms because the audience has no frame for it, so attaching it to imagery that already carries authority supplies one. It is Rajagopal's claim, reported without a specific citation in the passage, and the author then extends it himself to 2010s celebrity endorsement as a likelihood. It must not be treated as a primary source because it is second-hand throughout: the author is reporting a scholar, not observing the material, so if a primary source on Indian calendar art were ever admitted this could not count as independently corroborating it.

source_terms: darshan
darshan lena
darshan dena
item.claim: Dwyer describes darshan as a structure of spectation drawn from Hindu religious practice in which the look runs both ways: the beholder TAKES darshan (darshan lena) and the object GIVES darshan (darshan dena). The distinctive feature she draws out is that the image, not the person looking, holds the power — the image "authorizes the look (rather than merely being its object), thereby benefiting the beholder." She reports that this is used in Hindi cinema to construct the star: the star appears in tableau scenes that invite darshan, which hierarchises the look and lends the star the associations of the traditional granters of darshan, kings and gods.

mechanism.text: A look that is authorised by its object rather than by its subject inverts the usual direction of power in spectatorship. Stasis and the tableau hold the figure still and frontal long enough for the exchange to be legible as an exchange rather than as narrative action, which is why Dwyer (following Vasudevan) ties darshan to stasis and tableaux rather than to continuity editing.

scope.conditions: Stated for Hindi commercial cinema and for viewers who hold the code. Dwyer is careful that this is a contested topic: she reports it as Prasad's and Vasudevan's argument, says Vasudevan's contention that stasis and tableaux permit hierarchical darshan is one "I find persuasive," and immediately bounds her own agreement — "while it may operate within the film to produce the star, I cannot otherwise see any culturally specific ways in which the star is produced."

caveats.text: Dwyer explicitly limits her endorsement: she accepts darshan as operating INSIDE the film to produce the star and otherwise finds the Hindi star produced no differently from the Hollywood star. An extraction that reported darshan as a general theory of Indian spectatorship would overstate what she signs up to
the source describes a reading practice available to viewers who hold the code; it reports no measurement that viewers in fact respond this way
Patel, in chapter 4, applies the term to poster design but explicitly downgrades it there, calling it a 'secular darshan' — the two authors do not use the term at equal strength

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: The source presents this as a disputed topic and marks the dispute. Dwyer calls it "this much disputed topic of darshan" and accepts it only in a bounded form. No measurement supports it.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3, printed p. 171; Ch. 4, printed pp. 187-192
item.question: Describe overpainting as this source documents it: the technique, who introduced it, what it was for, and where it came from.
item.answer: The technique is applying oil or gouache over a photographic still, often with a knife in thick textured strokes, and it is documented as the defining technique of Indian film poster art in the 1970s and '80s. Its principal practitioner is named — Diwakar Karkare, trained at the Bombay School of Art, who introduced it on Daag in 1973. Its purpose is stated: it 'provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion'. Its lineage is traced to nineteenth-century Indian painted photography, where studios employed up to six artists to paint a single photograph, and to the one surviving branch of that practice, memorial photographs of the deceased, which produce 'hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze through the sharp reworking of the eyes'. The knife-laid impasto over photographic underlay was confirmed by direct inspection of the plates in this pass.
item.support: it 'provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion.'
item.confounders: Overpainting is not retouching. The point is not to correct the photograph but to add an interpretation the photograph cannot supply.

item.question: Where do the figures 18 point and 14 point bold come from? What does the source say about how the equivalent sizes are established for Chinese, Japanese and Korean?
item.answer: They are not derived from a contrast experiment. Note 5 states that the 18 and 14 point sizes for roman text are taken from existing large-print conventions: 14 point is the minimum size for large print and 18 point the larger standard font size. For other scripts such as CJK, the "equivalent" sizes are defined the same way — the minimum large-print size used for those languages, and the next larger standard large-print size. item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation, Note 1; SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing, Note 1
item.question: SC 1.4.8 and SC 1.4.12 both mention line spacing at around one and a half times. Why are they not the same requirement, and what would it take to satisfy each?
item.answer: They impose different kinds of obligation on different objects. SC 1.4.8 concerns blocks of text — defined as more than one sentence — and requires that a *mechanism be available* to achieve line spacing of at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs, with paragraph spacing at least 1.5 times the line spacing, alongside four other presentation aspects. Its Note 1 says content is not required to use these values, and that the mechanism may be provided by the browser or another user agent rather than by the content — so a page can satisfy it without the author doing anything to the type, if a user agent supplies the mechanism. SC 1.4.12 concerns whether content *survives* a user setting line height to at least 1.5 times the font size, along with three other properties, changing no other property. Its Note 1 likewise says content need not use the values. Satisfying SC 1.4.8 is about availability of control; satisfying SC 1.4.12 is about the layout not cutting off or overlapping when control is exercised. SC 1.4.8 is Level AAA, SC 1.4.12 Level AA.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.8 and its Note 1; SC 1.4.12 and its Note 1.
confounders: reading either as an instruction to set 1.5 line height
assuming that meeting one implies meeting the other
missing that SC 1.4.8's mechanism may be supplied by the user agent, not the content

item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal, 'Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting' (spine 6)
item.question: You want depth and directional ambiguity in a poster but not incoherence. Samara names a way to get ordered ambiguity from layering. What is it, and what detail does he say strengthens it?
item.answer: Use more than one grid rather than none. He says a conventional grid structure repeated in different orientations can be used to explore a more dynamic architectural space by creating different axes of alignment, and that overlapping grids with modules of different proportions, or running at right angles to each other, can introduce a kind of order to the spatial and directional ambiguity that layering creates. The detail that strengthens it is that some elements should be oriented on both layers simultaneously — an element belonging to two structures at once is what ties the layers together instead of leaving them as separate sheets.

item.question: SC 1.4.8 sets a line width of no more than 80 characters, but 40 if CJK. Why half, and what reason does the source give for limiting line width at all?
item.answer: The stated reason for halving is width per character: the note says studies have shown CJK characters are approximately twice as wide as non-CJK characters when both are displayed with characteristics that achieve the same readability, so the maximum line width for CJK is half. The reason for limiting line width at all is a reading-process failure rather than an aesthetic one: for people with some reading or vision disabilities, long lines are a significant barrier because they have trouble keeping their place and following the flow of text, and a narrow block makes it easier to continue to the next line. The criterion's word is "glyphs", defined in the note as the element of writing in the writing system for the text — so the limit is counted in units of the script, not in characters of English. Note that the studies behind the CJK claim are not cited in the document.

item.rationale: Patel separates, explicitly and in the same passage, an attentional effect she offers as general (a human face draws the glance whether or not the person is recognised) from a recognition effect she says does not travel (an Indian star "will be unknown to the wider Western audience ... and the poster will not evoke the same response"). She draws the same line again for character types, which "are not universally recognized". This project generates and evaluates media for audiences it does not choose, and the distinction between what a design does for any viewer and what it does only for a viewer holding the code is exactly the distinction that gets collapsed when a convention is lifted out of its context. The binding is to that DISTINCTION, not to either effect.

applicability.when: assessing whether an observed or intended effect of a design is available to a viewer outside the culture that produced the convention
applicability.limits: The source measures neither effect. The attentional claim is asserted from developmental and expressive premises with no test of any kind, and must not be cited as evidence that faces draw attention. What is usable is the two-level distinction and the source's insistence that the second level is culture-bound. It supports asking which level an effect belongs to; it supports no prediction about either level, and no threshold.

item.question: "Large scale text is text at 18 point or above." Why is that statement of the definition incomplete in at least three separate ways?
item.answer: First, weight is part of the test: 14 point bold also qualifies, so a 14 point setting can be large scale or not depending only on its weight. Second, script is part of the test: the definition ends with "or font size that would yield equivalent size for Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK) fonts", so CJK is settled by equivalence rather than by the same numbers. Third, which measurement of size counts is specified: Note 2 says font size means the size when the content is delivered and excludes resizing done by the user, and Note 3 says the point size should be obtained from the user agent, or calculated from font metrics the way a user agent does, because the size a reader sees depends on the author's setting and on the user's display and user-agent settings together. Note 3 gives working equivalences — for many mainstream body fonts, 14 and 18 point are roughly 1.2 and 1.5 em, or 120% and 150% of the default body size — and instructs authors to check them for the particular fonts in use rather than treat them as constants.
item.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "large scale (text)" and its Notes 2, 3 and 4.
confounders: treating the definition as a single point-size cutoff

source_terms: A brand name is nothing but a word in the mind
Any and every proper noun is a brand
item.claim: The authors reject every distinction the marketing trade draws between company names, division names, brand names, model names, subbrands, megabrands and flanker brands. On paper there is no difference; inside the prospect's mind all of the variations vanish, because people do not talk or think in those categories. A brand, for them, is simply a proper noun lodged in a mind — which makes brands not limited to registered trademarks, and makes places, people and individuals brands too. The power of a brand is defined narrowly as its ability to influence purchasing behaviour, and they insist a brand name on a package is not the same thing as a brand name in a mind: the same shopper buys milk and bread as commodities and beer and cigarettes by brand in the same trip.

mechanism.text: The test they apply is conversational: imagine a customer saying to a friend "what do you think of this new flanker brand?" Nobody talks that way, so the distinction has no existence in the only place the authors regard as real, which is the mind of the prospect. Everything that cannot be spoken by an ordinary customer is treated as an internal fiction.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3 'The Art of Advertising', printed pp. 101-182; thesis stated at p. 101
item.question: What is chapter 3's organising claim about how film-advertising style changed, and why does the Art Deco phase matter to that claim?
item.answer: That Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'. The sequence given: text-only newspaper notices and handbills from 1896; the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique on Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to the Ajanta revival, used when a studio wanted to signal a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; computer-aided design from the 1990s. Art Deco matters because of how it ended: it 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s' in India because it came to be seen as Western cultural imperialism. That is a style displaced by a political meaning attaching to it rather than by a better style, which is the strongest evidence for the chapter's claim that these are period vocabularies rather than steps toward a solution.
item.support: each phase borrows 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'; Art Deco 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s'

item.source_locator: Glossary: large scale (text), Notes 2-4; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
item.question: A designer says: "The subhead is 20px, so it is large text and 3:1 is enough." Diagnose everything wrong with that reasoning using the source's own definition.
item.answer: Three problems. First, the unit: the definition is in points, not pixels. The Understanding note gives the conversion — 1pt = 1.333px, so 14pt and 18pt are approximately 18.5px and 24px. At 20px the subhead is about 15pt, below the 18 point threshold. Second, weight: 14 point bold also qualifies, so if the subhead is bold the question becomes whether it reaches roughly 18.5px, which 20px does. The claim cannot be settled without knowing the weight, and the designer has not stated it. Third, the measurement: Note 2 says the size meant is the size when the content is delivered, excluding user resizing, and Note 3 says the point size should be obtained from the user agent or calculated from font metrics as user agents do — so a figure taken from a design file is not automatically the figure the criterion is asking about, particularly where sizes are set in relative units and the user agent computes them. The correct answer is therefore: 20px regular is not large scale and needs 4.5:1; 20px bold plausibly is, subject to confirming the computed size.
item.support: Normative — Glossary: "large scale (text)" and its Notes 2, 3 and 4. The 1pt = 1.333px conversion and the 18.5px / 24px equivalences are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".

ignoring weight, which can move 14pt into the large-scale category

item.source_locator: SC 1.4.3, 'Large Text'; Glossary: large scale (text), Note 1; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
item.question: Taking the 3:1 large-text branch buys something and costs something. State both sides as the source presents them, and say when the trade goes bad.
item.answer: What it buys is stated openly: a lower requirement lets authors use a wider range of colour choices for large text, which the note says is helpful for the design of pages and particularly for titles. What it costs is contrast headroom — the type is now permitted to sit at a ratio the standard itself considers insufficient for body text, and there is no margin left for anything that reduces effective contrast. The source names when the trade goes bad. Note 1 to the definition of large scale states that fonts with extraordinarily thin strokes, or unusual features that reduce the familiarity of their letterforms, are harder to read, especially at lower contrast levels — which is exactly the condition the branch creates. The Understanding note reinforces it: "18 point" and "bold" can mean different things in different fonts but should be sufficient except for very thin or unusual fonts. So the branch is safest for a large, conventionally weighted face and least safe for the thin display face a designer is most likely to want at title size.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3's Large Text exception and Note 1 to the glossary definition of "large scale (text)". The colour-latitude benefit and the thin-font caution are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".

item.question: Godin says two paragraphs of his book should have paid for it. What is the separation they make, what opposite disciplines follow, and what does he say the real danger is?
item.answer: Direct marketing is action-oriented and is measured; brand marketing is culturally oriented and cannot be measured. The disciplines that follow are opposites, and he states both as instructions. For direct: measure everything — what attention costs, what a click costs, what an order costs — and if you cannot measure it, it does not count. For brand: be patient, refuse to measure, engage with the culture, focus and above all be consistent — and if you cannot afford to be consistent and patient, do not buy brand advertising at all. The danger he names is neither discipline done badly but the confusion of the two, which is what makes a shift to a measured environment destroy a business built on unmeasurable brand advertising. He adds the gate: if you cannot see the funnel, do not buy the ads, and if you can see it and it costs too much, fix the funnel first. And the narrowing rule still applies — you cannot afford to build a brand for everyone, so be specific.

item.answer: Both fail. The source illustrates three failure types under this criterion — text cut off vertically, text cut off horizontally, and text overlapping other content — and the described case contains two of them. The repairs the source accepts stop short of redesign in one specific circumstance: where a text container cannot expand because of a design constraint, such as a maximum width for a left navigation or a table column header, truncation with an ellipsis can still meet the requirement provided the content remains available. The source names two acceptable routes: a mechanism reveals the truncated text on the page, for instance on focus or on activation; or, where the ellipsis is part of a section containing a link, the truncated text is revealed on the linked page. item.question: The authors say brands are brands and companies are companies, then recommend using the company name as the brand name. Explain how both positions sit together, and give the two-question test they offer.
item.answer: The separation is about whose point of view governs: a company is the organisation that produces a brand and is not the brand, but customers are brand-oriented while managers, being employees, are company-oriented, so the brand name should almost always take precedence. The recommendation follows from that rather than contradicting it — unless there are compelling reasons otherwise, the cleanest arrangement is for company and brand to be one name, so that the question has one answer: what is a Coca-Cola, a Zippo, a WD-40? Cola, windproof lighter, lubricating spray. Their test is a pair of questions: what is the name of the brand, and what is the name of the stuff inside the packaging? Both had better be the same or you have big problems. They push the identification hard — the liquid itself is Coca-Cola, not a cola made by a company — which is why they say a company that understood branding could never have introduced New Coke. They add a symptom: when customers feel they must say both names together, there is usually a branding problem, normally because a generic word was used as the brand name.
