item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 143-144 (Chapter Thirteen, the repricing of Puffed Rice and Wheat Berries)
item.question: Two products are in decline, their makers are convinced they cannot succeed, and there is no money for a campaign. Hopkins's first act on this exact brief was not a creative one. What was it, how does the arithmetic work, and what did he assert rather than establish?
item.answer: His first act was to raise the prices. Puffed Rice went from ten cents to fifteen and Wheat Berries from seven cents to ten — renamed Puffed Wheat so the two could be advertised together — and he states that this added an average of $1.25 per case to the billing price. That increment was the advertising appropriation: the fund to develop new users came out of the price rather than out of the client's existing margin, on a line the client had already written off. What he asserts rather than establishes is the demand side. He says he was sure the extra price would not reduce the sale in view of the advertising effort, and reports no test of the price change on its own, no before-and-after unit figures, and no attempt to separate the price effect from the campaign effect. He is also candid on the following pages that the same campaign then wasted large sums in newspapers, so the appropriation he created was partly spent on a medium he later proved could not pay for this line.

item.question: Two layouts are equally chaotic on first impression; one is praised in this book and the other would not be. Reading the exhibit commentaries, what does Samara consistently credit for the difference — and what is the honest limit on that reading?
item.answer: He consistently credits a restricted substructure. In one commentary the designers attend to the parallel or divergent nature of axes and their junctures, distributing them along a limited selection of planar levels and directions, which he says ensures well-crafted, rhythmic cohesion instead of chaotic randomness. In another, spatial confusion and complicated interference between overlapping shapes and text are said to be underpinned by a rigorously controlled network of geometric axes in which the edges of every element line up with, or point to, those of other elements. item.claim: Godin's most operational claim is a separation. Direct marketing is action-oriented and is measured; brand marketing is culturally oriented and cannot be measured. The disciplines that follow are opposites and he states both as instructions: if you are buying direct ads, measure everything — what attention costs, what a click costs, what an order costs — and if you cannot measure it, it does not count; if you are buying brand ads, be patient, refuse to measure, be consistent, and if you cannot afford to be consistent and patient, do not buy them at all. The danger he names is not doing either badly but confusing the two, which is what makes a shift to a measured environment destroy a business built on unmeasurable brand advertising. He adds the gate: if you cannot see the funnel, do not buy the ads, and if you can see it and it costs too much, fix the funnel first. And he insists brand marketing is subject to the same narrowing rule as everything else — you cannot afford to build a brand for everyone.

mechanism.text: The two do different work on different timescales, so they require opposite decision rules. Applying measurement to culturally-oriented spending kills it before it accumulates; declining to measure action-oriented spending removes the only control it has.

item.source_locator: printed p. 24 (Ch. 5, 'you can't become generic by overtaking the leader')
item.question: A challenger brand outsells the category leader and its marketing director expects the brand name to become the generic term for the category. What boundary condition do the authors state, and what test do they give for whether a brand has actually got there?
item.answer: The boundary is absolute in their statement of it: you cannot become generic by overtaking the leader. A brand can own the category word only by having been the first brand and having established the category, and they say Pepsi would not become generic for cola even if it outsold Coke — noting that it once did outsell it in the supermarket distribution channel. item.question: A caption is set in a hairline geometric sans at 11pt, in a grey computing to 4.6:1 against white. A reviewer says WCAG has nothing to say about it because it passes. What does the source actually say about this case, and what does it stop short of saying?
item.answer: It passes SC 1.4.3 as computed — 4.6:1 exceeds 4.5:1, and computed values are not rounded, so it is a real pass rather than a marginal one. But the source raises two related concerns and states both as concerns rather than requirements. Note 1 to the definition of large scale says fonts with extraordinarily thin strokes or unusual features that reduce the familiarity of their letterforms are harder to read, especially at lower contrast levels. And the Understanding note explains why the number can flatter this setting: because the contrast ratio may be evaluated with anti-aliasing turned off, and because evaluation refers to the colours in the markup rather than the text as presented, a thin face rendered by a user agent with anti-aliasing may appear much fainter than its declared colour — producing text that nominally passes while having much lower contrast in practice. The note's response is best practice, not obligation: choose a font with stronger, thicker lines, or aim for a combination that exceeds the normative requirement. What the source stops short of saying is that this caption fails anything. It has no test for stroke weight, no requirement to exceed a threshold, and no claim about whether the caption reads well.

item.answer: The variable is how long the audience dwells with the medium. For roadside boards he reports the received limit of about seven words, notes the logo adds two or three, calls ten pushing it, and says eleven can work with the right execution — helped by having no visual. For subway postings and bus stops he says concepts can risk a slightly longer fuse, because the audience dwells. The two tests: show it to someone for two seconds, take it away and ask what it said; and view the layout from ten feet away as a legibility check. Their reason is that a brand's power is confined to the meaning attached to its name and cannot be extended past it, which they argue through Kodak: Kodak stands for conventional photography, so the Kodak name has no power over videotape and, they predict, none over digital imaging. item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. item.question: You are laying out a transcript of a heated argument between three speakers. Using Samara's verbal deconstruction, what is the source of the layout's structure, and what specifically does he warn you are exchanging?
item.answer: The structure comes from the speech itself. Samara says the natural rhythm of spoken language is often used as a guide for changing weight, size, colour or alignment among lines of type, with louder or faster words set larger, bolder or in italics to correspond to stresses and lulls in actual speech; giving a voice to visual language can push words out of paragraphs or force columns into relationships where the natural logic of the writing creates a visual order. His own example is a book of dialogue in which each character's voice is coded typographically and the columns are deconstructed by the quality of the speech — falling apart, becoming confused, interrupting each other. item.label: the_brand_life_cycle_from_publicity_to_euthanasia
item.description: Four of the laws describe successive phases in the life of a single brand, and the source itself supplies the connective tissue for the first transition and the last. A brand is born with publicity, generated by being first in a new category (Law 3). Once the category launch and the pioneer's rise have both been told, the publicity potential is exhausted, and the authors state the sequence explicitly: "First publicity, then advertising is the general rule" (printed p. 19); advertising thereafter defends rather than builds (Law 4). Through the long middle the brand is held still — success measured in decades, not years (Law 19). Change is possible only under three narrow conditions (Law 20). And finally the brand dies, at which point the authors say the money should go to a new brand rather than to life support (Law 21), because a new category will be won by a new name.

whole_system_claim.text: What a brand should do depends on where it is in this sequence, and the authors' most counter-conventional prescriptions are phase-specific rather than general. Advertising is useless for building and necessary for defending — the same activity, opposite verdicts, separated only by phase. The instruction to hold absolutely still applies to a brand that has already taken a position and not to one that has none, which is why Law 20's first permitted change is for a brand that is weak or non-existent in the mind. Reading any of these four laws without its phase produces the wrong advice: a start-up that takes Law 4 literally will spend on defence it has nothing to defend, and an established leader that takes Law 21 literally will kill a brand that has not finished.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states the publicity-to-advertising transition and its cause directly (printed pp. 18-19), states that brands are born, grow up, mature and die (p. 105), and states that Law 20's first permitted change applies where there is effectively no brand (p. 101). It does NOT present these four laws as a life cycle, does not number them as phases, and does not warn that a law read out of phase misleads. The assembly into a sequence, and the warning, are OURS.

source_terms: The Law of Expansion

item.answer: A see-say advertisement — the rookie error of showing the headline. He describes the symptom as every element trying too hard and either repeating or tripping over one another, and states the rule in both directions: never show what you are saying or say what you are showing. The fault is not in either element individually but in the relation: he treats the distance between what is said and what is shown as the variable that sets the size of the shift in the reader's head, so a visual that closes that distance to zero leaves the reader nothing to do and wastes the second element. His requirement is that the visual amplify the headline or reinterpret it. He grants that a supporting element may be deliberately straight — his own preferred pattern is one clever element and one straight one — but the straight element must still add something, and he supplies no test for where support becomes restatement.

Once a brand occupies a position in a mind, its essential characteristics should never be changed, though they may be bent slightly or given a new slant. When the market swings elsewhere the choice is to follow the fad and destroy the brand, or to hang on and hope the market swings back — and the authors say hanging on is the better approach. They supply a specific verbal cue for the failure: the sentence "why should we limit ourselves?", which they say should raise a red flag, because limitation is the essence of branding. Brands are used as personality statements or badges, and people change badges as they grow up, so a brand that follows its customers through their life stages ends up making a statement no group wants. item.question: A designer claims an image of text qualifies for the "Essential" exception because the typeface is central to the brand's identity. What does the glossary definition of essential actually require, and which half of the test does that claim not address?
item.answer: The definition has two conjoined halves. Removing the thing would have to fundamentally change the information or functionality of the content — and the information and functionality must be unachievable in another way that would conform. The brand-identity claim speaks only to the first half. It says nothing about whether the same information could be delivered by a conforming route, which is the half that usually defeats such claims. The source does grant one case by fiat rather than by test: a note under SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 declares logotypes — text that is part of a logo or brand name — to be essential, which short-circuits the test for the mark itself. The Understanding note for SC 1.4.3 draws the boundary explicitly: corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.
item.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "essential", and the notes to SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 declaring logotypes essential. The statement that brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are excluded is non-normative, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: treating 'essential' as a synonym for 'important to us', which is the first half only
extending the logotype note to a whole brand type system — the source explicitly excludes it
confusing 'essential' with 'pure decoration'; both exempt, on opposite grounds

source_terms: The Law of the Category

item.claim: Law 8. The authors take the Law of Contraction to its limit and treat the result as the best situation available: narrow the focus until no market remains, and you have created the chance to introduce a new category. They then prescribe two things done at once — launch so as to create the perception that the brand is the first, the leader, the pioneer or the original, and promote the category rather than the brand. Their reason is that customers care about categories, not brands: not about Domino's but about whether the pizza arrives in thirty minutes. They state plainly that the most useful aspect of branding has nothing to do with increasing a company's share of an existing market.

Berger's account is that the brand latched onto something people already wanted to talk about — unrealistic beauty norms — and which was emotional but controversial enough that people had been reluctant to raise it. The film gave them the occasion. He explicitly names the other drivers it recruited: it made the issue more PUBLIC, giving people an excuse to discuss what had been private, and it was highly EMOTIONAL. And it got people talking about the brand along the way, because the brand was smuggled in as part of the discussion rather than attached to it. item.label: the_growth_problem_and_the_four_permitted_answers
item.description: The book returns repeatedly to one situation: a company believes its home-market share cannot rise much further and believes it must grow, and therefore extends its brand. The authors state this belief pair verbatim at printed p. 91 and treat it as the origin of the violations the book catalogues. Against the one forbidden answer — put the existing name on more things (Law 10) — they permit four. Grow the market for the narrow thing the brand already owns rather than the brand itself (Law 5, printed p. 26). Narrow further until a new category exists, then promote the category (Law 8). Take the unchanged narrow brand across borders (Law 18). Launch a separate sibling brand, under six conditions, when the market has genuinely moved or when share would otherwise pass about fifty per cent (Laws 10, 11 and 15).

whole_system_claim.text: The permitted answers are not alternatives of equal standing but a ladder the authors expect to be climbed in order of how little the existing brand is disturbed: expand the category around the brand, create an adjacent category, carry the brand abroad unchanged, and only then add a name. What unifies all four, and separates them from the forbidden answer, is a single test — does the growth move require the existing name to stand for anything new? If it does not, the authors permit it; if it does, they forbid it, whatever it is called. This test is what makes the difference between the sibling brand they license and the subbrand they condemn: both add a product, but only one adds meaning to an existing name.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Every member is the source's, and the source itself connects three of the links: Law 18 names the belief pair and offers going global as the answer to it, Law 11 points forward to Law 15 for shares above fifty per cent, and Law 10 states the two-branch rule about launching a second brand. The unifying test — whether the move requires the existing name to carry new meaning — is OURS. So is the ordering of the four answers as a ladder. The authors state no order among them and never give a single test for what separates permitted from forbidden growth; they argue case by case.

dependencies: the sibling answer depends on the six conditions in Law 15; without them the authors say a second brand dilutes the first
the go-global answer depends on two stated conditions — being first, and fitting the perceptions of the country of origin
the create-a-category answer depends on the publicity engine of Law 3
tradeoffs: each permitted answer costs more management effort than the forbidden one; the authors say a sibling family needs more top-management supervision, not less
conflicts: the authors give no test for when a market has 'really' moved, which is the judgement that selects between the two branches of sk_r22_0033 and therefore between doing nothing and launching a brand

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The members and three of the links are the source's; the framework, the ordering and the unifying test are OURS and should be attributed to this lane, not to Ries & Ries. No answer in this framework has been measured against any other anywhere in the book, and the whole rests on cases chosen after their outcomes were known.

item.claim: Law 12. A generic name cannot separate a brand from its competitors, and the authors ground this in a claim about processing. Most brand communication happens verbally rather than visually — they say the average person spends nine times as long listening to radio and television as reading print — and even the printed word is processed through the sound it generates, so a reader cannot hear the difference between "general" and "General". Capitalising a generic word does not make it a name. They use this to explain why line extensions fare poorly: an extension typically pairs a brand name with a generic descriptor, and the descriptor cannot create the separate identity the branding process needs.

mechanism.text: Sound is the channel. Because the mind processes the printed word through its sound, the orthographic marking that distinguishes a proper noun from a common one is lost, and the generic word is heard as generic however it is set. The naming process, the authors say, goes wrong because it is conducted visually — logotypes mounted on foamcore and passed round a boardroom — rather than by ear.

item.rationale: The Law of Color's operative property is not "is this colour good" but "is this colour held, and is it the one the competitor does not have". Both halves are relational and temporal. A single execution cannot answer either: a brand's colour is differentiating only relative to a named competitor's, and it is an asset only if it has been held long enough to be recognised, which is the whole of the source's Tiffany argument. So the honest observable is the colour distribution across a brand's output over a period, checked against the leading competitor's. Again a single asset cannot carry the property — every individual piece can be on-palette while the palette itself has been changing, or while it collides with the category leader's.

applicability.when: reviewing colour use across a brand's accumulated output over a period, with the competitor's palette available
applicability.limits: The source's rule is for a brand's whole visual identity, decided once and held for decades by a company, not for the palette of a production run. Its physiological justification — wavelengths focusing in front of or behind the retina, producing the emotional readings of red and blue — is offered without a source and does not support the cultural meanings the chapter derives from it. The colour associations listed are Western conventions. Nothing here should be applied to a brand whose market this project has not looked at.

item.question: Hopkins names two specific phrases-and-postures he says kill advertisements. Name both families, quote the short phrases he gives for the first, and state the single mechanism that condemns both.
item.answer: The first family is brand insistence: insist on this brand, avoid imitations, look out for substitution — to which he adds buy my brand, mine is the original, be sure to get the genuine. He says such appeals have no good effect and indicate a motive with which buyers cannot sympathise, and that he has seen many an advertisement killed by a single unfortunate phrase of this kind. The second family is institutional boasting: about the plant, the output, the age of the firm, anything more interesting to you than to your prospect. Boasting is repulsive, he says, and he identifies it as the recurring reason he lost large accounts. The single mechanism is that both make the advertiser's own interest the visible content of the appeal. Every such phrase is in substance a request to transfer money from a competitor for the advertiser's benefit — a grocer would not say come to my store rather than the next store, he offers an advantage. His estimate that nine-tenths of advertising money is lost to selfish purposes openly displayed is rhetorical, with no computation given, and he elsewhere concedes that name-crying may sometimes pay to an extent.

item.answer: A narrow focus, a better name and a higher price. Narrowing makes the brand a specialist and a specialist is perceived to know more — their analogy is the cardiologist against the general practitioner, and they add that from a marketing point of view it does not matter whether the perception is true. item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 109-110 (Ch. 22, 'The Law of Singularity')
item.question: The book closes with two answers to the question 'what is a brand?'. Give both, explain the test that goes with them, and state the caveat the authors attach about brands that have failed the test and are still trading.
item.answer: A brand is a proper noun that can be used in place of a common word — instead of an imported beer you ask for a Heineken, instead of a safe car a Volvo, instead of a thick spaghetti sauce a Prego. And a brand is a singular idea or concept that you own inside the mind of the prospect. The test is the one that opened the book: say the name and see what comes back. What is a Chevrolet? A large, small, cheap, expensive car or truck. What is a Miller? A regular, light, draft, cheap, expensive beer. A name that returns a list of contradictory attributes has lost its singularity and, in their word, is burned out. The caveat is that such brands can remain on the marketing scene for many years because of the line-extension generosity of their competitors. Survival is therefore not evidence that singularity was retained — which is the fourth time in this span the authors use competitor weakness to keep an outcome from counting against them.
item.support: Printed pp. 109-110. The definitions and the caveat are the authors'. The observation that the caveat repeats the weak-competition move a fourth time is the extractor's; the other three are at printed pp. 7, 36 and 66.

treating this chapter as introducing something new; it restates the Law of Expansion and the Law of the Word, and was extracted for the closing definitions and the caveat

item.question: The authors say General Motors' five brands were once instantly identifiable and later were not. What mechanism do they name for the decay, and what management conclusion do they draw from it?
item.answer: The mechanism is sibling rivalry: a pattern of corporate behaviour in which each brand copies the best features of its sibling competitors, so that a portfolio of distinct brands converges. They pair it with a second cause — control over the brands was lifted and each division allowed to set its own course, after which each division broadened the scope of its own brand, producing expensive Chevrolets, cheap Cadillacs and general confusion. Their summary is that all General Motors cars ended up with fins. The management conclusion runs directly against the common belief they quote, that a sibling strategy works best in a decentralised organisation: a sibling strategy requires more top-management supervision, not less, because the urgent long-term need is to maintain the separation between brands and human instincts work in the opposite direction.

item.source_locator: printed pp. 101-103 (Ch. 20, 'The Law of Change')
item.question: Name the three situations in which the authors say changing a brand is feasible, and explain the mechanism they give for the third — including why they say it will not work in a fast-moving field.
item.answer: First, where the brand is weak or non-existent in the mind: there is effectively no brand, so it can be used on any product in any category — who is to know? Intel leaving memory chips for microprocessors is their case, on the grounds that outside a handful of computer executives and purchasing agents nobody knew what Intel had stood for. Second, moving the brand permanently down the price ladder, which customers read as value received; going the other way, up the food chain, they call much harder if not impossible. Third, a slow-moving field where the change can be spread over a long period. The mechanism for the third is not persuasion but forgetting: Citicorp moved Citibank from a corporate to a consumer perception over twenty-five years, and the authors say little change actually occurred in any prospect's mind — instead of changing minds, enough time was allowed to pass for the natural process of forgetting to take place. That is why it will not work in computers or consumer electronics: there is not enough time for forgetting.

item.claim: Sullivan's account of branded content has a durable core and a datable surface, and he marks the boundary himself in places. The core claim is that the work must satisfy two criteria at once: focus too much on the narrative and viewers may enjoy it without receiving any brand message, so the entertained audience must not leave without knowing the brand was involved. He states the strong form of the requirement — the idea cannot be a "brought to you by" attachment; it must come from and carry the brand's own material, and be relevant to the audience — and reports PJ Pereira's test: if it is impossible to talk about the idea without the brand, yet interesting enough to generate buzz, you have something. He records Edward Boches's participation sequence — do something interesting that communicates the brand's value, invite people into it, capture what they make, make it shareable — and notes the hard step is the first, which requires an idea worth advertising rather than an advertising idea. He states a bounding condition: whenever customers are asked for time or effort there must be a payoff commensurate with what was asked, or usage rates are very low. Everything platform-specific around this core — hashtag ceilings, which network's features to exploit, the stock-and-flow content vocabulary he footnotes as already out of use, the influencer arrangements — is contingent on the state of specific commercial platforms at the time of writing.

mechanism.text: The two criteria pull against each other because the entertainment must be good enough to be chosen voluntarily while the brand must remain inseparable from it. Sullivan's own image is giving a dog a pill: the medicine cannot sit beside the treat, the two have to be one thing. The participation sequence works by converting the audience into producers, which he says yields material that can outlast and outgrow the original idea.

scope.conditions: content a customer chooses rather than encounters; the durable claim is about the double criterion, not about any platform

caveats.text: everything in these chapters that names a platform, a feature, a format limit or a content-scheduling vocabulary is contingent on the commercial platforms of the writing period and must not be read as durable; the source himself footnotes one of his own terms as no longer in wide use

the founding example — a car brand spending a year's whole budget on short films — is the single most celebrated case of its kind and is presented as having changed the field; no comparable attempt that failed is discussed anywhere

source_terms: The Law of Credentials
The crucial ingredient in the success of any brand is its claim to authenticity.
Credentials are the collateral you put up to guarantee the performance of your brand.
item.claim: Law 6. The authors start from customer disbelief: prospects are suspicious and discount most product claims. They argue one claim takes precedence over all others because it makes the others credible — the claim to authenticity, to being the real thing. Benefit claims made without credentials are, on their account, generally ignored, because every competitor makes the same sort of claim; the same benefit claims attached to a credential carry much more weight. They extend the point to buyer behaviour generally with the empty-restaurant observation: people prefer to wait for a table where there is a queue rather than eat in an empty room.

mechanism.text: Credentials work as collateral. A claim about performance is unverifiable at the point of choice, so the prospect looks for something that stands behind it; where a brand supplies that, the prospect will believe almost anything else it says. Absent it, benefit claims fall into the undifferentiated mass that provokes "that's what they all say".

item.question: What do the authors mean by credentials, what problem do credentials solve, and what do they say happens to benefit claims that lack them?
item.answer: Credentials are the collateral a brand puts up to guarantee its own performance — most often a claim to authenticity or to leadership. The problem they solve is disbelief: customers are suspicious and discount most product claims, so a brand needs one claim that takes precedence over the others and makes them believable. Where the credentials are right, they say, the prospect will believe almost anything else the brand says. Benefit claims without credentials fall into an undifferentiated mass — tastes great, saves money, whitens teeth, bigger, smaller, lighter, faster, cheaper — which prospects meet with "that's what they all say" and generally ignore. item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 181-182 (Chapter Seventeen, on type size and on capitals)
item.question: A designer argues for large display type and all-capital headlines so the advertisement will command attention. Hopkins answers both. What are his two arguments, and on what basis does he make them — which is not the basis a modern reader will assume?
item.answer: On size he argues from habit and from cost. Ordinary reading of the period was done in 8-point type; most mail-order advertisers, presenting something more interesting than ordinary reading matter, had gone down to 6-point. The easiest type to read, he says, is the ordinary, because anything unusual presents difficulties; advertisers use big type because they are trying to demand attention rather than induce it; and anyone who traces results can quickly prove that oversize type does not pay, because doubling the space you need doubles your cost. His summary is that if the story is interesting people will read it in their accustomed type, and if it is not they will not read it in any size. On capitals he argues from habit alone: all our reading is done in upper-and-lower case, so lines set in capitals have to be studied out — a detriment always, though he concedes it may not be a severe one. The basis is what readers are accustomed to, plus space economy, and not legibility as a measurable property of the letterforms. He runs no vision experiment, cites no study, and the point sizes he names are the reading conventions of 1920s American print rather than thresholds.
item.support: Printed pp. 181-182. The 8-point ordinary reading, the 6-point mail-order convention, the demand-versus-induce framing, the doubling of cost with space, and the all-caps habituation argument are all stated there. Argued from habit and cost; the claim that traced results prove it is asserted without figures.

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 3, 6-7 (Ch. 1, 'The Law of Expansion')
item.question: State the Law of Expansion in the authors' own terms, and then explain the distinction they draw in the same chapter that stops market-share numbers from settling the question either way.
item.answer: The law is "the power of a brand is inversely proportional to its scope" — put the name on everything and the name loses its power. The distinction is between a brand's power and its sales. Sales, they say, are a function not only of a brand's power but of the strength or weakness of its competition, so if the competition is weak or non-existent you can often increase sales by weakening your brand, that is by extending it. A share gain following an extension therefore demonstrates only the weakness of the competitor, on their account. Their worked instance is Diet Coke: Coca-Cola had nothing to lose because Pepsi had already line-extended into Diet Pepsi. The practical consequence is that neither a rise nor a fall in share can settle whether the law held in a given case.

item.question: Why do the authors say a dominant brand should welcome competitors rather than merely tolerate them? Give the three mechanisms in the chapter.
item.answer: First, attention: competition increases the noise level in a category, makes customers more conscious of it and raises consumption per head — the best thing that happened to Coca-Cola, on their reading, was Pepsi-Cola, and they call it ironic that Coke fought Pepsi over the use of "cola" and fortunate that it lost. Second, comparison: choice is itself read by customers as a benefit, and where there is none they become suspicious — maybe the category has flaws, maybe the price is too high; who wants to buy a brand with nothing to compare it against? Third, focus preservation: two competing brands can each stay narrow and powerful while between them covering a market neither could cover alone, their example being one brand appealing to older customers and one to younger. source_terms: The Law of Siblings
There is a time and a place to launch a second brand.
You don't want to create a family of brands, you want to create a family of different brands.
item.claim: Law 15. The authors open by conceding that their own laws seem to suggest a company should concentrate everything on one brand for one market, agree that this is true, and then license an exception: there comes a time to launch a second brand, and perhaps a third and fourth. They set six conditions — focus the family on a common product area; segment on a single attribute, price being the most common; set rigid, non-overlapping distinctions, which price makes easiest because numbers can be attached to it; give the siblings different rather than similar names, since alliteration is the curse of a sibling family; launch a new sibling only when it can create a new category, never to fill a hole in the line or block a competitor; and keep control at the highest level. They are explicit that a sibling strategy requires more top-management supervision, not less, because the natural drift is toward making the brands alike.

mechanism.text: Separation is what makes a portfolio work, and separation decays without enforcement. The authors name the decay mechanism as sibling rivalry: each brand copies the best features of its siblings, and if control has been decentralised each division also broadens its own scope, so the portfolio converges on a single indistinct offering. Their case is General Motors, whose five brands they say a child could once tell apart from a block away.

caveats.text: the exception is granted without any test for when the 'time and place' has arrived, so the licence and the prohibition it qualifies cannot both be applied to a given case without judgement the book does not supply

the authors themselves note that Wrigley's approach is imperfect, since three of its brands need the parent name to support generic descriptors, and that Time Inc. has since produced names that break the rule — the exemplars are graded rather than clean

item.answer: The connecting rule closes Chapter 10, and both of its branches begin the same way: if the market is moving out from under you, stay where you are and launch a second brand; if it is not, stay where you are and continue building your brand. source_terms:
part of the status quo of designing
It's a convention and, like all conventions, it is suitable for achieving particular goals.
Using a grid may not offer the best solution toward that end; assuming that one should be imposed may, in fact, compromise the information's integrity.
item.claim: Using a grid to organise text and imagery is the status quo of designing, but it is a convention and, like all conventions, is suitable for achieving particular goals rather than all of them. The designer's purpose is to facilitate the clearest and most compelling experience for the audience; a grid may not be the best route to that end, and assuming one should be imposed may compromise the information's integrity. There are numerous ways of delivering understandable, meaningful experiences that are equally valid and that run counter to the rationalist approach of grid-based structure; exploring them often creates opportunities to transcend the content's literal, pragmatic meaning and to engage with a richer, more specific and more memorable visual language.

mechanism.text: A convention is fitted to the goals it was developed for. Imposing it where those goals do not hold makes the structure a cost paid against the content rather than a service to it.

scope.conditions: any project where a grid would be the default choice

caveats.text: This is the same author's own qualification of the position his chapter 1 argues. It is not a retraction — chapter 2 does not say grids are wrong, only that grid use is a choice with conditions. It must never be presented as a second source disagreeing with the first.

item.label: the_four_rules_of_critique
item.description: The source states four key rules for a critique session and says it is the facilitator's job to see they are adhered to, that they should be shared with the team, and that they can be reviewed at the start or posted in the room. They are: everyone is equal; everyone is a critic; avoid problem solving; and don't rush to make decisions on the changes to be made. The source summarises them at the end of Chapter 5 as: everyone is equal, everyone participates, avoid problem solving, don't rush to make decisions.

whole_system_claim.text: The four rules divide cleanly into two that protect the input and two that protect the output, and each pair fails in a characteristic way if the other is enforced alone. Equality and participation govern what enters the session — they exist because deference and silence remove observations before they are voiced. Avoiding problem solving and refusing to decide govern what leaves it — they exist because a session that produces a change list has substituted a remedy for the diagnosis. Enforcing only the input rules yields a full, noisy room that still emits a to-do list; enforcing only the output rules yields a well-formed set of findings drawn from a fraction of the knowledge present.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source presents four rules in sequence with no grouping and no statement of how they interact. The input/output division and the two failure modes of partial enforcement are entirely ours. What the source does supply, and what the reading rests on, is a mechanism for each rule individually: suppression under hierarchy (p. 111), concerns surfacing too late (p. 112), fragmentation of mental process (p. 113), and premature decision closing the option space (p. 115).

item.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Logos
item.question: Under SC 1.4.11, when does a logo *lose* its exemption from the contrast requirement? Give the source's stated condition and its worked case.
item.answer: The exemption rests on the assumption that logos must comply with stricter colour choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines — that is, on a constraint the author cannot alter. The source states the consequence directly: where a logo is presented with insufficient contrast but that presentation was an author choice rather than mandated by brand guidelines, the low-contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt. The worked case is an author who displays partner or company logos at low contrast by default and raises the contrast only on hover; being logos does not rescue that, because the initial low-contrast presentation was chosen, not mandated. The source separately flags that the exemption is problematic when a logo acts as a user interface component such as a link, and recommends as best practice a higher-contrast logo variant where brand guidelines allow, or an equivalent control that meets the requirements. item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 44-45 (Ch. 9, 'The Law of the Name')
item.question: What do the authors say a brand needs in the short term as against the long term, and what is the argument that gets them from one to the other?
item.answer: In the short term a brand needs a unique idea or concept: it needs to be first in a new category and to own a word in the mind. In the long term the unique idea disappears and all that is left is the difference between your name and your competitors' names — or rather the perception of those names. The argument connecting the two is erosion by imitation. Xerox was the first plain-paper copier and in the beginning you could sell one by showing the difference between a Xerox copy and an ordinary copy; today all copiers are plain-paper copiers, so the technical asymmetry is gone. What remains is the name, which competitors cannot copy, and that is why they say the most important branding decision anyone makes is what to call the product, and that the most valuable asset of the Xerox Corporation is the Xerox name itself.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed p. 125 (Chapter Eleven, after rivals adopted the same tire construction)
item.question: Hopkins's most successful differentiation campaign forced every rival to copy the feature. What happened next, what did he do, and what does his successor argument require that makes it unavailable to most advertisers?
item.answer: Within two or three years the advantage the campaign had been built on no longer existed, because the campaign itself had forced all rivals to that type of tire and Goodyear could no longer claim it. His response had three parts: he gradually reduced the coined product name, promoted the house name in its place, and shifted the argument to a different and, he says, more impressive talking point — the demonstrable growth of demand. He reports the same pattern in sampling, where rivals adopted the coupon plan and a new mechanism had to be invented, and states generally that few who dominate a field have any exclusive advantage and there are few advertised products which cannot be imitated. What the successor argument requires is a visible lead in demand, which is available only to a brand that is already winning. He offers no successor at all for a brand whose differentiator expires while it is behind. The two-or-three-year timing is one observation in one category in one period and he does not offer it as a general figure.

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed p. 91 (Ch. 18, 'The Law of Borders', the two ironclad beliefs)
item.question: Chapter 18 opens with two beliefs the authors say most of their clients hold. Name both, explain why the pair produces line extension, and give the authors' alternative resolution.
item.answer: The beliefs are that the brand's market share cannot be substantially increased in its home country, and that the company needs to grow. Together they close off the obvious route and leave only one apparent exit: extend the brand into other categories, which the clients defend by saying it may be dangerous but it is the only way to grow. The authors say that reasoning falls victim to the first law of branding, the Law of Expansion. Their resolution satisfies both beliefs without breaking it: keep the brand's narrow focus in its home country, and go global. Growth comes from more geography rather than from more categories, and nothing about what the brand means has to change. Heineken is their case — the leading brewery in a country of fifteen million becoming the second-largest brewery in the world by going global.

item.question: Sullivan reports that audiences in every city he has lectured in answer "safety" when asked what Volvo stands for, and adds that Volvo has not recently appeared in lists of the safest cars. He reads this as evidence of one thing. What second reading does his own evidence permit that he does not draw?
item.answer: He reads it as the power of simplicity: a brand that successfully welded one adjective to its marque rides the benefit of that position in customers' minds long after its products stopped meriting the distinction. The reading he does not draw is the uncomfortable one — that a successfully installed brand adjective can survive the loss of the underlying truth, which makes the same mechanism a way of sustaining a claim the product no longer supports. Two consequences follow: because the optimal count puts an average number of average-length words on each line, hyphens are greatly reduced; and the same consistency makes a ragged setting fall into a rhythmically regular rag shape, and a justified setting space regularly, minimising dark and light spottiness and the appearance of rivers.

item.question: The authors connect the Law of Color to the Law of Extensions through a single comparison. What is the comparison, and what does it claim?
item.answer: They compare Miller with Tiffany. Miller's line extensions each need to be told apart from one another, so the brand uses an array of colour combinations, and in the process it loses the chance to differentiate its core brand from Budweiser, its key competitor — one of the many problems the authors attribute to those extensions is that they destroy the brand's colour identity. Tiffany, by contrast, holds a single colour and holds it even at Christmas when every other brand and retailer turns to red and green, which they say makes it more noticeable under the tree rather than less. The claim they draw is a wager about recall: you have probably seen many more Miller cans than Tiffany boxes, but they would bet you know the hue of a Tiffany box and are not quite sure about Miller's. item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 63, 65-66 (Ch. 12, 'The Law of the Generic')
item.question: What is the authors' mechanism for why a generic brand name cannot differentiate, and what does it imply about how naming decisions are usually made?
item.answer: Their mechanism is that the mind deals in sounds rather than letters. Most brand communication happens verbally — they claim the average person spends nine times as long listening to radio and television as reading print — and even the printed word is processed through the sound it generates, so a reader cannot hear the difference between "general" and "General". Capitalising a common word therefore does not make it a proper noun in a mind. What it implies about practice is the chapter's sharpest point: the naming process is usually conducted visually, with logotypes set in type, mounted on foamcore and passed round a boardroom, which is exactly the wrong sense for a decision that will be settled by ear. The same mechanism is their explanation for why line extensions fare poorly, since an extension typically pairs a brand name with a generic descriptor and the descriptor cannot create a separate identity — "Michelob Light" being heard as "Michelob light", a watered-down version of the regular beer.
item.support: Printed pp. 63 and 65-66. The nine-to-one listening ratio is cited without source and concerns media time, not name processing. The historical objection — that General Electric and its peers succeeded — is handled by asserting they succeeded in spite of their names because they were first.
confounders: assuming this is about descriptive versus suggestive marks in trademark practice; the concern here is retrieval from memory, not registrability
reading the Vaseline Intensive Care case as a counter-example the authors accept; they concede it and explain it as customers happening to treat the descriptor as a name
supposing the historical successes are counted against the law; they are reassigned to priority, so neither outcome can disconfirm it

source_terms: the star must appear as a star, not as a character playing a role
impersonation
personification
item.claim: Dwyer reports Barry King's distinction between two forms of acting — impersonation, where the actor transforms body and voice, and personification, where the actor's persona retains significant similarities across performances — and states that the latter is found most often in Hindi cinema. She draws the consequence for the image directly: personification "creates and maintains the star's text, RESTRICTING THE WAY IN WHICH AN IMAGE CAN BE PRESENTED," and melodrama reinforces this because "the star must appear as a star, not as a character playing a role."

mechanism.text: If the persona persists across films, then each image of the performer is read against the accumulated persona rather than only against the current role. The persona therefore becomes a constraint on what any single image is permitted to show, because an image that contradicts it reads as an error rather than as characterisation.

scope.conditions: Stated for Hindi cinema as against Hollywood, but Dwyer immediately qualifies the contrast: "it seems that there is little difference between the creation of the star in a Hindi film and in a Hollywood film," and says Hindi film stars seem to fit Dyer's theory of the star, "which has barely been challenged in twenty years."

caveats.text: Dwyer herself declines the strong culturally-specific reading of stardom, saying the Hindi star is created much as the Hollywood star is. The constraint is real; its Indian specificity is explicitly NOT claimed
no evidence is offered that images which violate a persona in fact fail; the constraint is asserted

item.source_locator: Essay 'Indian Traffic as Metaphor'
item.question: A brand plans to lead on safety in a market where no competitor does. What observation and what explanation does this source offer, and how much weight does each carry?
item.answer: The observation is that in India at the time of writing, 'not a single brand of vehicle is sold on the basis of safety'. The explanation is that safety is a meaningful proposition only for a buyer who accepts a link between an action and its consequence, which he argues Indian traffic conditions do not train — a benefit claim requires the audience to hold the premise that makes the benefit meaningful. The two carry very different weight. The observation is a checkable claim about a category's advertising, though it is an absolute stated with no supporting survey and it is dated — the essays are late-2000s columns and this is exactly the kind of claim that changes. The explanation is the author's interpretation, offered without evidence and embedded in a sustained metaphorical essay whose metaphysics of time the extraction does not take.
item.support: 'not a single brand of vehicle is sold on the basis of safety. The idea of safety is relevant only for those who acknowledge the relationship between cause and effect…'
item.confounders: It must never be used as a current market statement. The general shape — check whether the audience holds the enabling premise — is what survives.

source_terms: The Law of Extensions
The easiest way to destroy a brand is to put its name on everything.
management measures results with the wrong end of the ruler
item.claim: Law 10. The authors' central prohibition, stated in absolute terms. Their principal diagnostic is a measurement error: management measures only the success of the extension and never measures the erosion of the core brand, so the decision is taken on half the ledger. They add a second, subtler cost — foregone opportunity, since the new brand that could have been launched instead was not. Their test question for where an extension's volume comes from is directed at the core: they say a Coors Light drinker is more likely to have come from Coors than from a rival, and that after the three light beers launched, the three regular brands all declined substantially.

mechanism.text: Cannibalisation plus an accounting blind spot. The extension is nearest in the mind to its own parent, so it draws its volume from the parent rather than from competitors, while the management measurement system records only the extension's sales. The authors add "manufacturer logic" as the reason the error persists: when volume is flat the manufacturer concludes it needs more brands, and when the category is growing it concludes it does not — exactly the reverse, they say, of what the market requires.

scope.conditions: stated as a law without conditions; the demonstration material is US grocery, drug and beer

caveats.text: the Kroger scanner figures (23,000 items in a store, 5,500 selling nothing in a month) are third-party data reported second-hand with no method given, and they describe slow-moving stock, not the erosion of core brands that the law claims
'more than 90 percent of all new products introduced in the U.S. grocery and drug trade are line extensions' is cited without source and does not by itself say anything about whether extensions work

the beer case turns on the assertion that the three regular brands declined because of the light launches; no comparison group and no other cause is considered, and the authors themselves note a real market shift from regular to light beer
the authors state the shift from regular to light is genuine and say it is 'really two markets' — which is a concession that the demand the extensions served was real

source_terms: To get into the consumer's mind you have to sacrifice.

item.claim: The authors ground the one-word rule in a capacity argument about minds. The average adult knows perhaps fifty thousand words while some two and a half million trademarks are registered in the United States, so a brand cannot expect to be associated with a list of attributes; it is a physical impossibility for most brands to go beyond a single word. source_terms: Official Marketing Bullshit mode
stop 'writing ads'; don't write, talk
the bar stool test
item.claim: Sullivan holds that being asked to write for publication makes most people adopt a scholarly, authoritative register in the belief it is more persuasive than plain English, and that the resulting voice communicates nothing. He supplies a portable diagnostic: imagine sitting with a friend in a bar who asks why they should use the product, and try to say your line to her face with a straight expression. Copy that cannot survive that delivery has failed. He demonstrates with a real 143-word corporate memo whose entire content was a nine-word sentence, and with the generic restaurant line he says most briefs produce.

mechanism.text: The test works by changing the audience from an imagined public to a specific person who can react. Sullivan's stated reason is that the register is adopted for an audience the writer cannot see, and that a visible listener makes its emptiness audible. He recommends the same move structurally — write the copy as a letter to one named person, then delete the salutation — reporting that this was how a famous brand voice was actually produced.

scope.conditions: any brand copy; the source applies it to headlines, body copy and brand voice alike

caveats.text: the bar-stool test detects a register failure but says nothing about whether the claim is true or the strategy right; the source does not claim otherwise but the test is easily over-read
the conversational register he prescribes is itself a convention of a particular market and period, not a neutral default

source_stated_problems: we seem to default to a kind of Official Marketing Bullshit mode we think sounds impressive but actually telegraphs overly packaged half-truths
four out of five people decide a scholarly and authoritarian tone is somehow more persuasive than clear English
companies that speak in the language of the pitch, the dog-and-pony show, are no longer speaking to anyone
source_stated_remedies: pretend you're talking to an actual human being who's capable of detecting bullshit
write like people talk; obey the rules of grammar and go easy on the adjectives
pretend you're writing a letter — put 'Dear Charlie' at the top and your name at the bottom, then delete them

positive.description: the reported method behind a famous car brand's copy voice: written as a letter to a named friend, then with the salutation and sign-off removed

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 87-88 (Ch. 17, 'The Law of Color', the Maxion tractor case)
item.question: A new entrant in a category where the leader owns the category's natural colour asks which colour to take. Apply the authors' rule, and state the trade they say you should accept.
item.answer: Take the colour opposite the major competitor's, not the one symbolic of the category — the leader has first choice, and the leader normally takes the symbolic colour. Their own worked case is a Brazilian tractor brand they named Maxion. John Deere, the leading tractor brand, had green, the colour of grass and agriculture; the second brand had red; so they made Maxion blue. The trade they say to accept is stated plainly: is blue a good colour for a farm tractor? No — but it is more important to create a separate brand identity than to use the right symbolic colour. They run the same logic through car rental (Hertz yellow, so Avis red, National green) and hold up Pepsi as the counter-case, having taken red and blue together and so struggled for decades against a world that seems awash in Coca-Cola red. They add that whatever colour is chosen must be held consistently over years, which is their reading of the Tiffany box.
item.support: Printed pp. 87-89. The rule and the trade are the authors'; the chapter's physiological justification — wavelengths focusing behind or in front of the retina — is offered without a source and does not support the cultural colour meanings the chapter derives from it. The associations listed are Western conventions.
confounders: choosing the category-symbolic colour for recognisability, which is the move the passage explicitly rejects for a non-leader
assuming the leader's rule and the follower's rule are the same; the chapter separates them, and only the leader is told to take the symbolic colour
reading the red/blue physiology as established; it is asserted, and the emotional readings drawn from it are conventions rather than consequences of optics

item.label: the_mail_order_copy_prescriptions
item.description: The concrete copy rules chapter 4 draws from mail order practice: small type, every line utilised, no borders, no palaver or entertainment, a coupon because readers forget, pictures that earn their space, the complete story, returns that scale with fully used space, and the long-running unchanged advertisement as the model — closed by the concession that advertisers routinely depart from all of it for pride, and should at least price the departure.

whole_system_claim.text: These are not independent craft preferences. Every one of them is warranted by the same argument — that mail order advertising is continuously measured, so whatever mail order advertisers do universally has been selected by results — and each is therefore only as sound as that argument is.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states each prescription separately and repeats the phrase "in mail order advertising" at the head of most of them, and it states the warrant once at the start of the chapter. It never says that the prescriptions stand or fall together. Grouping them by their shared warrant is ours, and it is the property that matters, because the warrant is inference from observed practice rather than a reported comparison — only the incubator picture case carries an actual before-and-after result.

source_terms: Most retail category killers follow the same five-step pattern.

item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.source_locator: printed p. 185, tip 13 'Be consistent'
item.question: Whose responsibility does Airey say brand style guides are, and what chain of consequences does he attach to consistency?
item.answer: The designer's — he states that many logos are accompanied by style guides and that creating them is your responsibility. Their function is to make sure anyone inside the client's company who uses the design does so consistently. The chain he attaches is two links and he states it compactly: consistency breeds trust, and trust wins customers. He makes the same claim in the earlier chapter, that the same visual identity seen over and over generates trust and trust makes customers come back for more, and his historical case is the Kellogg signature, used on the front of every packet since 1906. Neither link is evidenced; Kellogg is a survivorship case with a century of confounded marketing behind it.

item.label: the_twenty_two_immutable_laws_of_branding
item.description: The twenty-two named laws, numbered and titled by the authors, each opening with a one-line epigram beneath its chapter title. The book presents them as a body, not as a list: laws are invoked by name inside other laws' chapters, one law is described as the biggest exception to the rest, another is introduced by conceding what "the laws seem to suggest" before departing from it, and one pair is given an explicit temporal order. What the authors do NOT claim anywhere in this span is that the laws are independent, mutually exclusive, or ranked; the numbering is presentational and only once is a law given an ordinal ("the first law of branding, the law of expansion", printed p. 91). Nor do they claim a procedure for applying them in sequence. The set is asserted to be universal — the Introduction says the laws apply equally to the Internet and the real world — while three chapters inside it limit that assertion.

whole_system_claim.text: The twenty-two laws cannot be read as twenty-two separable rules, because several of them are stated as qualifications of others and at least three pairs point in opposite directions without the book reconciling them. Read singly, a law will mislead: the Law of Contraction taken alone tells a retailer to dominate its category, while the Law of Fellowship and the Law of the Category both cap a leading brand at about half of it; the Law of Advertising tells a leader to smother competitors while the Law of Fellowship tells it to welcome them; the Law of Consistency says brands should never change while the Law of Change says they can. The set behaves as a body of mutually qualifying practitioner advice in which the reader supplies the judgement about which law governs a given case — and the book supplies no criterion for that judgement. Anyone using these laws must therefore hold the qualifying partner of each law alongside it.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states the membership, the names and the epigrams; it states that the Law of Change is the biggest exception to the laws of branding (printed p. 101); it states that the laws are immutable while brands are not (p. 105); it states what the laws seem to suggest about single-brand concentration and then licenses a second brand (p. 77); and it invokes laws by name inside other chapters (pp. 35, 39, 56, 60, 91). All of that is the authors'. What is OURS is the characterisation of the whole as mutual qualification, the identification of the three unreconciled conflicts recorded below, and the conclusion that a law read alone will mislead. The authors nowhere say their laws conflict, and they nowhere tell the reader to hold a law's qualifying partner alongside it. Do not attribute that instruction to them.

dependencies: Law 2 (Contraction) is the positive statement of Law 1 (Expansion); the authors restate the pair as a single sentence at printed p. 47 — expand and you reduce power, contract and you increase it

Law 8 (Category) is explicitly derived from Law 2 in its opening sentence: 'according to the law of contraction a brand becomes stronger when you narrow its focus. What happens when you narrow the focus to such a degree that there is no longer any market?' (printed p. 39)
Law 7 (Quality) is explicitly derived from the others: 'the best way to build a quality perception in the mind is by following the laws of branding. Take the law of contraction' (printed p. 35)
Law 11 (Fellowship) invokes Law 1 by name — 'the law of expansion suggests the opposite' (printed p. 56) — and points the reader forward to Law 15 for shares above fifty per cent (printed p. 60)
Law 18 (Borders) invokes Law 1 by name as 'the first law of branding' (printed p. 91)
Law 4 (Advertising) refers the reader back to Law 3's chapter by number (printed p. 19)
Law 12 (Generic) supplies the naming mechanism for Law 10's prohibition on extensions (printed p. 65)
Law 6 (Credentials) depends on Law 8: a brand without leadership is told to invent a category in which it can claim it (printed p. 30)
tradeoffs: short-term sales against long-term brand meaning — the authors' own framing of Law 1, and the trade that most of the book turns on (sk_r22_0006)
focus against growth — the pressure that produces every violation the book records; the authors permit four answers to it and forbid one (see scs_r22_003)
a brand's interests against its owner's: at printed p. 25 the authors say Federal Express's expansion hurts the brand and may not hurt the company, which concedes the two can come apart
conflicts: DOMINATION AGAINST THE SHARE CEILING. Law 2's five-step pattern names 'dominate the category' as the ultimate objective of any branding programme and cites 95, 80 and 70 per cent approvingly (printed pp. 10-11), while Law 8 states that a leading brand's rightful share is never more than 50 per cent (p. 42) and Law 11 gives about 50 per cent as the researched upper limit (p. 60). The book never addresses the conflict, and the Coca-Cola figure differs between the two passages without comment. UNRESOLVED — recorded, not adjudicated.

SMOTHER AGAINST WELCOME. Law 4 tells a leader to use massive advertising to smother the competition and make competitors pay through the nose (printed p. 21); Law 11 tells the dominant brand to welcome competitors because they build the category (p. 56). Both are stated as laws. UNRESOLVED.

NEVER CHANGE AGAINST CHANGE CAREFULLY. Law 19 says markets may change but brands should not, ever (printed p. 97); Law 20 opens by saying nothing in branding is absolute and sets out three situations in which a brand can be changed (p. 101), and names itself the biggest exception to the laws of branding. The authors present this as a stated exception rather than a conflict, but they give no criterion for identifying which of the three situations a brand is in. RECORDED AS THE AUTHORS' OWN EXCEPTION.

ONE BRAND AGAINST A FAMILY. Law 2 and Law 22 point to a single narrowly focused brand; Law 15 opens by conceding that the laws seem to require exactly that, agreeing it is true, and then licensing a second, third and fourth brand (printed p. 77). Again an authors' concession, with no test for when the 'time and place' has come.

NARROWING AGAINST STOCKING IN DEPTH. Inside Law 2 itself, step 1 is to narrow the focus and step 2 is to stock the narrowed category in depth — ten thousand toys against a department store's three thousand (printed p. 10). The brand contracts what it is about while expanding what it carries, and the book does not say where one stops and the other begins.

THE WORD AGAINST THE VISUAL. Laws 16 and 17 devote two of the twenty-two to logotype and colour while both chapters argue that the visual is secondary and the meaning lies in the word (printed pp. 84-85).

item.source_warning_ref: printed p. 101 — 'nothing in life, nothing in branding, is ever absolute. There are always exceptions to every rule. And the law of change is the biggest exception to the laws of branding.' Also printed p. 77 and p. 105. This is the closest the source comes to warning against isolated use; it is not framed as such a warning.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The membership, the names, the numbering, the epigrams and every cross-reference listed under dependencies are the SOURCE'S. The classification as mutual_qualification, the six conflicts, the three trade-offs and the whole_system_claim are OURS. The authors never say their laws conflict; on the contrary the Introduction asserts them as universally applicable. Any downstream reader should treat the conflicts as this lane's reading of the text — checkable against the pages cited, since each conflict is a pair of passages, but a reading nonetheless. And the word "immutable" carries no evidential weight anywhere in this system: the entire set rests on selected corporate anecdote, and the book reports no measurement of its own (see sk_r22_0049 and PROVENANCE.md §6-7).

source_terms: Many pioneers in a line establish large demands. Then, through some fault in their foundations, lose a large share of the harvest.

Vaseline is an example. That product established a new demand, then almost monopolized that demand through wisdom at the start. To have called it some brand of petroleum jelly might have made a difference of millions in results.

item.claim: Substitution is a structural exposure that must be closed before a campaign begins, not argued away afterwards. The source states that many pioneers establish large demand and then, through some fault in their foundations, lose a large share of the harvest — typically because what they built was a mere brand where it might have stood for an exclusive product. Vaseline is given as the counter-case: it established a new demand and almost monopolised it through wisdom at the start, and calling it some brand of petroleum jelly might have made a difference of millions. Royal Baking Powder, Toasted Corn Flakes and Horlick's Malted Milk are named as pioneers who left the way open to perpetual substitution. The prescription is foresight to see all eventualities and defences established in advance.

mechanism.text: A pioneer creates demand that attaches to whatever name the market can use for the thing. If that name is available to everyone, competitors inherit the demand the pioneer paid for; if it is exclusive, they cannot.

scope.conditions: products that create a new category and must own the demand they create

"To have called it some brand of petroleum jelly MIGHT have made a difference of millions" is an untestable counterfactual, and the failures are diagnosed by the same reasoning that the successes are explained by. The chapter contains no case where an exclusive name failed or a generic name succeeded.

source_terms: One cannot establish or claim an advantage on natural or standard products.

Its stated diagnosis of the category was that dominance was not produced by advertising at all — certain brands held certain markets for years against every effort to displace them, and the only apparent reason was familiarity. Its conclusion was therefore not to argue superiority but to manufacture familiarity, and it redirected the campaign accordingly.

source_terms: The first stage of this process is to find a universal width increment that all of the optimally styled text specimens can share.
This universal increment will be the column width.
item.claim: Once each kind of text has been styled optimally, the column width is derived from them rather than chosen. Find a universal width increment that all the optimally styled specimens can share: stack them left-aligned, draw guides at their left edges and at each specimen's longest line, then shift the long-line guides slightly to discover a fractional relationship between the styles' widths — the caption perhaps one half or one third of the running text. Combine those fractions, splitting differences where needed, to yield a single width increment that governs every style as a multiple of itself: two for the caption, four for running text and so on. That increment is the column width. The fastest version compares only the narrowest and widest specimens, usually caption and headline; but running text is the most important style because it appears in the greatest volume and its readability matters most, so narrowest, widest and running text should be compared, and comparing all of them is better still.

mechanism.text: If every style's width is a whole multiple of one increment, every style can be placed on the same column structure without any of them being distorted to fit it.

source_terms: The Law of Advertising

item.claim: Law 4. The authors assign advertising a purely defensive role for an established leader. source_terms: Everyone is equal
HiPPO (Highest Paid Person's Opinion); it's a killer when it comes to effective critique
it isn't inherently true that their opinions are more accurate just because they're executives
item.claim: The first of the source's four rules holds that in a critique everyone's observations are listened to equally, and that more attention must not be paid to a perspective because of the speaker's position. The argument is careful: the authors concede that an organisation may legitimately make its decisions on what its leaders think, but deny that seniority makes an observation more accurate, and insist the two be kept separate and sequenced — "we want to keep that separate, and hopefully after a critique." The named harm is suppression: where participants sense inequality they either stay quiet or go along with what was already said, and the group loses information. Crucially the authors state the rule must hold in both directions — contributors must also see themselves and others as equal contributors. The remedies are behavioural: ask quiet people directly during the session, speak to a weight-throwing participant afterwards, and, in Adam's practice, call a break to raise the problem with the organisation's leaders present. Weighing expertise is permitted, but later, when the collected feedback is reviewed.

mechanism.text: Deference removes independent observations from the pool before they are voiced, so the session's output is narrower than the room's actual knowledge. Separating collection from decision preserves the observations while leaving the organisation's authority structure intact for the decision that follows.

scope.conditions: a session including participants of differing organisational seniority

caveats.text: the authors concede the rule is hard to implement depending on culture, and that it is a 'key element' rather than an achievable default
they note that many executives do not want the deference and have helped address it when asked — which is an observation about the executives they worked with, not a general finding
the rule concerns the weight given during collection; it explicitly permits expertise to be weighted afterwards, which is a distinction easy to lose when the rule is quoted alone

they might decide to just go along with the feedback expressed by someone else instead of voicing their own perspectives
source_stated_remedies: if you notice that people are being quiet because of a 'superior's' participation, ask for feedback directly from those people
as we review the feedback collected, we can take into consideration an individual's expertise and experience, and not focus solely on her position in the hierarchy

source_terms: Most importantly, the scooter hid the machine from view. Unlike the bike, which revels in displaying its muscular architecture, the scooter covers up the beast within with rotund blandness.

item.claim: Desai's central reading of the scooter is that it signifies by concealment and by refusal: it hides its machinery under a rounded shell where the motorcycle displays its architecture, and it means what it means precisely by advertising its *lack* of ambition. An object can therefore carry meaning by what it declines to claim as much as by what it asserts, and the decision to show or hide the mechanism is one of the carriers.
