The physical facts — the scooter's enclosing bodywork, the motorcycle's exposed engine — are uncontroversial; the argument that the enclosure is a social signal, and that refusal signifies, is interpretive throughout, and is developed in a sustained metaphorical passage ("if the bike is an untamed stallion, the scooter a recalcitrant mule").

item.claim: A structure's intervals may be sourced from outside the page. item.claim: The source's constructive rule, and the sharpest usable test in the book: the thing you want transmitted must be load-bearing in the story, such that removing it makes the story unretellable or unfunny. item.claim: Sullivan offers a two-step generator he says he has watched work repeatedly in teaching, while explicitly refusing to call it a rule. Step one: state the truest thing that can be said about the brand — which he notes is almost never in the brief, because it is usually the thing clients are taught to deny or minimise. The first is operational and the third is political — a simple mark is cheap-looking in the sense that matters when a newspaper is costing your identity programme. item.question: What argument do the authors give for why a brand cannot own more than one word, and what is the problem with the two quantities they compare?
item.answer: They give a capacity argument. The average adult knows the meanings of perhaps fifty thousand words, while about two and a half million trademarks are registered in the United States, and from that they conclude it is a physical impossibility for most brands to go beyond a single word — a limit they say could only be lifted if science replaced brain tissue with silicon chips. The problem is that the two figures are not comparable quantities. One is an individual person's vocabulary; the other is a national register of legal marks, the overwhelming majority of which no individual will ever encounter. source_terms: If you don't have anything nice to say, don't say anything at all

item.claim: The source names a bias that operates on the supply of judgement itself and a matching error in reading it. On the supply side: people raised to withhold anything not nice hold back honest critique they fear will upset the recipient, or worse, validate a direction they do not believe in. On the reading side: in cultures where challenging or speaking up is seen as rude, silence is not agreement, and participants who assume it is will record a consensus that does not exist; conversely, participants used to straightforwardness can be misread as combative. Adam's own account is of a project with a team from India where he repeatedly discovered afterwards that the alignment he thought he had seen in meetings was not there, and that where he thought there had been disagreement there had been none. item.claim: Sullivan holds that a brand story requires an opposing force, and that most briefs remove it. item.question: Where do the authors bound their own Law of Fellowship, and what is the weakest link in the case they use to bound it?
item.answer: They bound it at the point where choice becomes confusion: customers can have too much choice, and the more brands, flavours and varieties, the more confusion in the category and the lower the consumption per head. They name two major brands per category as apparently ideal and give five paired examples. Their case for the failure mode is wine — more than a thousand wineries and five thousand brands in California alone, an annual magazine ranking some twenty-four thousand individual wines, and no major brand having emerged. The weakest link is the inference they draw from American consumption being a tenth of France's, a ninth of Italy's and under a third of Germany's. That comparison is cited without source and is used to make brand structure the cause of low consumption, with no consideration of drinking culture, licensing, taxation, price, climate or history — any of which a reader would reach for first. The five ideal pairs are also the five categories that fit.

item.question: The authors say a leader should advertise its leadership rather than its superiority. Set out the loop they describe, and explain why they say leadership claims are nevertheless rare.
item.answer: The loop: everyone believes the better product wins in the marketplace; most people want the better product, so most people buy the leading brand; buying it keeps it the leader; and its leadership sustains the perception that it is better. The claims land differently for that reason — "our product is better" gets the response "that's what they all say", while "our product is the leader" gets "it must be better". Leadership is the one premise a prospect will accept on the advertiser's word, because it is a fact about the market rather than a claim about the product. Such claims are rare, they say, because companies do consumer research and customers insist they would never buy a brand just because it leads, going out of their way to deny it and saying instead that they buy it because it is better. The authors treat the stated reason as unreliable and the circle as real; they also root the whole inference in an American belief that the better product always wins.

item.question: A brand has a fact about its product that is genuinely useful and that nobody ever repeats. Berger's diagnosis is not that the fact is dull. What is it, and what does his contrasting case show?
item.answer: The diagnosis is that the fact has no occasion. His example is a sandwich chain's low-fat range: the information is practically valuable to someone trying to lose weight, but nobody walks up to a friend and states it — it would be strange and out of context, and unless weight loss is already the topic or something has cued it, it never comes up. People do not think in terms of information, they think in terms of narratives, so the fact needs a carrier. His contrast is the story of one man losing 245 pounds while eating at that chain, which people bring up even when weight loss is not the subject, because the story is worth telling for its own sake. Listeners take away four things about the brand — that it has healthy options, healthy enough to lose weight on, a lot of weight, and food someone could eat for three months and still want. item.claim: Law 17. The authors give a rule with an order of precedence. The leader in a category should take the colour most symbolic of the category. item.question: Hopkins advised a client against advertising a standard product on a superiority basis. What is his stated reason, what did he do instead, and where does this sit against his own commonplace-facts doctrine?
item.answer: His reason is that one cannot establish or claim an advantage on natural or standard products — evaporated milk was made to government requirements — and he names eggs, butter, lard, flour and oatmeal as the same case, saying many millions have been wasted trying to tie people to a brand of a staple. His diagnosis of the category was that dominance there was not produced by advertising at all: certain brands held certain markets for years against every effort to displace them, and the only apparent reason was familiarity. So instead of arguing superiority he set out to manufacture familiarity. Where it sits is awkwardly: his commonplace-facts doctrine at printed pp. 79-82 was applied to beer and to canned beans, both arguably standard products. He does not draw the line, and the practical difference appears to be whether the production process is unfamiliar enough to the public to be worth publishing. Note also that the advice was not taken as stated — the campaign ran on the familiarity basis instead, so the rule itself was never tested.

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed p. 10 (Ch. 2, 'The Law of Contraction', the five-step pattern)
item.question: Give the five steps the authors say most retail category killers follow, in their order. Then identify the tension that steps 2 and 5 create with step 1 — a tension the book does not address.
item.answer: Narrow the focus; stock in depth; buy cheap; sell cheap; dominate the category. The authors chain them causally: narrowing permits depth, depth permits buying power, buying power permits low prices at maintained margin, and the result is domination, which they call the ultimate objective of any branding programme. The tension is that steps 2 and 5 are both expansions. Step 2 widens assortment inside the narrowed category — a Toys "R" Us store carrying ten thousand toys against a department store's three thousand — and step 5 enlarges the brand's share of it, with Microsoft at 95 per cent, Intel at 80 and Coca-Cola at 70 cited approvingly on the following page. So the brand contracts what it is about while expanding what it carries and how much of the category it takes, and the book never says where narrowing stops and depth begins. The domination figures also sit against the roughly 50 per cent ceiling the same authors state twice later.

item.claim: Law 11. The dominant brand should not merely tolerate competitors but welcome them, because competition raises the noise level, makes customers more conscious of the category, and lifts consumption per head. item.answer: First, a publicity stunt at the 2004 Olympics: a man in a tutu and polka-dot tights with an online casino's name across his chest interrupted the diving. Millions watched, news outlets worldwide covered it, and the word of mouth was enormous — about Olympic security, about the Chinese divers who flubbed their next dive, about the perpetrator's trial. Nobody talked about the casino. Second, a bottled-water brand's roller-skating babies film: more than 50 million views and declared by Guinness the most viewed online advertisement in history, and the same year the brand lost market share and sales fell almost 25 percent. What the two have in common is that the sponsor was irrelevant to the content — a tutu and roller-skating babies are great story material and neither has anything to do with a casino or with water. There is a big difference between people talking about content and people talking about the company that made it.

item.claim: The source gives a typographic rule grounded in habituation rather than in legibility science. Ordinary reading of the period was done in 8-point type; most mail-order advertisers had adopted 6-point, and the source says advertisers nonetheless use larger type, that it does not know the theory, and that anyone tracing results can quickly prove oversize type does not pay because doubling the necessary space doubles the cost. Its argument is that the easiest type to read is the ordinary and anything unusual presents difficulty; if the story is interesting people will read it in the type they are used to, and if it is not they will not read it in any size. It applies the same reasoning to capitals: all reading is done in upper and lower case, so lines set in capitals have to be studied out, which it calls not a severe handicap but always a detriment. It attributes large type to advertisers demanding attention rather than inducing it.

mechanism.text: Reading is a habit, and deviation from the habitual form imposes effort on the reader. The cost is therefore twofold — the reader works harder and the advertiser buys more space — while the benefit, attention demanded rather than induced, does not convert.

scope.conditions: Attributed to a global study of 11,000 ads dated April 2021; the source does not state the markets, categories, ad formats, lengths or comparison baseline behind either figure.

caveats.text: The three Google pages phrase the identical finding differently and the difference is not cosmetic. Google Ads Help says "Deliver as much as a 30% lift ... and a 17% lift", which is an upper bound. Think with Google says "On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift ... and a 17% lift", which is a central tendency. The Google for Business resources article prints the two numbers as bare callouts ("30% lift in short-term sales likelihood", "17% lift in long-term brand contribution") with no qualifier at all, above a page-footer line reading "Actual results will vary by advertiser". An upper bound and an average are different statistics. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved; nothing in any of the three pages settles which is correct.

Citation detail also differs by page. Only the Google for Business resources article gives the sample size, "n=11,000 ads". Google Ads Help gives the same study, publisher, scope and month with no sample size. Think with Google cites it as "Google/Kantar Link AI, Global, The Short and the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, 2021" — naming Kantar's Link AI, dropping the month and giving no sample size.

The underlying study is not published on any of the three pages and is not linked. No method, comparison baseline, definition of "short-term sales likelihood" or "long-term brand contribution", confidence interval or dispersion is given. These are reported results, but they are reported by an interested party from a study the source does not let the reader inspect.

item.question: You are briefed to make a wordmark for a new prepaid-billing product with no existing recognition, to be used at favicon size, on a dark dashboard, in a one-colour invoice header, and on printed collateral. Which of Airey's requirements bind hardest here, and where does his advice stop being usable?
item.answer: Four bind hard and they compound. The dark dashboard and the one-colour header together mean the mark must be designed for the reduced case, not adapted to it: he requires a supplied one-colour version (tip 15) and a version that works on dark backgrounds (tip 19), and his generation argument at printed p. 30 says to work only in black and white anyway, because contrast puts the emphasis on the shape and colour is secondary to form. Favicon size is the extreme of his "think small" case — he names the favicon explicitly as the small end of the media range, and his one-inch rule with no loss of detail sets the floor. And because the brand is unknown, tip 12's legibility gate applies at full strength by his own scoping — if most people cannot read it straight away, do not use it as a logo. Where his advice stops being usable: he gives no threshold for the dark-ground case beyond "clearly identified", no test for whether a mark survives reversal at all, nothing about screen rendering below one inch, and no way to administer the legibility gate — no population, no exposure time, no distance. Everything past those points is your judgement and must not be attributed to him.
item.support: Printed p. 30 (work in black; colour secondary to form), p. 34 (think small; favicon; one inch), p. 185 (legibility gate and its scoping clause), p. 186 (one-colour version), pp. 187-188 (contrast; reverse it). The gaps named are gaps in the source, not omissions from the answer.

treating the dark-ground and one-colour requirements as delivery formats rather than as constraints on the design
dropping the legibility gate because the mark is a wordmark; the unknown-brand condition is exactly when he says it binds hardest

source_terms: morphing change
molting change
Force = Mass x Acceleration
change confluence
item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a framework for reading change in this market, built on a distinction she draws: MOLTING change, in which the old is shed for the new like a snake's skin, against MORPHING change, slow and from within, "like an amoeba which, with every tiny particle it ingests, infinitesimally changes shape." She argues Indian change is of the second kind and gives the reason in a physics analogy: since Force = Mass x Acceleration, "a small acceleration (small changes over long periods of time) can also unleash a large force of change, if the mass that is changing is very large." She names the detection problem it creates — "this change is not visible through the usual run of the mill 'usage and attitude' type surveys that most companies ritualistically engage in" — and reports the executive's experience: watching for change annually and finding none worth mentioning, then five years later finding the market distinctly different and asking "when did we blink and not see this happening?" Her proposed unit of observation is the CHANGE CONFLUENCE: a collection of individually insignificant changes occurring simultaneously, which together reshape a market.

mechanism.text: An instrument that reports a rate per period will report a small number every period when the per-period change is small, regardless of how large the accumulated change becomes or how large the population it applies to. The change is therefore invisible to the instrument and visible only in the cumulative state, which is why it is discovered retrospectively.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets. The Force = Mass x Acceleration formulation is an analogy, and the author uses it as one.

caveats.text: the physics analogy is rhetorical. Nothing is multiplied and no quantity is computed; it is a memorable way of saying that a small rate over a large base is a large absolute number. It should not be mistaken for a model

the bicycle case that anchors the argument — a declining share explained by a confluence of rising rural incomes, a younger and more school-going buyer, better public transport and widened geographic footprints — is told without dates, figures or client, and without saying whether the recommended response worked. The author reports the category's subsequent state as unresolved: 'it appears that the traditional bicycle has had its day, and the new one has not yet been innovated to everyone's satisfaction'
no method is offered for detecting a change confluence prospectively. The two worked cases are both retrospective diagnoses, which is precisely the failure the object describes

source_terms: an enabling technique rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation

item.claim: Jain reports Geeta Kapur's observation, and builds on it, that "realism" was construed in nineteenth-century Indian discourse "to mean an ENABLING TECHNIQUE rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation within a specific historical context." She draws the distinction out: there is a difference between naturalist TECHNIQUES — perspective, anatomy, modelling, the rendering of light and shadow — and the institutionally sanctioned "post-sacred" schemata of signification through which they entered the colonial context: romanticism and the picturesque, neoclassicism, bourgeois realism, ethnographic documentation. The techniques were taken up; the schemata largely were not. She records the vernacular word some artists used instead of the English "realism" — sajivta, "livingness" or "lifelikeness" — and states what it puts at issue: "at issue here is not the reality of the gods, but how alive they are: how the image brings them to life."

mechanism.text: A technique and the worldview that historically carried it are separable, because a technique is a way of making marks and a worldview is a set of commitments about what marks are for. Where the receiving context has its own commitments, the technique can be adopted to serve those instead. Jain's instance: naturalist modelling was taken up not in its techno-rationalist aspect but in its "personalizing, affective, libidinal aspect, making the divine accessible to devotees as an empathetic presence."

scope.conditions: Nineteenth and twentieth century Indian commercial image-making, principally chromolithography, Nathdwara and the calendar industry.

caveats.text: Jain positions this against Christopher Pinney's account of a 'naturalist blip' between 1878 and 1927 and against readings that align naturalism with disenchantment. She is arguing with named colleagues, and the object should be read as her position in a live scholarly disagreement rather than as settled fact
the separability claim is historical and interpretive. No mechanism is tested; the evidence is the pattern of what was and was not adopted

the same chapter shows the separation is not clean in practice: artists trained in anatomy report frustration at being unable to use it, and 'realism' in their discourse is, in Jain's words, 'an often contradictory, highly overdetermined term'

item.label: composition_techniques_subordinated_to_the_essence_test
item.description: The nine composition spreads — leading lines, internal framing, foreground interest, proximity, symmetry, thirds, working the frame, visual weight — together with the closing spread that tells the reader to break them. Read as a system, the techniques are the lower layer and the essence test is the layer above, deciding when the lower layer applies.

whole_system_claim.text: The composition techniques are a default that produces a settled, competent reading, and the essence test overrides them: where the subject is not settled, a settled composition misdescribes it, and the same features that are ordinarily faults become the means of a true reading. The techniques therefore have no standing of their own — each is in force only until the subject gives a reason to break it.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Carroll never states this as a system. He presents nine independent spreads, then a tenth spread which calls them "essential building blocks", warns that too much of them makes photographs "safe and predictable", names the rule of thirds specifically as breakable, and tells the reader to concentrate instead on capturing "the essence of your subject". The two-layer structure — techniques below, essence test above — is our reading of that sequence. Two facts make the reading contestable and are recorded rather than smoothed over: Carroll leaves symmetry (centre the subject) and thirds (do not centre the subject) side by side without ranking them, and the essence test as he states it is unfalsifiable, since any broken rule can be justified after the fact by asserting the discomfort suits the subject.

dependencies.nature: the essence test is stated with the rule of thirds named as breakable
leading lines are named among the building blocks the test may override

tradeoffs.nature: isolating one region against accounting for the whole frame

item.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Essential Exception
item.question: Name the categories W3C gives for the Essential exception to SC 1.4.11, and state the underlying principle that unites them.
item.answer: The principle is destructive interference: the exception is intended to apply where there is no way of presenting the graphic with sufficient contrast without undermining the meaning. Since the remedy for low contrast is to change colours, the exception covers cases where changing colours destroys what the graphic exists to carry. The named categories are logos and logotypes, presented in a brand's specific colours; flags, which may not be identifiable if their colours are changed; sensory content — the source states there is no requirement to change pictures of real-life scenes such as photos of people or scenery; and things that cannot be represented any other way, for which it names screenshots demonstrating how a website appeared, medical diagrams using the colours found in biology, and colour gradients representing a measurement such as heat maps. As with the logo case, the exception is an exemption from a requirement, not a finding that these graphics are easily perceived.

source_terms: Deformation and Distortion
altering the actual shapes of columns and rows produces a compositional effect that is far more organic, where the orthogonal underpinning of the base grid's structure becomes less apparent
Pulling edges of columns and rows out of parallel alignment emphasizes diagonal axes.

item.claim: In contrast to splicing and shifting, which keep the orthogonal frame, altering the actual shapes of columns and rows produces a far more organic effect in which the orthogonal underpinning becomes less apparent. Pulling edges out of parallel alignment emphasises diagonal axes; deformed structures may sit side by side as though on one surface, or be shifted and rotated to move over and under each other. Deformation often produces an illusion of perspective as the new angles converge, and that illusion is greatly enhanced if the content inside the columns changes in size or spacing to correspond with the perceived near-to-far position. Columns and rows may also be deformed curvilinearly — circles, waves or free-form organic shapes — not only angularly.

item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Make People Feel Like Insiders' (spine 6)
item.question: Berger distinguishes scarcity from exclusivity, which are usually run together. What is the distinction, and what does he insist about what can serve as the basis for exclusivity?
item.answer: Scarcity restricts HOW MUCH is offered — through high demand, limited production, or limits on the time or place something can be acquired. Exclusivity restricts WHO may have it, by criteria. His insistence is that the criterion need not be money or celebrity: exclusivity is also about knowledge — knowing certain information, or being connected to people who do. That is why a bar with no sign, reachable only through a phone booth inside a hot dog restaurant, is exclusive without being expensive, and why an invitation-only site is exclusive in a way money cannot purchase. Both raise perceived desirability, by two inferences he names: difficulty of acquisition is read as evidence of worth, and unavailability is read as evidence that many other people wanted it.

item.question: Sullivan reports a four-step participation sequence and one bounding condition that is easy to skip. Give the sequence, say which step he calls the hard one, and give the condition.
item.answer: Edward Boches's sequence: do something really interesting that communicates the value of your brand; conceive the idea so people can participate and find a way to invite them in; capture what is created or document the event so it lives beyond it; and make it shareable across every relevant channel. He names the first step as the hard one, because it cannot be an advertisement — it has to be, in his phrase, radioactively creative — and it is where his idea-worth-advertising reframe applies. The bounding condition, quoted from Scott Prindle, is about the exchange: whenever you ask customers for time or effort you must come through with a payoff, and it needs to be equal to or greater in value than the time contributed, or usage rates are very low.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 'Logotypes' and 'Incidental' exceptions
item.question: WCAG says logotype text "has no contrast requirement". What exactly does that sentence assert, and what does it not assert?
item.answer: It asserts that the criterion does not apply — the text is removed from the scope of the measurement. It does not assert that the text is readable, that it is readable enough, or that its contrast is acceptable. The standard withdraws its test; it does not certify the outcome. The same reading applies to the Incidental group: text in an inactive user interface component, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, and text inside a picture with significant other visual content all have "no contrast requirement" in exactly this sense. The source's own non-normative notes make the gap explicit for logos: the exemption is granted on the assumption that logos must comply with stricter colour choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines, and the notes go on to call the situation problematic when a logo also acts as a user interface component, recommending a higher-contrast variant or an equivalent control. An evaluator should therefore record such cases as excluded, not as passed.
item.support: Normative — the "Logotypes" and "Incidental" exceptions in SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6. The rationale and the best-practice recommendation are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent", and Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Logos".

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed p. 99 (Chapter Nine, 'Try Our Rivals, Too')
item.question: Faced with substitution once imitators arrived, rival advertisers insisted on their own brands. Hopkins did the opposite. What did he do, what is his stated reading of why it worked, and what does the move presuppose?
item.answer: He came out with headlines urging readers to buy the named competing brands and compare them with his own. His stated reading is that the willingness to invite comparison is itself the evidence: if we were certain enough of our advantage to invite such comparisons, people were certain enough to buy. So the operative effect is the buyer's inference from a costly signal — directing a buyer to a rival is expensive to fake — rather than the comparison itself. He reports the rivals' brand insistence fell on deaf ears. What it presupposes is a genuine advantage, or at least a strongly held claim; and here his own account of the category cuts against him, since he says the product was materially like its rivals and that in a blind serving of half a dozen brands nobody present could identify it. No response figures are given; the outcome is reported only as the appeal winning over others.

item.answer: Step one is the truest thing that can be said about the brand — not the client's preferred truth. For his worked case the client's truth was "comfortable" and the class's truth was "ugly". Step two is to look for the conflicts that arise as a consequence of that truth: wearing ugly shoes makes you look stupid, or costs you your evening. item.question: A team is choosing a cue to link a product to and proposes the colour red because everyone sees red constantly. State the trade-off Berger names, his image for it, and what he says about how to resolve it.
item.answer: The trade-off is frequency against strength of link. A cue must occur often or it will rarely fire — his case is a beer brand moving from "Holidays are made for Michelob" to "Weekends are made for Michelob" because holidays are too rare. But the more things a cue is already associated with, the weaker any one association becomes, and red is his own example of the failure: roses, love, Coca-Cola, fast cars, so it retrieves none of them strongly. His image is a paper cup with holes punched in the bottom — one hole gives a strong stream, many holes give a trickle from each. His recommendation is a fresher, more original link, with peanut butter reliably retrieving jelly as the standard to aim at. On how to resolve it: he names the two failure modes and stops. He gives no procedure for locating the balance point, which is exactly the decision a practitioner faces.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum); Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent and Rationale for the Ratios Chosen
item.question: A brand team asks: "Our campaign key visual has a headline at 3.8:1. Does WCAG say our advertisement is illegible?" Answer using only what the source claims.
item.answer: No. WCAG makes no claim of that kind about anything. SC 1.4.3 is a conformance criterion for web content, and what a shortfall means is that the content does not satisfy that criterion at Level AA — assuming the headline is not large scale, in which case the applicable figure would be 3:1 and 3.8:1 would meet it. The criterion's stated purpose is narrow and specific: to provide enough contrast between text and its background so it can be read by people with moderately low vision or impaired contrast perception, without contrast-enhancing assistive technology. The numbers are derived as compensation for a stated contrast sensitivity loss at a given visual acuity. There is no claim in the document that meeting a threshold makes a message effective, noticeable or attractive, and no claim that missing one makes a design bad. The honest statement to the brand team is: at this size the headline would not meet the Level AA web threshold, which concerns readers with low vision; whether it works as advertising is a question this standard does not address and does not answer.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3 and its Large Text exception. The purpose statement and the derivation are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent" and "Rationale for the Ratios Chosen".
confounders: translating 'fails WCAG' into 'is illegible' or 'is bad advertising'
forgetting to check whether the large-scale branch applies, which would change the applicable figure

item.question: The authors say a brand cannot simply claim prestige. Give their two-part procedure for building a prestige position, and the reason they give for the second part.
item.answer: First, make the product or service more expensive than the competition. Second, find a code word for prestige. The reason for the second part is a social one: the connotations of prestige work in brand building but the word itself does not, because it is not that people are not dying to own prestige brands — they just hate to admit it. "Which logos do you think will appeal to your customers, and why?" — the point is the redirection: by shifting the focus off the client's individual design tastes and onto their customers', the process stays oriented to the interest of the business as a whole rather than one person's preference. item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Inner Remarkability'; Ch. 2 'Triggers', sections 'Why Do People Buzz About Some Products More Than Others?' and 'Triggered to Talk' (spine 6, spine 7)
item.question: A team has built something genuinely remarkable and asks how long the resulting conversation will last. Answer from Berger's own two findings, and note the tension between them that he never resolves.
item.answer: On his BzzAgent evidence: not long, unless something in the audience's environment brings it back. Interesting, novel and surprising products got more IMMEDIATE word of mouth and no more ONGOING word of mouth than boring ones; what predicted ongoing talk was how frequently the thing was cued in the environment. So the practical answer is that remarkability buys the opening and triggers buy the duration, and a remarkable thing with no habitat behaves like his pirate costume — discussed all day and gone by the next month. The tension he never resolves is that his other study, with Raghu Iyengar across 6,500 brands, found more remarkable brands discussed almost twice as often, with no immediate-versus-ongoing split applied. The two findings are never placed side by side, and the resolution he offers later concerns INTEREST rather than REMARKABILITY, and is asserted rather than shown to apply to the brand study.

item.question: Sullivan warns against the gimmick and then names what he claims is the only legitimate source of material. What is the distinction, and what does he say you already have to work with?

What you already have, on his list, is more than enough: the client's product with its brand equities and benefits, the competitor's product and its weaknesses, the price-quality-value arithmetic of the two, and what the customer brings — pride, greed, vanity, envy, insecurity and a hundred other wants, one of which the product satisfies. item.question: A restaurant reads the chapter on scarcity and starts turning away most callers, on the grounds that difficulty of access builds demand. Bookings rise briefly and then customers stop calling. What does Berger's own footnote say about this, and what operating rule does he report?
item.answer: His footnote bounds exactly this. Making access difficult is different from making it impossible: getting a reservation at Please Don't Tell is hard, but people who keep calling should be able to get one. He warns that restricting availability can come off as snooty or standoffish, and that people are used to getting what they want and will go elsewhere if they hear no too often. The operating rule he reports, from Jim Meehan, is to convert every refusal into a "no, but" — no at eight-thirty, but how about eleven; no to that brand, but would you try this one. Managing the disappointment preserves the allure while preserving satisfaction. He also adds a lifecycle qualification: using scarcity and exclusivity early and relaxing them later is a particularly good way to build demand, which makes restriction a launch phase rather than a permanent setting.

item.question: What does Berger mean by a habitat, and what evidence does he offer that one can be deliberately grown rather than inherited? Be precise about who the reported effect applies to.
item.answer: A habitat is the set of triggers that cause people to think of a product or idea, on an analogy with the environment that sustains an organism. Hot dogs have a thick habitat — barbecues, summer, baseball, dachshunds; he says Ethiopian food has a thin one. item.question: Starbucks is one of the book's showcase cases for the Law of Contraction and again for the Law of Publicity. What does the same book note about Starbucks in passing, and why does that note matter to a reader assessing the Law of Contraction?
item.answer: In the middle of arguing that marketers wrongly copy what successful companies currently do, the authors note parenthetically that Starbucks "currently is busy getting into everything from ice cream to bottled drinks to tea". By their own Law of Expansion that is a brand widening its scope, and the note appears in the very chapter in which Starbucks stands as the demonstration of narrowing. It matters because the book's central case is presented in a snapshot: the narrowing is credited for the success, and the subsequent broadening — which on the book's own account should weaken the brand — is mentioned and dropped. item.question: In Airey's FedEx account, research changed something bigger than the mark. What did the research find, what did it change, and what makes this his strongest example of research?
item.answer: A nine-month global study by the two organisations' research groups found that businesses and consumers were unaware of the company's global reach and full-service capabilities, believing it shipped only overnight and only within the United States. Further research on the name itself found that many people associated "federal" negatively with government and bureaucracy, and that "express" was over-used — more than 900 company names in the US alone employed it. What it changed was the name: Landor advised adopting "FedEx" as the communicative name while keeping "Federal Express Corporation" as the legal one. It is his strongest research example because it is the only place in the book where a finding contradicted the obvious move and the research output was a decision above the designer's own remit — with over 300 designs then created in the exploratory phase, ranging from evolutionary to revolutionary.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 'Incidental' and 'Logotypes'; Glossary: pure decoration; Glossary: image of text
item.question: Four pieces of text appear in one page. (a) A wordmark in the header. (b) A street sign visible in a photograph of a high street. (c) A heading saved as a PNG so a licensed display face could be used. (d) Faint words tiled behind a hero section, chosen at random from a thesaurus. Which have a contrast requirement under SC 1.4.3, and on what ground?
item.answer: Only (c). (a) is exempt under the Logotypes exception — text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement. (b) is exempt under the Incidental exception as text that is part of a picture containing significant other visual content; the Understanding note uses almost this example, saying incidental text such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign is not included. (d) is exempt as pure decoration, but only because the words satisfy the substitution test — chosen at random, they can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose; had they been the brand's values or a tagline, the exemption would fail. (c) is squarely in scope: it is an image of text under the glossary definition, text rendered in a non-text form to achieve a particular visual effect, and the criterion applies to images of text as it does to text. Note that (c) would additionally engage SC 1.4.5, since the presentation could be achieved with a web font.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3's Incidental and Logotypes exceptions, and the glossary definitions of "pure decoration" and "image of text". The street-sign illustration is NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".

item.source_locator: printed pp. 98-100 (Ch. 19, the boredom passage and the Arch Deluxe)
item.question: What cause do the authors give for most violations of the Law of Consistency, and what diagnostic error do they say a company makes after such a violation fails?
item.answer: Boredom. Brand building is boring work, what works best is absolute consistency over an extended period, and when people do boring work they get bored — so every so often someone at a company like Volvo has a bright idea about branching out into exciting sports cars. They supply a verbal cue for the moment: run up a red flag whenever you hear the words "why should we limit ourselves?", because you should limit your brand, and that limitation is the essence of branding. The diagnostic error afterwards is misattribution: it is always the product that is declared a failure, never the branding concept. Their case is the Arch Deluxe — a hundred and fifty million dollars of advertising later it was declared a disaster and dropped, when on their reading McDonald's is understood as a kid-oriented family restaurant, so an adult hamburger might taste good in the mouth but was never going to taste good in the mind.

item.answer: It recommends asking, through the client. The designer, aware that the Zia sun symbol was an ancient and sacred design belonging to Zia Pueblo, encouraged the doctors to request an audience with the elders at Zia Pueblo to ask for permission to use their identifying mark, rather than simply using it. The harm she names is concrete and current: people slapping the Zia at random onto the side of any old work van as an identity, which she says happens often in New Mexico — so the objection is not abstract offence but a pattern of appropriation she could see. Airey generalises it only as far as being sensitive to that kind of thing, adding that respecting traditions and differences can bring unexpected parties together, which matters for collective acceptance. What not to generalise: this is one narrated project with a favourable outcome recounted rather than tested, the Pueblo granted use and blessed the hospital grounds, and Airey frankly notes the public-relations benefit — so the case cannot be read as evidence that asking pays. It is a boundary condition on borrowing heritage symbols, and it is specific to a community that can be identified and asked.

item.answer: Three different strengths for one finding. item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 64-65 (Ch. 12, 'take a regular word and use it out of context')
item.question: A start-up in office supplies has shortlisted three names: General Office Products, Staples, and Supply Systems Inc. Apply the authors' two constructive naming procedures to explain which they would choose and why the other two fail.
item.answer: They would choose Staples. It is their own worked example of the first procedure — take a regular word and use it out of context so that it connotes the brand's primary attribute — and they point to the double entendre as making it particularly powerful: buy your office staples from Staples. The other two are the failure the chapter is about: common descriptive words that cannot separate the brand from anything, because the mind hears "general office products" and "supply systems" as descriptions no matter how they are capitalised, and every competitor can use the same words. The second procedure they offer is truncation — cutting a generic phrase down to something short and distinctive, as Intelligent Chip Company becomes Intel, with the point that all computers have intelligent chips inside but only some have Intel inside. Their warning case is the company that dropped McAfee, the only real name it owned, for Network Associates, and then spent $10 million including a Super Bowl spot trying to make two generics register.

item.question: A small organisation with no advertising budget wants existing users to generate awareness. Berger's remedy is not to ask them to. What is it, and what are the non-textual forms he gives?
item.answer: Build the signal into the act of use, so that consumption broadcasts without anyone being asked to do anything. His paradigm case is the free email service that appended a line and a link to every outgoing message, so each user sent prospective customers an implicit endorsement in the course of writing to exactly the people they already wrote to. The non-textual forms matter more for his general claim: distinctive shape, in a crisp packaging tube; distinctive sound, in an operating system's startup chime; unexpected colour, in white earphone cords in a market where every competitor shipped black ones, and in red-lacquered shoe soles that make a brand recognisable to people who know nothing about it; and enlarged logos. He notes the white cords did double duty — they also supplied visible social proof of how many people had switched, in a market where the standard was contested. He stresses this is disproportionately valuable to organisations with no advertising money, because existing customers become the medium.
item.support: Recounted business cases with company and press outcome figures that are uncontrolled and given for the whole business rather than for the mechanism. Berger concedes in passing that such signals can be switched off — device signature lines can be changed and mostly are not — which makes the mechanism partly a default-setting effect; he attributes the low switch-off rate to social currency without evidence. Period-bound to the late 1990s and early 2000s.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 116-117 (Chapter Ten, the trend of the crowd)
item.question: Hopkins names one device the single most effective thing he ever found in advertising. Which, on what reasoning, and what does every case he reports have in common that limits the claim?
item.answer: The trend of the crowd — the observable direction of other buyers. His reasoning is that people cannot judge values and know they cannot, so they accept the verdict of the majority; it is hard for them to analyse reasons and worth, so they follow the crowd. He built whole campaigns on it: a car sold on the story of demand outrunning a bankrupt factory until production moved into tents; a tire brand whose growth in demand was featured in pictures and type until it seemed the whole motor world was turning to it; a car sold on multiplying sales and the production economies they permitted. He adds a variant for categories where ordinary buyers cannot measure — cite the choices of commercial users who do measure, since the ordinary buyer knows fleet operators do not choose on guesswork. What every case has in common is a brand that was already growing. The device requires a real trend to point at, so on his own evidence it amplifies momentum rather than creating it, and he does not distinguish it from a claim that the crowd is right. He also concedes that the figures in the Overland story may not be accurate and that he tells it from memory.

item.source_locator: printed p. 51 (Ch. 10, 'management measures results with the wrong end of the ruler')
item.question: The authors say one reason 90 per cent of new brands are line extensions is a measurement error. State the error precisely, name the second cost they say goes unmeasured, and give the question they use to expose it.
item.answer: The error is that management measures only the success of the extension and never measures the erosion of the core brand — the ledger records the new item's sales and not what the new item took from the old one. The second unmeasured cost is opportunity: the new separate brand that could have been launched instead was not, so its foregone value never appears anywhere. The exposing question is about source of volume. When Coors was planning Coors Light they asked an executive where the business would come from and were told it would be taken from Budweiser and Miller; Budweiser said the same about Miller and Coors when planning Bud Light, and Miller said the same about the other two. The authors' reply is that the Coors Light drinker is more likely to come from Coors, the Bud Light drinker from Budweiser and the Miller Lite drinker from Miller High Life — and they note the three regular brands all declined substantially after the three lights launched.

item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', the cheese advertisements and blender passages in 'Making Virality Valuable' (spine 11)
item.question: Berger tests his own favourite advertisement destructively before endorsing it. What is the test he applies, what does the destructive step establish, and how do you run the same test on any artefact?
item.answer: The test is whether the thing you want transmitted is load-bearing in the story — whether people can tell the story without mentioning it. The destructive step is that he points out the cheese commercials would be exactly as funny with a chicken suit and a used-car tagline: someone in an animal costume kicking over groceries is funny regardless of which animal or which product. That establishes that the humour is not what makes them work as advertising, because the humour is detachable. The brand passes anyway, on a different ground: the story cannot be told or understood without the panda, so mentioning it is unavoidable. He runs the same test on the blender films — impossible to recount the clip destroying a phone without saying a blender did it, and without conveying that the blender is extraordinarily strong, which is exactly what the company wanted communicated. To run it: retell the artefact aloud without naming the subject. If the account still makes sense and still lands, the subject is detachable and will be dropped.
item.support: Berger's argument, not measured. The claim that audiences remember the brand days or weeks later is asserted rather than measured, and the test as stated is binary with no way to grade partial integration. His counterfactual is unusually rigorous for this book — it holds the entertainment constant and varies only whether the subject is load-bearing — but it is an argument, not an experiment: he did not build the chicken-suit version and measure anything.

assuming heavy branding satisfies the test; a logo can be prominent and still detachable from the plot

item.claim: The source's second route to social currency is to turn an activity into a game with recorded standing. He states two requirements. Performance must be quantified — where a domain has no built-in metric, one must be created, as airlines created recorded miles and status tiers out of flying. And the resulting status must be readable by people outside the domain: a system whose levels an outsider cannot rank confers no currency, because the whole payoff is being seen to be ahead. He argues game mechanics work on two levels at once, internal achievement and interpersonal comparison, and that the second is the one that produces talk, because boasting about the achievement necessarily names the brand or domain where it was earned.

mechanism.text: Status is inherently relational — being leader of the pack requires a pack — so a level tells people both where they stand absolutely and where they stand relative to others. People publicise the achievement for its own sake, and the sponsoring brand travels with it as an unavoidable part of the boast.

scope.conditions: domains where performance can be recorded and where standing is socially visible

caveats.text: NOT Berger's research. The relative-standing study is a third-party experiment on Harvard students choosing between earning $50,000 while others earn $25,000 and earning $100,000 while others earn $200,000, with a majority reported as choosing the lower absolute income. The source names neither the researchers nor a citation for it, so the design cannot be checked from this book.

The legibility requirement is argued from constructed contrasts, not measured: Olympic medals and British traffic-light nutrition labels as legible, Foursquare's hundred-plus badges and the platinum-sapphire-diamond credit card tiers as illegible. Persuasive, but no comparison of outcomes is reported.

The outcome figures offered are single-case and company-reported — Burberry's Art of the Trench site with millions of views and a 50 percent sales increase — with no attempt to isolate the contest from everything else the brand was doing.
Heavily period-bound: Foursquare mayorships and badges, airline status tiers as described, and the display of both on Facebook belong to roughly 2011-2012.

source_terms: There is great advantage in a name that tells a story. The name is usually prominently displayed. To justify the space it occupies, it should aid the advertising.

item.claim: A brand name is treated as an item of purchased display space subject to the same test as any other. Since the name is usually prominently displayed, it must aid the advertising in order to justify the space it occupies, and some names — May Breath, Cream of Wheat, Dutch Cleanser, Minute Tapioca, 3-in-One Oil, Holeproof — are almost complete advertisements in themselves, with Cream of Wheat said to have been worth a fortune on its own. item.label: the_copy_finishing_sequence
item.description: The copywriting chapter's back half is ordered, and the source states the ordering at the points where it matters. Tone is decided before writing and is constrained by product and audience, with the standing correction that funny is a subset of interesting rather than a goal (sk_whip_0058). Voice is acquired by study of the brand's own published work rather than invented (sk_whip_0054). The draft is then written, and only afterwards worked: rhythm varied and the joints filled until no sentence can be removed without damage (sk_whip_0055), the whole cut by a third and read aloud (sk_whip_0056). The tagline is written last, explicitly — save it until the campaign is well started, possibly to the very end — and must survive alone with the logo (sk_whip_0057). The final requirement is that each piece stands alone and ends by moving the reader somewhere (sk_whip_0059).

whole_system_claim.text: The ordering carries the claim. Each step operates on material the previous step produced, and three of the steps are explicitly retrospective — you cannot vary a rhythm, cut a third, or summarise an idea into a tagline before the thing exists. Taken together they say that copywriting in this source is mostly editing, which is Sullivan's own summary: all first drafts are crap and all good copywriting is rewriting.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The individual steps and two of the orderings are the source's — the tagline is explicitly last, and reading aloud and cutting are explicitly after the writing. The unification of the tone and voice material at the head of the same sequence is ours; he presents those under a separate heading and does not say they precede the draft, though his own account of voice emerging from the brand truth implies it.

source_terms: Chance Operations
Random Physical Effect
Programmatic Effect
Conducting a chance operation implies that the chance is being controlled to a certain degree, and this is usually the case.

By selecting the type of chance operation to use, a designer can skew the results in their favor to some degree, ensuring appropriateness in the form while allowing the unpredictability to create new visual relationships that structured thinking about layout won't achieve.
item.claim: Chance as an organising principle may seem counterintuitive, but unpredictable results can aid communication conceptually by bringing out juxtapositions of material that would otherwise have escaped notice; introducing chance sometimes helps the designer see the material more clearly and yields less predictable but more illuminating solutions. The crucial qualification is that conducting a chance operation implies the chance is being controlled to a degree, and the source says this is usually the case. Control falls into two categories. Random physical effect involves randomness to a greater degree, based on an action that prevents explicit control of the outcome — flinging paint at a surface, or scattering or dropping cropped images over a format from a certain height, knowing that certain kinds of pattern will occur because of the brush size or the gesture, but unable to predict or effect a specific result. Programmatic effect uses planned procedures, usually mechanical or mathematical; these equally deny explicit control, but their mechanical nature guarantees greater foreknowledge of the results. Named programmatic procedures include dissecting an image on an arbitrarily applied grid or a mathematical formula; photographing or scanning a layout in progress from a fixed viewpoint at predetermined times and inserting the results as images; augmenting the point sizes of successive lines of type by an arbitrary multiplier; and printing two layouts over one another then deleting the overlaps. By choosing which type of operation to use, the designer skews the results in their favour and ensures appropriateness of form while letting unpredictability create relationships structured thinking will not reach.

mechanism.text: Chance is admitted at the level of the specific outcome and withheld at the level of the operation. The designer chooses the generator, which fixes the family of results, and gives up only the individual result — which is what makes the juxtapositions new without making them arbitrary.

scope.conditions: physical and pre-digital or digital procedures applied to layout material

caveats.text: The two named kinds are distinguished by degree of foreknowledge, not by whether control is exercised; in both the operation is chosen deliberately. Reading this section as a licence for arbitrary placement inverts its actual claim.
The source's stated benefit — that chance can make a solution more illuminating — is a practitioner assertion with no evidence attached and no failure case discussed.

The illustration for this section is itself a chance operation performed on the page, a list of possibilities dropped onto the layout. That demonstration exists only as a printed page and was not available to this extraction.

source_stated_remedies: choose the type of chance operation so as to skew the family of results toward appropriateness
random physical effect: fling, scatter or drop material with knowledge of what the gesture tends to produce
programmatic effect: dissect on an arbitrary grid or formula, capture at predetermined times, multiply successive point sizes, or overprint two layouts and delete the overlaps

item.source_locator: Ch. 'I am a Complan Girl…', Colgate sachet passage
item.question: A brand plans to extend the sachet format from shampoo into toothpaste. What does this source predict, what is the proposed mechanism, and how confident is the author?
item.answer: It predicts failure, and reports that Colgate's sachet attempt did fail. The proposed mechanism is that a sachet prices a single occasion, which suits occasion-shaped consumption and not continuous consumption: shampooing was an occasional act in many Indian homes so a sachet could be bought for a special occasion, whereas a consumer ready to adopt a daily-use category would buy the full pack instead. The author's confidence is explicitly low — he writes 'I suspect', proposes no test, and extends the same conjecture to hair oil 'probably for the same reason' without new evidence. The underlying usage-frequency premise is asserted, not measured.
item.support: 'I suspect consumers did not see toothpaste as an occasional use product.'
item.confounders: This is the author's conjecture about an observed commercial pattern, not a reported study. Do not upgrade 'I suspect' to a finding.

source_terms: There are some fields which are almost impregnable. They are usually lines which created a new habit or custom and which typify that custom with consumers.

item.claim: The source gives a diagnostic for how hard a market will be to enter: the near-impregnable fields are those whose incumbent created a new habit or custom and has come to typify that custom for consumers, which combines category identification with the volume and profit to fund a heavy defence. It immediately qualifies the diagnosis — such fields are constantly invaded — and names the only two routes it accepts: some convincing advantage, or very superior salesmanship in print. A second, lesser tier is named as well: lines like a new shaving soap, where nearly every possible customer already uses a rival, most are satisfied and many are wedded to it, so the appeal must be strong enough to break long-established favour.

mechanism.text: Typifying a custom means the brand name is how consumers think of the behaviour itself, so a challenger must displace a category concept and not merely a preference; and the incumbent's volume funds the defence of that position.

scope.conditions: entry into an established category

caveats.text: No field is named as impregnable and no invasion is named as successful. The diagnostic is offered as observation and no case is attached to either half of it.

The qualification effectively empties the claim: fields are almost impregnable, and are constantly invaded, and the invasion routes given — a convincing advantage, or superior salesmanship in print — are the two things any challenger would attempt anyway. The diagnostic identifies difficulty; it does not discriminate between actions.

item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Human Behind the Client'
item.question: A creative team resents a client's approval process and treats it as an obstacle. What does this source argue instead, what is the mechanism, and what weakens the case?
item.answer: That the process should be accepted as a SHARED constraint rather than fought, because accepting it converts the relationship from adversarial to joint: if the client's requirement to test an idea is treated as a problem for the whole team, understanding deepens and the process eventually becomes 'a blur, a necessary chore'. The mechanism is that where two parties each treat the other's constraints as obstacles, effort goes into the conflict; adopting the constraint as shared redirects that effort at the brief, and the shared difficulty itself becomes what binds them. item.answer: Against being shown to have failed. His argument is that a specific audience makes the work accountable — it matched or it did not, it spread or it did not — whereas an unspecified audience cannot be contradicted by any outcome, so "everyone" functions as a place to hide. source_terms: Pattern match/pattern interrupt
A pattern interrupt, on the other hand, requires some sort of jolt ... The answer is no because the patterns are established, time is precious, and risk is something to be feared

item.claim: Godin distinguishes two situations that look alike and cost very different amounts. A pattern match slots a new offering into a routine that already exists — the family that cycles through breakfast cereals adds another one without deciding anything. A pattern interrupt requires the routine itself to be undone before any forward motion is possible, and the default answer to that request is no, because the pattern is established, time is precious and risk is feared. The operational consequence he draws is about timing rather than message: when a person's life has just changed — a new parent, someone recently engaged or recently moved — there is no pattern to match, so everything is an interrupt and you do not have to persuade them that their old choices were mistakes. The same logic makes a brand-new platform the best time to launch on it.

mechanism.text: Undoing a pattern requires the person to accept that their previous choice was wrong, which is a status cost on top of the switching cost. Where no pattern has formed, that cost is simply absent, so the same offer meets a much lower barrier.

scope.conditions: audiences with or without an established routine in the category

caveats.text: Godin notes the mirror case in organisations: a purchasing manager has been taught that matching the pattern is the way to keep a steady job with no surprises, so the same distinction predicts institutional resistance, not only consumer inertia.

The life-transition targeting claim is stated as a profitability fact with no source. It is also the point in the book where the method comes closest to the surveillance-driven practice Godin criticises elsewhere, and he does not address the tension.

item.claim: Sullivan reports Monahan's technique of listing forty or fifty data points about the brand's own subject, then building a second list from a subject chosen to be as far from it as possible, and connecting points across the two. He passes on Monahan's selection criterion for the second domain — familiar, unrelated to your work, and rich in data points — and his named rejects, which are unrelated but thin. Sullivan then offers a variant with the opposite setting: use a nearby domain instead, drawn from the truths of the product, category or customer, and use the collision to produce the campaign's name first, then write the campaign from the name. item.question: Samara opens the chapter by describing grid use as "part of the status quo of designing." What exactly is his objection, and what is the harm he says follows from getting it wrong?
item.answer: His objection is not to the grid but to defaulting to it. He calls grid use a convention and says that, like all conventions, it is suitable for achieving particular goals — not every goal. The designer's purpose is to facilitate the clearest and most compelling experience for the audience, and a grid may not be the best route there. item.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 16, the four lettered shortcomings (spine 21)
item.question: Give Ogilvy's four objections to recall testing, and say which is a mechanism rather than an absence of evidence.
item.answer: First, nobody has demonstrated a relationship between recall and sales. Second, some commercials scoring about average on recall score below average on changing brand preference, with celebrity commercials the standing case of high recall and low persuasion. Third, it is too easy for the copywriter to cheat, and he quotes a colleague saying that when he wants a high recall score all he has to do is show a gorilla in a jock strap. Fourth, he doubts recall tests even measure recall, believing they measure the viewer's ability to articulate what is recalled, which is a very different thing. Nobody can hold two hundred and fifty motorcycles or nineteen thousand drink combinations in mind, so we remember the best one — and "best" is always best-for- me on the dimension I happen to care about. Memory holds one slot per person per dimension, not one ranking per category, so the same category has a different winner in each head. item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed p. 53 (Chapter 17, 'Individuality')
item.question: Chapter 9 rules out eccentricity; chapter 17 requires standing out. How does Hopkins hold both, and what selection rule does he give?

item.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Forcing a focus" (spine 11)

item.answer: The mechanism runs through the artefact, not the audience. Pursuing mass means aiming at the centre of the curve, which requires you to offend no one and satisfy everyone, and those are constraints on the thing you make: they force compromises and generalisations, and produce work that is average. item.source_locator: printed p. 33, 'Commit to memory'; and printed p. 36, 'Focus on one thing'
item.question: Airey converts a claim about how a mark is SEEN into a constraint on how the designer WORKS. What is the exposure claim, what is the working constraint, and what is the inferential step between them that he does not defend?
item.answer: The exposure claim is that very often a quick glance is all the time you get to make an impression — his examples are a bus passenger looking out of the window at a billboard and a pedestrian looking up as a branded truck drives past, and he adds that the client's customers are not going to spend long studying the logo. The working constraint is to limit the time spent on each idea sketch, trying about thirty seconds. The step between them is his rhetorical question: otherwise, how can you expect a viewer to remember it with a quick glance? item.question: Sullivan proposes replacing the key message on a brief with a key question. What is his argument, and what does he say the word "message" quietly presupposes?

A key message is fully cooked and asks nothing of the maker; a question is unfinished, which is what gives it spring — it is a riddle that produces an itch a creative person will want to scratch with ideas. He also names the presupposition: the word "messaging" presupposes that the solution to the client's business problem is a message, which it may not be, and creatives compound this by reading the line item on the brief as the solution rather than as an input. item.answer: Mind mapping is for considering as many different design directions as possible, at the stage where that matters most: you write a word central to the brief, branch outward, and build the largest thought cloud you can. Sketching is for volume and freedom: paper is less restrictive and adds no intermediate steps, so more ideas get out before the computer is opened, and he says drawing skill is irrelevant because the point is documenting ideas so they can be built on or discarded. item.question: Hopkins says no single orange or raisin grower could increase consumption of those fruits. What is the mechanism, and what exception does he name?

item.answer: They tell leaders not to think of advertising as an investment that will pay dividends but as insurance protecting against losses caused by competitive attack. Their analogy is a national defence budget: "your advertising budget is like a country's defense budget" — the tanks, planes and missiles buy nothing, they only keep the country from being overrun. item.question: Airey ends his criteria chapter by weakening it. What exactly does he withdraw, what precondition does he attach, and what does he claim the benefit is?
item.answer: He withdraws necessity. Having given the seven elements, he asks whether you always have to play by the rules and answers that rules are made to be broken — it is up to you to break new ground and cross boundaries in attempting designs that are a cut above the rest. The precondition is stated a chapter-opening earlier and is not decorative: you have to know the rules in any creative endeavour before you can successfully break them, illustrated by a Michelin-starred chef who does not pull ingredients out of thin air but takes a proven recipe and adapts it. The benefit he claims is not a better outcome — he is explicit that whether your results are successful will obviously be an open question — but a faster one: you will learn much more and much faster when the potential mistakes are your own rather than someone else's. item.question: Airey rules against trends and then makes one concession that keeps the rule workable. State the rule, the standard it replaces, the concession, and the problem the rule cannot solve.
item.answer: The rule: leave trends to the fashion industry — trends come and go like the wind, and the last thing you want is to invest a significant amount of your time and your client's money in a design that will look dated overnight. His own example of the error — the period in the nineties when Helvetica Neue seemed to be used on every new design — is identified only in retrospect, and the book offers no way to make that identification prospectively. The quoted designer's version, "I don't want to be in vogue, I want to set the standard and not follow others", is a statement of ambition, not a test.

item.question: Sullivan sets a volume target rather than a quality target for headline writing. State the target and the two conditions he attaches, one of which is usually dropped when this advice is repeated.
item.answer: Write a hundred lines, across several sessions. The first condition is that they all have to be pretty good — the target is a hundred workable lines ranging from decent to very strong, not a hundred attempts, and this is the condition usually dropped. The second is that between rounds you start over on a clean page and constantly pretend you have nothing so far. His argument for the number is that we cannot seriously believe a ticket-selling, brand-building campaign has been crafted after nineteen tries, and that a couple of hundred will be needed. He also gives the reason the target has to be set in advance: around half past two in the morning, "good" starts to look like "great", and volume produced earlier is what lets you refuse it.

item.label: value_located_in_circulation_and_what_follows_for_reading_this_market
item.description: Jain's political-economy argument, assembled: an image's value is held to emanate from its circulation and exchange rather than from its production, which is why authorship registers so weakly, why the same industrial system can address many segments without homogenising them, why the catalogue is not a demand curve, and why publicness itself adds value.

whole_system_claim.text: In this arena the artefact's value does not sit in it and was not put there by its maker. It accrues through movement — through being gifted, displayed, worshipped, recognised as recognised. That single relocation explains a cluster of otherwise disconnected observations: that buyers choose by subject and not by artist; that signatures work as brand names; that catalogues encode self-presentation rather than preference; and that an image's exposure to a public gaze both creates its power and makes it vulnerable to desecration.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Jain states the location of value in circulation as her own thesis (chs. 5 and 6) and connects it to the fetish, to the gift economy of the bazaar and to meta-popularity. She does not join it to the subject-over-author finding or to the layered-catalogue finding, which sit in chapters 1 and 4. Assembling them under one relocation is the extractor's synthesis. What the grouping ADDS, and what must be attributed to CANON-014, is the observation that four findings which look like quirks of one trade are consequences of one premise about where value sits.

dependencies.nature: if value accrues in circulation rather than in production, the producer's identity is not what is being bought, which is why the signature migrates from an authorship mark to a brand name
meta-popularity is only visible once the image is treated as a circulating object rather than as a representation

conflicts.nature: the post-liberalisation object describes a partial re-import of the production-centred regime — proprietary analytical templates, patenting pressure, corporate signage — into an arena the earlier chapters characterise as circulation-centred. Jain does not treat this as refuting her thesis, but the two describe different states of the same system and should not be read as simultaneous

item.source_warning_ref: Ch. 3, printed p. 119, and Conclusion, printed p. 369: the bazaar ethos 'is a hegemonic formation in itself and therefore should not be romanticized in the name of the popular'

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate-to-high. This is the most theoretically loaded grouping in the record and the one where an extractor is most likely to over-systematise a book that is arguing with other scholars rather than laying down a model. Two of the five members are joined to the thesis by the extractor and not by the author. It is recorded as a hypothesis about how Jain's political economy connects to her trade observations, not as her stated system.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 77-78 (Chapter Seven, the conditions for entering an occupied field)
item.question: State Hopkins's entry condition for a new advertiser, including the softening clause that makes it far easier to satisfy than it first appears.
item.answer: Before committing, one must know the competition, know what others offer, know what people want, and be able to outbid the field in some way — on qualities, on service, or on terms. Crying a name or a brand does not satisfy the condition, and until one feels sure the advantages are strongly on his side it is folly to risk a battle. He adds a second constraint: never pay the cost of acquiring customers without seeing how they will be kept. The softening clause is that, failing a real advantage, one may create a seeming advantage by citing facts which others fail to cite. That makes the condition satisfiable by communication alone, and it is the clause his Schlitz and Van Camp campaigns actually run on. He gives no method for judging in advance whether an available claim is exceptional enough; his operational answer is elsewhere — run a cheap local test and read the repeat sales.

item.question: Sullivan prefers an "-est" to an "-er". What is the argument, and what does he say happens when the absolute is not available?
item.answer: His argument is a claim about what is retained: quietest, fastest and cleanest are what people are going to remember, and all the claims in the middle ground — quieter, faster, cleaner — are grey and forgettable. Best is better than good, and where the product genuinely is the best, set up camp there. What happens when it is not available is the failure he describes rather than a remedy he offers: the client or agency ends up trying to leverage some rice-paper-thin difference nobody cares about, often because legal will not permit anything stronger.
