item.question: You have produced twenty sketches for a wordmark and they all look like each other. Which of Airey's moves apply, and what account does he give of why you are stuck?
item.answer: His account of the problem is mechanical rather than mystical: the brain forms routine patterns, and the more often you perform the same task the more entrenched and natural the pattern becomes, so before you know it you are in a rut. Four moves follow. Turn your design concepts upside down. Look at them from a distance. Ask someone else to share some thoughts on your sketches. And the one from his own practice: sketch every idea that comes, then study those sketches WITH THE DESIGN BRIEF IN HAND, which he says produces further sketches that would not have come to mind without that analysis. item.question: Godin argues that saying "it's not for you" is an act of respect. Set out the argument, and give the case in his own book that shows what it costs.
item.answer: The argument has two parts. Refusing to pursue someone respects them: you are not wasting their time, pandering to them, or insisting they change their beliefs, and "I made this for you, not for the other folks" and "it's not for you" are two sides of one coin. And the alternative is unavailable anyway — every bestselling book has one-star reviews, and it is impossible to create work that both matters and pleases everyone. The cost shows in his restaurant case: a group that eliminated tipping had to accept that diners who enjoyed the status of leaving a large tip could no longer get it, and the honest formulation is "it's not for you, sorry". So the choice is not how to avoid disappointing people; it is which people to disappoint.
item.support: It's not for you: shows the ability to respect someone enough that you're not going to waste their time, pander to them, or insist that they change their beliefs; it's impossible to create work that both matters and pleases everyone. No tipping at USHG: some diners find joy in the status of leaving a big tip and the group can no longer offer that thrill.
confounders: reading exclusion as a marketing tactic for creating exclusivity rather than as an unavoidable consequence stated plainly
assuming the excluded group is unimportant; in his case they were paying customers with a preference he removed

item.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Headlines' (spine 13)
item.question: Ogilvy states that five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy, and then immediately draws a much stronger conclusion from it. What is that conclusion, and what step is hidden inside it?
item.answer: His conclusion is that unless the headline sells the product, ninety per cent of the money has been wasted. The hidden step is a move from a readership ratio to a spending ratio: the five-to- one figure is about how many people read two parts of an advertisement, and the ninety per cent is a claim about wasted expenditure, which requires the further assumption that readership of the headline is what the money buys. He also derives from the same ratio that the brand name must appear in the headline, since eighty per cent of readers never reach the body copy and would otherwise never learn what is being advertised.
item.support: Chapter 7 opens by naming its evidence base — factor analyses commissioned from Gallup and Robinson, the Starch Readership Service, direct-response test results and the author's own observation — then gives the five-times figure and the ninety per cent conclusion in adjacent sentences. The readership figure is a reported measurement; the ninety per cent is his inference, not a measured waste.
confounders: reading the ninety per cent as a measured finding rather than as an inference from the readership ratio
assuming the claim is about attention span; it is about the fall-off between two elements of one advertisement
confusing this with the chapter-2 doctrine that advertising must sell rather than please — that is a different claim, about the criterion, not about where readership sits

item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.source_locator: printed p. 190, tip 22 'Don't neglect the substrate'; and printed pp. 175-176, 'Tools of the trade'
item.question: Two of Airey's cautions are about the artwork's physical fate rather than its design. What are they, and why does he say each matters?
item.answer: The substrate: the paper or card a logo appears on can make a big difference to how it appears in the final presentation, because the colour and the sharpness of the mark can change drastically — so discuss all the possibilities for variation with the commercial printer, or advise the client to, before final production. And scalability: the delivered artwork must be scalable to any size, for use on posters or on the side of buildings, which is his reason for producing marks as vector artwork rather than in a photo editor. The failure case for the second is named earlier and is the sharper illustration: a low-resolution "save for web" logo file scaled up and used on the cover of a printed sales manual, which he says defeats the purpose of hiring a specialist. Both are physical-production cautions in his own frame, tied to 2010 commercial print, and neither comes with a method or a tolerance.

item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 139-140, the Yellow Pages dart concept, 'Swallow that pride'
item.question: A client group is convinced an element should be added that you believe will weaken the mark. What does Airey do instead of arguing, and what is the mechanism he says makes it work?
item.answer: He builds their request. On a Yellow Pages redesign, committee members were convinced that adding a dart beside the walking fingers would improve the design and he was sure it would not. Rather than becoming defensive, he executed the dart version — and paired it with another idea he believed was a better improvement, explaining why when he presented it. He reports that once the two results could be compared, it was easier for the committee to see that its own idea was unsuitable. The mechanism he generalises is that clients are much less likely to resist your ideas going forward if they have seen a graphic representation of how their own strategic interpretation filters out. He also records the reason the demonstration was needed: the committee was unaware of the "focus on one thing" idea from Chapter 3 — which is as much an argument for explaining the principle as for showing the comparison.
item.support: Printed pp. 139-140. Both concepts are printed on p. 140, the dart version above and the alternative below. One narrated project, no measurement of whether the method changes outcomes.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 37-38 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
item.question: Hopkins treats price as having more than one regime. Set out the three he describes and what determines which applies.
item.answer: Volume: the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit — Campbell's Soups, Palmolive Soap, Karo Syrup, Ford cars — and a price that appeals only to, say, 10 per cent multiplies the cost of selling. Low consumption: on some lines high price is unimportant but high profit is essential, because sale per customer is small; a buyer hardly cares what he pays for a corn remedy because he uses little, so the maker must have a large margin. Judgement: on other lines a higher price is itself an inducement, because the line is judged largely by price and a product costing more than the ordinary is considered above the ordinary. What determines the regime is how much the customer consumes and whether he has any way to judge the product other than by price — though Hopkins never states a test for placing a new product, which is the decision the passage is about.
item.support: p.38: "the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit... A price which appeals only to—say 10 per cent—multiplies the cost of selling." "The maker must have a large margin because of small consumption." "A product which costs more than the ordinary is considered above the ordinary."
confounders: Reducing him to 'low price wins volume', which is only the first regime.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Get the visual clichés out of your system right away'; and Ch. 3 'Look at the competitors' advertising' (spines 15, 13)
item.question: Sullivan says visual clichés are not general but category-specific. What working procedure does that imply, and what stops this from being a blanket ban on familiar imagery?
item.answer: It implies research rather than taste: go and learn which images your category is currently using — visit the competitors' sites, watch their videos, study what they post — and then do not use those. His examples are category-bound: grandfathers flying kites with grandchildren in insurance, earnest bespectacled people with a screen reflected in their glasses in technology. The mechanism is availability, the same argument he makes about early ideas: a cliché is what the whole category already reaches for, so using it puts the brand inside the category's existing visual field rather than distinguishing it from it. What stops it being a blanket ban is his own endorsement of borrowed image equity: an established image given a spin and used in a new and unexpected way that relates to the product advantage is the metaphor he recommends. The prohibition is on unmodified reuse, not on familiar imagery.
item.support: Stated procedure and stated examples. Which images count as tired is judged by inspection and is time- and market-bound; his examples are American category conventions of his period.
confounders: treating the cliché list as universal rather than as something to be assembled per category
reading it as a prohibition on recognisable imagery, which his metaphor advice contradicts
assuming novelty alone resolves it — his metaphor condition requires the new use to relate to the product advantage

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Narrative Allusions: Vernacularism' (spine 6)
item.question: You are designing an invitation to an exclusive art auction and propose using the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. What is the mechanism Samara says makes this work, and what is the limit an extractor should attach to it?
item.answer: That is Samara's own example. The mechanism is that vernacular imagery, or a vernacular compositional conceit, imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated. Because "vernacular" means the ordinary, such gestures often trade on forms associated with low culture or with undesigned visual experience, and the distance between the borrowed world and the actual subject is what carries the comment. He traces the practice to Pop Art, citing Warhol's Brillo boxes and Rosenquist's paintings of spaghetti and cleaning products. The limit is that the effect is entirely dependent on the audience holding the association: Hatch Show Prints signify the American Midwest, and Victorian illustrated books signify small independent trade, only to people who already read them that way. Samara does not discuss what happens when the borrowed style is simply read as itself.
item.support: "Vernacularism": the auction-invitation example; imposing the look of something else to draw a comparison or comment; the low-culture note; the Pop Art lineage; the Hatch Show Prints and Victorian-illustration examples.
confounders: treating vernacular borrowing as retro styling for its own sake
assuming the association transfers across cultures — every one of his examples is culture-specific
confusing it with pictorialisation; vernacularism borrows a style, it does not depict the subject

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Rewiring Your Brain', section 'Tom Monahan's wonderful exercise: Ask a better question' (spine 23)
item.question: Monahan's ladder has a precise terminal condition. State the three rungs by what kind of answer each admits, and say what Sullivan instructs the first question and first answer to be.
item.answer: Rung one is a basic question relevant to the problem for which there is a correct answer, so no creativity is involved. Rung two is derived from the previous answer and admits only an educated guess, so some creativity is involved. Rung three is derived again and has no correct answer that can be known or even guessed, so creativity is required — and that is the better question. Sullivan instructs that the first question always be "why should people buy this brand?" and the first answer be the key message you were given, so the ladder starts inside the brief and climbs out of it. He notes the search is not linear: many threads dead-end, and the move is to back up, rephrase the last question and continue. He calls it, in his own coinage, the Toddler Socratic Method.
item.support: Lifted whole from Monahan's book with permission; the teaching frame and the worked cases are Sullivan's. Monahan's own stated mechanism is that ordinary questions let the answerer stay inside the known, because an answer is by definition something that already exists.

item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', sub-section 'Building a Good Game' within 'Leverage Game Mechanics' (spine 6)
item.question: A membership scheme awards more than a hundred differently named badges for different kinds of activity, and users are proud of them. On Berger's account, what is wrong with it and what is his contrasting case?
item.answer: It fails his legibility requirement. Berger says effective status systems are easy to understand even by people unfamiliar with the domain, and a scheme with a hundred unrankable badges fails that: he asks whether anyone on the street could say whether being the mayor of a location beats a School Night badge or a Super User badge. Since the whole payoff of a status system is being SEEN to be ahead, standing that an outsider cannot read confers no social currency, and the achievement produces no talk. His contrasting case is Olympic medals — tell someone you won silver and they know exactly how you did, even if they know nothing about the sport. He gives credit card tiers as the same failure: once gold was issued broadly, companies added platinum, sapphire and diamond, and nobody can rank them, producing what he calls a chaos of consumer confusion. He also cites British supermarket traffic-light nutrition labels as an intuitive system anyone can read immediately.
item.support: Berger's argument from constructed contrasts, not measured. No comparison of outcomes between legible and illegible schemes is reported anywhere. Heavily period-bound to roughly 2011-2012.
confounders: diagnosing the problem as too many badges rather than as unrankable ones; Berger's criterion is legibility to outsiders, not count
assuming internal satisfaction is enough — his mechanism runs through interpersonal comparison, so private pride produces no word of mouth

item.source_locator: printed pp. 63-64 (Ch. 3, 'The end game: goals and principles'), with the negative form at printed p. 165 (Ch. 6, 'Step 4: Critique together')
item.question: A team's design principles are "delightful", "modern" and "fun". Applying this source's own test, what is wrong with them, and what is the test — stated both in its positive and its negative form?
item.answer: They are too broad. The positive form of the test is that a good principle is specific and, by virtue of being specific, eliminates more design ideas than it retains — the source names "fun" and "amusing" as exactly the kind of quality that fails, because every member of a team interprets them differently and none of them rejects any candidate. item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 96-97, 'The fundamental need for the sketchpad'; printed p. 149; printed p. 155
item.question: A designer says they think faster on screen than on paper. Reconstruct Airey's reasons for excluding the computer anyway, and state precisely where his exclusion stops.
item.answer: Three reasons, from three places. Friction: translating the same process to a computer requires unnecessary intermediate steps that hinder creative flow, whereas on paper you want a circle here, a stroke there — no problem, just do it. Volume: what matters is beating out as many ideas as possible before turning to the computer, sketching from a single mapped word, then combining two, then a group. Disinhibition: keep an open mind and do not limit yourself, make a visual note of every thought that passes even if the ideas seem far-fetched, and do not let weak drawing skill stop you, because the point is documenting ideas so you can build on them or discard them. He repeats it at printed p. 149 with a designer's addition that drawing "will teach you how to see". Where the exclusion stops is stated precisely: eventually your concept develops structure, and only then are you ready to use a computer. It is a stage rule, not a prohibition — and it is practitioner assertion throughout, with no comparison and no measurement anywhere in the book.

item.source_locator: printed pp. 114-116, 'Where Photoshop comes into play'
item.question: Airey requires concepts to be shown in context. What is his analogy, what is his stated reason, and what does he concede about what the practice is for?
item.answer: The analogy is a car: it might have a fresh paint job and that new-car smell, but unless you take a test drive you will not be entirely convinced. The stated reason is about the client's attention rather than the design's quality — most clients do not have the time to follow every step of the process and will be focused on the final result, so the more tangible your concepts appear, the more the client will be able to visualise the benefits. He also claims a variety effect: the greater the range of applications you create, the more consistent the use appears and the more attractive the result. What he concedes, and it is worth keeping, is the purpose: showing your logo designs in context may be what finally seals the deal with the client. item.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
item.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', items 6, 7, 8 and 9 (spine 14)
item.question: Set out Ogilvy's four findings about the sound layer of a commercial, and say which one he reports as a genuine null result.
item.answer: Voice-over holds the audience less well than actors talking on camera, and he reports a manufacturer who made two commercials identical except for this and found the on-camera version sold more. Supers — the promise set in type over the picture while the soundtrack speaks it — pay, but the words must be exactly the same as the spoken words, because any divergence confuses the viewer. Sound effects, such as sausages sizzling, can make a positive difference; he instances a commercial built round the sound of coffee percolating that ran five years. The null result is background music: research shows it is neither a positive nor a negative factor, doing no harm and no measurable good. Jingles, separately, are below average at changing brand preference and should never go on air until people who have not read the script can make out the words.
item.support: The voice-over comparison is the closest thing to a controlled pair in the chapter — two commercials identical except for one variable, tested, direction reported — though the magnitude, product and method are not given. The music null is stated as a null, which is unusual in this book. His argument against background music is rhetorical rather than evidential.

conflating jingles with background music; he treats them as separate findings with different verdicts

item.question: What is the strongest piece of evidence the authors offer for the claim that measured quality does not track market success, and what exactly is wrong with it as evidence?
item.answer: It is a Consumer Reports ranking of sixteen small cars, from which they report that the number-one brand in quality was twelfth in sales, the number two was ninth, and the number three was last. item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', sections 'To spark story, start with this versus that' and 'If a conflict isn't immediately apparent, make one up' (spine 21)
item.question: You are handed an undifferentiated commodity — bananas — and asked for a campaign. Sullivan says the open assignment freezes his pen. What device does he impose, and what does he do when the category itself contains no conflict?
item.answer: He draws a rectangle with a line down the middle, treats the line as the word "versus", and fills either side with any opposition that comes to mind — life with the product versus without it, our product versus theirs, or anything else. He reports that the same assignment stated as an opposition ("Coke versus Pepsi") starts producing ideas where the open version produced nothing. When no in-category conflict exists, his instruction is to invent one, and for bananas specifically to go outside the category: good food versus junk food, has its own wrapper versus canned foods, ready to eat versus food you have to cook. item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 173-174 (Chapter Sixteen, the reason is rarely economy)
item.question: A brand aimed at buyers of limited means proposes to lead on how much money the product saves them. State Hopkins's objection, his substitute, and the character of the evidence he offers.
item.answer: His objection is that the reason for a purchase is rarely economy, and that where economy is a necessity most people like to defy it: suggest a thing because it is economical and you arouse opposition, you hurt their pride. A price appeal classifies the buyer, and buyers who must economise experience that classification as an injury. His substitute is to direct the appeal to those who do not consider cost, so that the buyer who must economise can include herself without accepting the classification — she demands what the best people use. His evidence is his own observation of the gardeners, their families and the village folk near his country home, whom he presents as typifying the ninety-five per cent who are his customers; and a cosmetics experience in which a low price on perfume did not appeal to the girl who should have economised. The passage is heavily bounded by 1920s American assumptions about class, pride and gender, and is recorded as his framing, not as a finding about buyers.

item.source_locator: printed pp. 125-126 (Chapter Eleven, on names that tell a story)
item.question: Why does Hopkins treat naming as a principal creative decision rather than a labelling step, and what does he concede about names that succeeded without one?
item.answer: Because the name is the part always displayed — in every advertisement and on every package — so a name that states the claim forms an advertisement in itself and delivers the claim at every exposure, including exposures where nothing else is read. He says coining the right name is often the major step in good advertising and that no doubt such names often double the results of expenditures, which is offered as no doubt and carries no measurement. item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 13 "Semiotics, Symbols, and Vernacular", sections "What does this remind you of?" and "Why is Nigerian spam so sloppy?" (spine 20)
item.question: Godin argues that badly spelled advance-fee scam mail is not incompetent. What is his reading, and what general claim about form does it illustrate?
item.answer: His reading is that the errors are a filter. The mail is sending a signal to people who are skeptical, careful and well-informed: go away. Putting anyone else into the process wastes the sender's time, and they would rather lose you at the beginning than invest in you and lose you at the end. The general claim is that form acts before content does. Busy people scan rather than study, and while scanning they ask what this reminds them of — and the answer decides whether they are the audience and whether the maker is credible, before any argument is considered. So the vernacular of a category — typefaces, photo styles, copy — is a membership signal: you are not people like us if you do not talk the way we expect you to. Note this is an inference about the senders' intent, not a reported finding about their strategy.

The one-thing rule requires exactly one feature doing the work of standing out — one, not two, three or four — and the Eiffel Tower counterfactual at printed p. 37 is the same shape of case: an element everyone would immediately associate with the subject, excluded because the viewer would then be forced to consider an unnecessary element, making the design less memorable. item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Inner Remarkability', the passages on breaking expected patterns and on mystery (spine 6)
item.question: A brand in a category with rigid customer expectations wants remarkability and has no unusual product feature to point at. What two constructive routes does Berger offer, and what does each exploit?
item.answer: First, break an expected pattern. Remarkability is relative to an expectation, so the expectation itself is the raw material — which means a category with a firm norm is an advantage rather than an obstacle. His cases are a low-cost airline supplying a comfortable seat, varied snacks and seat-back television against no-frills expectations, and a hundred-dollar cheesesteak against what a cheesesteak is. Second, unresolved mystery or controversy, which works by a different mechanism: an open question that undermines a settled belief gives people a reason to ask others to help settle it, and the disagreement itself generates more discussion. He insists remarkability can be found in anything, and offers black toilet paper at a party as his cheapest demonstration.

item.question: A maker wants to price a small remedy low to widen its market, reasoning that volume is where the profit is. On Hopkins's chapter 12 reasoning, when is that right and when is it wrong?
item.answer: It is right in the volume regime — he does say the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit, and that a price appealing only to, say, 10 per cent multiplies the cost of selling. But he places small remedies in a different regime. Where sale per customer is small, high price is unimportant and high PROFIT is essential: a buyer hardly cares what he pays for a corn remedy because he uses little, so the maker must have a large margin precisely because consumption is small. Widening the market at a low margin does not help when each customer buys once or twice — which is the same variable, consumption per customer, that governs chapter 10's feasibility test. So the reasoning is wrong here, and Hopkins would want to know which regime the line is in first. He never states a test for placing a new product in a regime, which is the weakness of the framework.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 60-61 (Chapter 20, 'A Name That Helps')
item.question: You must choose between a descriptive name, a meaningless coined name, and an ingredient name. Set out the trade-off as Hopkins does, including the patent complication.
item.answer: Descriptive: protectable while still describing the product, so the display is valuable and the name sells in space spent anyway. Meaningless coined — Kodak, Karo, Mazda, Vaseline, Postum: also protectable, and long-continued advertising may give it a meaning, at which point it becomes very valuable, but the great majority never attain that status, so such names do not aid the advertising and it is very doubtful whether they justify display. Ingredient names — Syrup of Figs, Tar Soap, Palmolive Soap: may dominate a market if the price is reasonable, but they invite substitution and are naturally classified with other products having like ingredients, so the price must remain in that class. The patent complication is separate and severe: on a patented product the right to a name expires with the patent — Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit became common property — which he says often makes a patent an undesirable protection. And where a product must be called by a common name, the best auxiliary is a man's name, better than a coined one because it shows some man is proud of his creation.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 152-153 and printed p. 185 (Chapters Fourteen and Seventeen, on prevention and negative appeals)
item.question: A hygiene brand proposes a campaign showing the consequences of neglect in order to frighten people into buying. State Hopkins's objection in two parts — one psychological, one economic — and the exception he grants.
item.answer: The psychological part: people will do little to prevent troubles they do not have, because they do not cross bridges in advance; they are seeking happiness, safety, beauty and content, not avoiding hypothetical harms. He couples this with an absolute rule against negative presentation — never advertise negatively, do not picture or feature ills, show the happier results — and reports that every illustration he used showed attractive people and good teeth. The economic part is the sharper half and is usually missed: people will do anything to cure troubles which exist, but legitimate advertising has little scope there, because those who have met the misfortune form in most lines a percentage too small to consider. So the exception is real — fear works where the trouble already exists — and it is ruled out by audience size, not by psychology. His evidence is that scores tried to scare people into using a dentifrice and none succeeded so far as he knows, which is an absence of success in his own recall rather than a comparison.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', the laptop logo decision in the opening and the shirts-and-socks argument in 'The Power of Observability' (spine 9)
item.question: Berger opens this chapter with a company deliberately making its product worse for the person who bought it. What was the decision, what was traded for what, and what general claim does he build on it?
item.answer: The laptop logo. It had faced the owner when the machine was closed, so that a person pulling it from a bag could tell which way up it went — a small usability gain, consistent with the company's obsession with the buyer's experience. But once opened, the logo was upside down to everyone else in the room. The trade was made explicitly: the customer's orientation cue was given up so that the logo read correctly to onlookers. The general claim is that seeing others do something makes people more likely to do it themselves, and the operative word is SEEING — if it is hard to see what others are doing, it is hard to imitate it. So observability bounds how far social influence can carry anything, which he compresses into: if something is built to show, it is built to grow. His category test is shirts against socks, cars against toothpaste.

item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", section "Positioning as a service" (spine 12), with Ch. 6 "Beyond Commodities", section "But your story is a hook" (spine 13)
item.question: Godin's music-teacher example: one teacher claims rigour and competition results, another claims the whole student and refuses competitions. What does he say this costs the first teacher, and what general rule is the example there to demonstrate?
item.answer: It costs him his freedom of action. Having claimed rigour, he now has to actually be more rigorous and professional than other teachers, has to make the difficult decision of expelling students who are not serious enough, and has to persevere until his students really do win competitions. The general rule is that a position is an obligation: once you claim a story you are on the hook to deliver, and Godin contrasts this with merely offering an alternative, which he calls the low-risk path — take it or leave it. He also adds two modern conditions on the claims themselves: they must be true and continually doubled down on in all your actions, and they must be generous, existing as a service to the customer. And he notes, without softening it, that this is not a teacher he would have wanted himself — which is the "it's not for you" principle applied to his own example.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Required for Understanding and Pie Charts
item.question: Two pie charts convey the same data. Chart A labels each slice with a name only. Chart B labels each slice with a name and its value. In both, adjacent slices contrast at about 1.8:1. What does SC 1.4.11 say about each, and what does that reveal about how the criterion is scoped?
item.answer: Chart A fails. It passes SC 1.4.1 because the slices are labelled rather than distinguished by colour alone, but the reader still has to discern the edges between slices to grasp the proportions — so those edges are graphical objects required to understand the content, and at 1.8:1 they do not meet 3:1. Chart B is not applicable rather than passing: its visible labels and values convey information equivalent to the slices, so the slices are no longer required for understanding and the criterion has nothing to bite on. The scoping lesson is that SC 1.4.11 does not attach to graphics as such. It attaches to whatever is load-bearing for comprehension, and that set shrinks as information is supplied in other conforming ways. The source lists four such ways: text embedded or overlaid conveying the same information, aesthetic-only graphics, information available in another form such as a following table or long description, and logos or brand names. It adds that text within a graphic must itself meet SC 1.4.3.
item.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Required for Understanding" and the "Pie Charts" worked examples. The criterion's phrase "required to understand the content" is normative (SC 1.4.11). The figures themselves were not inspected; the captions state the verdicts.
confounders: assuming labelling a chart is always enough — labels alone leave the proportions to the slice edges
assuming every slice must contrast with every other slice regardless of what else is shown
reporting Chart B as a pass rather than as not applicable, which loses why it is out of scope

item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', sections 'Triggered to Talk' and 'Why Cheerios Gets More Word of Mouth Than Disney World' (spine 7)
item.question: In the same dataset that produced the interest null, what did predict word of mouth, by how much, and what mechanism does Berger give for why dull products can out-talk exciting ones?
item.answer: Trigger frequency. More frequently triggered products got 15 percent more word of mouth — and, unlike interest, they got more of BOTH kinds, immediate and ongoing. His mechanism is that most conversation is small talk whose purpose is to fill conversational space rather than to impress, and what fills it is whatever is accessible. If something is top of mind it is usually relevant to the situation at hand, so it is what people reach for. Frequent use or frequent environmental cues keep a thing accessible, so it keeps being reached for. This is why Ziploc bags and moisturiser get discussed week after week while a theme park visited once a year does not: the park has high social currency and emotion and almost no triggers. His summary is that social currency gets people talking and triggers keep them talking — top of mind means tip of tongue.

item.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", sections "Positioning as a service" and "Choose your axes, choose your future" (spine 12)
item.question: Set out Godin's XY positioning method, and state the trade-off he attaches to the choice of axes — including what he says happens to the customer in the wrong case.
item.answer: Draw two axes, each an attribute people care about; plot every available alternative on them; and take a position at an extreme rather than in the middle. The trade-off is in choosing which attributes. It is tempting to pick the ones most people care about, and it is hard work to claim an edge nobody wants — but picking the popular axes puts you in a crowded quadrant, and without the magic of advertising you cannot grow there. What happens to the customer is the specific part: he does not know what to do, so he does nothing. Inaction, not a random pick. The alternative is to build your own quadrant from two overlooked axes and be the clear and obvious choice on them. Note the method organises a decision it does not make — Godin prints two dozen candidate axes and says you know your space better than he does.

item.label: the_truth_plus_conflict_platform_generator
item.description: The storytelling chapter contains an explicit generative procedure with a stated entry point, a stated operation, a stated output and two stated acceptance tests. Entry: the truest thing that can be said about the brand, which is generally not in the brief because clients are taught to minimise it (sk_whip_0041, sk_whip_0012). Operation: cross that truth with the conflicts it produces (sk_whip_0012), a conflict being required because without one there is no story (sk_whip_0011); the conflict may be found in the category, invented outright, or imposed by the versus frame (sk_whip_0014), and its most reliable shape is deprivation — life without the product rather than with it (sk_whip_0013). Output: not a campaign but a world with rules, which then keeps generating (sk_whip_0009); casting the brand as an archetype rather than as the hero is one route into such a world (sk_whip_0015). Acceptance tests: it fits on a sticky note, and spoken aloud it starts talking (sk_whip_0010). Sullivan applies the whole sequence to branded content, where the output must additionally satisfy an entertainment criterion (sk_whip_0070).

whole_system_claim.text: The system's real claim is that a platform is produced rather than found, and that the production runs on constraint. Each step narrows: a truth eliminates most of what could be said, a conflict eliminates most of what could be dramatised, and the resulting rule set eliminates most of what could be executed — after which, by the source's account, executions arrive without further invention. Sullivan states the payoff of the middle step in one word, focus, and states the payoff of the last as the rules starting to talk.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Sullivan states the formula (TRUTH + CONFLICTS = possible platform), the definitions of campaign and platform, the two signs, and the deprivation and versus devices, all in the same chapter and in this order. What is ours is the reading of the whole as a narrowing sequence and the claim that constraint is what makes it work — he says only that it gave his student focus. He also refuses the word formula and calls it a tool, so presenting it as a procedure is already one step further than he goes.

the rule set is what the crossing produces
the two signs test for the property that object defines

conflicts.note: sk_whip_0059 requires every execution to be wholly self-sufficient, while a platform's value is that later stories draw on rules the earlier ones established; the source states both and reconciles neither

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The sequence is largely the SOURCE'S — he writes it in this order in one chapter and states the formula in a display line. Ours are: the framing of it as a progressive narrowing, the placement of sk_whip_0041 (from Chapter 3) as the system's input, and the inclusion of sk_whip_0070 as an extension. He explicitly hedges the whole thing as a tool rather than a rule, and every supporting case is classroom work or a celebrated campaign described after the fact.

item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 10 "Trust and Tension Create Forward Motion", section "Pattern match/pattern interrupt" (spine 17)
item.question: You are launching into a category where every buyer already has an established routine. What does Godin say you are up against, and what timing rule does he derive from it?
item.answer: A pattern interrupt. Where a pattern exists, the routine has to be undone before any forward motion is possible, and the default answer to that request is no — because the pattern is established, time is precious and risk is feared. His mechanism is that undoing a pattern requires the person to accept their previous choice was wrong, which is a status cost on top of the switching cost. The timing rule follows: market to people who do not have a pattern yet. When life interferes — a new parent, someone recently engaged, someone who has just moved — there is nothing to match, so it is all interrupt and you do not have to persuade anyone that their old choices were mistakes. The same logic makes a brand-new platform the best time to launch an app on it. He also notes the institutional mirror: a purchasing manager has been taught that matching the pattern is how you keep a steady job with no surprises.
item.support: Pattern match/pattern interrupt: a pattern interrupt requires some sort of jolt and most of the time the answer is no, because the patterns are established, time is precious and risk is feared; when life interferes, new patterns are established, which is why it's profitable to market to new dads, engaged women and people who have recently moved; when you market to someone who doesn't have a pattern yet, you don't have to persuade them their old choices were mistakes.

He explains why the first half is not laziness: most car ads look alike because the sameness signals that this is a car worth considering, a safe alternative for a large purchase, and most big-company logos resemble each other because the designers are trying to remind you of a solid company. item.question: Every advertiser in a category is arguing against the other brands. Hopkins investigated and concluded they were all fighting over the wrong thing. What did he find, what did he do, and what is the general principle?

And this sits in direct tension with his later Quaker Oats conclusion that habits cannot be changed profitably in paid print — a contradiction he never addresses.

item.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the loyalty-card passage closing 'Highlighting Incredible Value' and the packaging discussion in 'More Than Money' (spine 10)
item.question: A supermarket loyalty scheme saves customers real money and generates almost no word of mouth. Berger gives two form conditions that explain it. What are they, and what does his proposed fix for the first one actually change?
item.answer: First, visibility. The saving is real but it is printed among half a dozen other items on a till receipt, and since nobody shows anyone their receipts, no one but the card holder ever sees it — so there is nothing to talk about and nothing for a non-holder to observe. His proposed fix is to surface it at the checkout: a sign showing the queue how much the current customer saved, or a bell rung when someone saves more than twenty-five dollars. That changes two things at once — it demonstrates the value to people who have no card, and it gives the card holder a remarkable figure worth repeating. Second, packaging. Useful information travels when it is bounded and scannable, so it can be passed on whole: a one-page note with a header item and three or four links rather than a rambling multi-page mailing across fifteen topics, which is also why so many heavily shared articles are short lists built around one topic.

item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', the Telephone study at the end of 'Making Virality Valuable' (spine 11)
item.question: What is the empirical basis for Berger's integration rule? Describe the study, its figure, and the pattern — and say whose study it is and how old.
item.answer: Gordon Allport and Joseph Postman's rumour research, published in 1947 — not Berger's, and more than sixty years old when he wrote. One person viewed a detailed picture of a subway car: an Eighth Avenue Express passing Dyckman Street, advertisements on the walls, five seated passengers including a rabbi and a mother with a baby, and, as the focus, two men arguing with one pointing and holding a knife. That person described it to a second, who described it to a third, and so on to a sixth, none of whom had seen it, across dozens of chains. About 70 percent of the details were lost in the first five or six transmissions. The important part is that the loss was STRUCTURED, not random: across chains the same details were consistently dropped and the same consistently retained, and the account sharpened around the central event. The line and the street went; the argument and the knife stayed. That is why an integrated brand survives and a decorative one does not.

Limits: the stimulus is a picture, not an experience, and the transmission is a laboratory chain rather than conversation, so whether the same rates hold for stories people want to tell is not established. The argument that settled it is stated by the person who made the call: the wristband lives on and the ride does not; there will be photographs of the ride and people will talk about the ride, but even repeated annually it does not act as a daily reminder, and the band does. item.question: Hopkins built a famous campaign out of facts that were true of every competitor. Describe the mechanism, and state the precondition without which it does not work.

The discriminator he reports is what a trademark lawyer weighs most heavily: whether the two logos are used in the same industry or by the same profession. item.source_locator: Ch. 16 "Price Is a Story", sections "Cheap is another way to say scared" and "Trust and risk, trust and expense" (spine 23)
item.question: Godin argues against competing on price, and one of his claims runs against intuition. What are the two claims, and what exemption does he allow?
item.answer: The first is that cheapness promises no change: when you are the cheapest you are promising the same, but cheaper — which removes the only thing he says a marketer has to offer — and that the race to the bottom is tempting because nothing is easier to sell than cheaper, requiring no calculation or thought from the buyer. The counter-intuitive one is that lowering your price does not make you more trusted, it does the opposite: where a transaction is risky or expensive, people construct a story that justifies their commitment, and that story carries trust with it — which is why high-end restaurants and hotels survive bad reviews. The exemption is genuine efficiency: unless you have found an extraordinary new way to deliver, racing to be cheapest means you are not investing sufficiently in change. He is objecting to cheapness as a position, not to a real cost advantage. He also notes, without embarrassment, that every confidence trickster relies on the trust mechanism — which is reason enough to hold it loosely.
item.support: Cheap is another way to say scared: unless you've found an extraordinary new way to deliver, racing to be cheapest means you're not investing in change; when you're the cheapest you're promising the same, but cheaper; low price is the last refuge of a marketer who has run out of generous ideas. Trust and risk: when people are heavily invested they often make up a story to justify their commitment, and that story carries trust; lowering your price does the opposite.
confounders: missing the efficiency exemption and reading it as a blanket rule against low prices
treating the trust-from-cost mechanism as established; it is cognitive-dissonance reasoning with no citation

source_terms: the simplest solution is usually the most effective

item.claim: Simplicity is not one attribute among equals in this source: it is the one that buys the others. item.claim: The authors give a diagnostic for why line extension keeps being chosen: managers look at currently successful companies, observe that those companies are expanding, and infer that expansion causes success. item.label: the_division_of_labour_between_word_and_image
item.description: Sullivan's treatment of headline and visual is a set of interlocking constraints on a single quantity: how the burden of meaning is split between the two elements. The precondition is that one element is designated as the entry point (sk_whip_0053). The format decision is taken early and is set by message complexity — letter or postcard (sk_whip_0045) — and choosing the postcard transfers the whole selling idea into the image (sk_whip_0044). Within a piece carrying both, one element may be the clever one and the other must be straight (sk_whip_0043); the distance between what is said and what is shown is the variable that sets the size of the reader's shift (sk_whip_0048); and zero distance is the named failure, the see-say (sk_whip_0032). Three generative devices supply the image side: transformation of the product itself (sk_whip_0051), borrowed image equity re-angled into a metaphor (sk_whip_0046), and demonstration rather than assertion (sk_whip_0047), which can remove the need for a headline entirely. Two members govern the look rather than the split: the brand should own a visual territory (sk_whip_0049) pulled from its own material rather than from current fashion (sk_whip_0050). The environment the piece appears in can itself become the image (sk_whip_0052).

whole_system_claim.text: In this source the relation between word and image is a designed quantity, not a matter of composition. Its lower bound is duplication, which wastes an element; its upper bound is the fuse running past the medium's dwell time; and everything between is a deliberate choice about how much of the resolving the reader is asked to do. That is why "which element carries the idea" is a question the maker must answer before executing rather than discover afterwards.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Sullivan states each constraint separately, across two chapters, as headed advice. He does state the scaling claim about polarity, the see-say failure and the clever/straight rule in the same short run, which is the strongest evidence for reading them as one set. What is ours is the framing of all of it as governing a single quantity, the identification of duplication and fuse length as the two bounds, and the inclusion of the look and environment members, which concern recognisability rather than the split.

dependencies.note: the clever/straight split presupposes a designated boss
a visually led piece presupposes the visual is dominant
the see-say is polarity at zero
the owned look must come from the brand, not from fashion
the metaphor's boundary against the visual cliché is re-angling

tradeoffs.note: greater polarity means a longer fuse; this set is bounded by scs_whip_001
a distinctive owned look and indifference to current visual convention pull against each other in practice, and against sk_whip_0030's requirement to study the category's conventions closely

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The claims are the source's; the set is largely OURS. He himself puts the clever/straight rule, the see-say failure and the polarity claim together in one run, and repeats the dominance requirement inside the letter/postcard decision, so a core of four members is source-grouped. The devices and the two look constraints were pulled in by us from a different chapter. A material limitation: almost every member is demonstrated by a reproduced advertisement that this extraction could not see, so what the images actually do is taken on the source's word.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 103-105 (Chapter Nine, the Van Camp's Milk coupon page in New York)
item.question: A brand has almost no shelf presence in a city dominated by a rival, and no budget for salesmen to call on grocers. Apply Hopkins's Van Camp's Milk plan: what is the sequence, what makes the grocer stock, and what did he report it cost and return?
item.answer: The sequence is announce, then redeem. For three weeks he announced in the newspapers that a coupon good at any store for a ten-cent can would appear, and told housewives what to expect from the milk. In parallel he mailed proofs of those advertisements to grocers, telling them every one of their customers would receive a coupon. The grocer's own arithmetic does the stocking: each coupon is a ten-cent sale that goes to a competitor if he cannot fill it — the manufacturer pays the grocer his retail price on redemption, so the grocer takes his normal profit and carries no risk. Then the coupon ran on a single Sunday page. In New York he reports 97 per cent distribution secured within three weeks, largely by letter; 1,460,000 coupons presented from that one page; $146,000 paid out to grocers to redeem them; a total enterprise cost of $175,000 including the advertising; and the cost returned with a profit in under nine months. These are his own retrospective figures, unaudited, and he warns in a neighbouring chapter that his memory of dates and sums may be at fault.
item.support: Printed pp. 103-105. The three-week pre-announcement to consumers and to grocers, the 97 per cent distribution figure, the 1,460,000 coupons, the $146,000 redemption, the $175,000 total and the under-nine-months payback are all stated there. Era-bound: paper coupons redeemed at independent grocers, general-circulation newspapers, no targeting.
confounders: the modern digital-coupon or trade-listing analogy; the whole mechanism depends on the grocer physically fearing a lost ten-cent sale to the shop next door
treating the 1,460,000 coupons as 1,460,000 converted users; he claims homes trying the milk in a single day, and the repeat question is answered separately at p. 135
confusing it with promiscuous house-to-house sampling, which he attacks on the very next page as cheapening the product and offending grocers
assuming the figures were audited; they are his recollection two decades later

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed p. 101 (Ch. 20 opening), p. 105 (Ch. 21 opening), p. 77 (Ch. 15 opening)
item.question: Someone cites 'immutable law' as a reason to weight a claim from this book heavily. Using three passages from inside the book itself, show what the authors actually claim about the status of their laws, and say what those concessions do and do not fix.
item.answer: Chapter 20 opens by saying that nothing in life and nothing in branding is ever absolute, that there are always exceptions to every rule, and that the Law of Change is the biggest exception to the laws of branding — one member of the set is described as an exception to the others. Chapter 21 opens by narrowing immutability to the laws themselves and excluding brands, which are born, grow up, mature and die. Chapter 15 opens by stating what the laws seem to suggest about concentrating on a single brand, agreeing it is true, and then licensing a second, third and fourth. So the authors themselves do not hold the twenty-two as independent universal axioms. What the concessions fix is the reading that every law applies always. What they do not fix is testability: no criterion is given anywhere for when an exception applies, so the concessions widen the laws rather than making them checkable, and they are never reconciled with the Introduction, which asserts the laws apply equally everywhere and assigns each named failure to the violation of a numbered law. The word "immutable" is a title, and it supplies no evidence.
item.support: Printed pp. 77, 101 and 105 — all three concessions are the authors' own sentences. The reading that they widen rather than test the laws is the extractor's, recorded in sk_r22_0049 and PROVENANCE.md §6. Nothing in this book is supported by measurement; see PROVENANCE.md §7 for the four candidate cases examined and rejected.
confounders: concluding the laws are worthless; practitioner assertion is a real category of knowledge and this is an articulate instance of it — the point is only about how it should be weighted
assuming the concessions make the laws falsifiable; they name exceptions without giving any test for when one applies

treating the Introduction's universal framing as the authors' considered position and the concessions as slips, or the reverse; both appear in the book, unreconciled, and this lane did not choose between them

item.claim: Sullivan names the two things people fire back at an advertisement and attaches a different fix to each. item.label: displacement_of_the_product_by_a_borrowed_element
item.description: Four failures the source reports in four different chapters, in which something brought into an advertisement to help it takes the attention or the memory the product needed: the celebrity who is remembered while the product is forgotten, the analogy whose vehicle the reader thinks is what is for sale, the named competitor who is taken for the hero of the commercial, and the corporate slogan or graphic symbol that clutters the layout and depresses readership of the copy.

whole_system_claim.text: These are one failure shape, not four coincidences. In each case an element is added for a reason that is locally sound — fame borrows credibility, an analogy borrows vividness, naming a competitor borrows a comparison, a symbol borrows recognition — and in each case the borrowed element competes with the product for the same finite attention and wins. The diagnostic that follows is one question asked of any addition: after this element is in, what is the most memorable thing in the advertisement? If the answer is not the product, the addition is subtracting.

It is kept in because the source's stated mechanism for it, cluttering the layout and reducing readership of the copy, is still a claim that an added element takes something the copy needed. source_terms: ask a better question

item.claim: Sullivan reproduces Tom Monahan's exercise as a three-stage ladder with a precise terminal condition. Question one is basic and has a correct answer, so no creativity is involved; question two is derived from the previous answer and can be guessed at, so some is; question three is derived again and has no correct answer that can be known or guessed, so creativity is required — and that is the better question. He instructs the first question always to be why people should buy the brand and the first answer to be the key message, so the ladder starts from the brief and climbs away from it. He notes the search is not linear: many threads dead-end, and the move is to back up, rephrase the last question and continue, which he demonstrates on two worked student cases. He then generalises it into a proposal about briefs: hand the creative team a key question rather than a key message, on the stated ground that a question has more potential energy because it is unfinished, where a message is fully cooked and asks nothing.

mechanism.text: Monahan's own explanation, quoted at length, is that ordinary questions let the answerer stay inside the known, because an answer is by definition something that already exists; progressively more probing questions leave no known available, so the mind is forced somewhere it has not been. The question does the forcing, not the answerer's effort.

source_terms: Not every graphical object needs to contrast with its surroundings - only those that are required for a user to understand what the graphic is conveying.

item.claim: The Understanding note supplies an operational test for "required for understanding". Identify what part of an image is needed to grasp what it represents; where there are several colours or a gradient, test the least-contrasting area; if that area falls below 3:1, assume it is invisible and ask whether the graphical object is still understandable. If enough remains to understand it, it passes. The note names four situations in which a graphic is not required for understanding at all: where text embedded or overlaid conveys the same information, such as labels and values on a chart; where the graphic is aesthetic and need not be seen to understand the content or use the functionality; where the information is available in another form such as a following table or a long description; and where the graphic is part of a logo or brand name. It adds that text within a graphic must itself meet SC 1.4.3.

mechanism.text: Treating the sub-threshold region as absent converts a contrast question into a comprehension question, which is what the criterion is actually protecting; a graphic can therefore keep low-contrast parts as long as the parts that carry the meaning survive their removal.

scope.conditions: assessing icons, charts, diagrams and other graphics under SC 1.4.11

caveats.text: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11 is a W3C Working Group Note; the criterion's phrase 'required to understand the content' is normative but the test procedure is not

source_terms: We try to give each advertiser a becoming style. We make him distinctive, perhaps not in appearance, but in manner and in tone. He is given an individuality best suited to the people he addresses.

One man appears rugged and honest in a line where rugged honesty counts. One may be a good fellow where choice is a matter of favor. In other lines the man stands out by impressing himself as an authority.

item.claim: An advertiser's personality is treated as a deliberate construction, selected to fit the audience rather than to express the client. The source describes giving each advertiser a becoming style — distinctive in manner and tone rather than appearance — and an individuality best suited to the people he addresses, with three worked castings: rugged and honest in a line where rugged honesty counts, a good fellow where choice is a matter of favour, and an authority in other lines. The distinction that governs the whole choice is between two kinds of uniqueness: one that belittles and arouses resentment, and one that is refreshing, enhances, and is welcomed and remembered. Eccentricity and abnormality are not distinctions to covet; doing admirable things in a different way is. item.claim: The source claims that a superlative makes no impression whatever, because it is the expected claim and is classed as exaggeration rather than falsehood; worse, it costs the advertiser respect, so everything else he says is discounted. A definite figure, by contrast, is accepted at par, because a definite statement is either a fact or a lie and readers do not expect reputable firms to lie in the better publications. It reports the device in four forms: a lamp's exact light multiple against the alternative; a motor manufacturer answering a public belief in excessive profits with a stated nine per cent margin and itemised hidden-part costs exceeding $700; a shaving cream published with laboratory figures where rivals used atmosphere; and a mail-order house that, instead of joining a chorus of lowest-price guarantees, published its actual net margin of three per cent and undertook not to exceed it. On the last it argues that in a chorus of superlatives all claims are equally ineffective, and that a stated margin was accepted as proof of bottom prices where every guarantee was not.

mechanism.text: A superlative is uncheckable and therefore costless to make, so readers price it at nothing and infer looseness. A specific figure is checkable and legally exposed, so it is read as having been weighed and measured, and belief transfers to the rest of the claim.

scope.conditions: media with editorial standards against outright falsehood; a claim that can actually be quantified

caveats.text: The source's credibility argument depends on a specific institutional fact of its era — that the better publications would not carry deliberate falsehood. It states this twice.

The mechanism rewards whoever quantifies first, not whoever is better. The source is explicit that rivals could probably meet the same shaving-cream specifications and that it has no idea one maker far excels others in the line.

The three-per-cent margin claim was derived from the client's own historical figures and is reported without independent verification. It is also a claim about margin, which a reader cannot check at all.

item.claim: Bijapurkar's most sustained methodological argument is against using "the Indian middle class" as a business-planning input, on the ground that the category has no agreed definition and that its size is therefore a function of who is defining it. She assembles the range: Hansa Research's finding from interviewing senior marketing professionals that "everyone of them had a unique definition" and that "no one really has a fix on this nebulous entity"; estimates from 100 million to 500 million; roughly 50 million by a global-brand affordability lens, 250-300 million by an FMCG lens, 375 million by NCAER's consuming class, 300 million by a middle-majority-of-income lens, 230 million by Butel's own-transport-entertainment-communication lens, shrinking to 30 million if a computer is added. She states the consequence: "despite being notional and subjective, if treated as a gospel, it leads to non-exploitation of opportunity and lazy strategy," and quotes Dr A. S. Ganguli that arbitrary downward estimates "do not truly reflect a state of restricted opportunity, but rather non-exploration of opportunities".

item.claim: The book's founding argument is built on a case that runs against its own thesis, and Sullivan states both halves. He reports the campaign was measurably successful — it sold billions of rolls, displaced the category leader, ran 504 executions over 26 years, and its actor was reported in 1975 as the second most recognised face in America — and simultaneously that research found it among the most disliked commercials of its decade and last in believability across years of studies. His position is that effectiveness does not settle the question. He quotes Norman Berry against judging advertising exclusively on sales: advertising that does not sell is lousy by any definition, but sales achieved with work in bad taste should not be applauded however much it sells, because offensive and stupid advertising damages the industry and business generally. His own test is a personal one — whether he could describe the work to his son — and his rebuttal to the sales defence is a question: spitting on the table would also get attention, so would you?

mechanism.text: The argument is that an advertisement has two accounts to settle, only one of which sales measure. Sullivan's stated alternative route reaches the same commercial destination — enduring brands and market leadership — without the second cost, which is what makes it a claim about sufficiency rather than a rejection of effectiveness.

item.claim: Jain reports that consumers of these images choose by SUBJECT, not by artist: "clients, and their customers in turn, are primarily interested in the 'subject' of a calendar and are unconcerned about other issues of provenance," artists' names "almost never register in conversations between publishers and their clients," and most end-users could not name any calendar artist beyond Ravi Varma. She quotes an Old Delhi pharmaceuticals trader: "I have no relation with the artist, I have a relation with the picture." She then reports the production constraint this creates. Customers often want a picture of the same deity year after year, so artists and printers are obliged to supply a constant stream of "new" designs on the "same" subjects, while iconographic recognisability limits what can change. She quotes a Sivakasi printer: "mythological means gods. In that we cannot change anything. Only colors we can change, dress we can change. Subject means same." And J. P. Singhal: "whatever change there is, it's in the decoration."

mechanism.text: If the thing being bought is the subject and the subject is fixed by iconographic convention, then the axis along which a producer can differentiate is narrow by construction. Novelty is therefore forced into the residual dimensions — background, colour, dress, ornament — which is why the industry recycles existing designs with modifications in exactly those, and why "copy masters" exist as a role.

scope.conditions: Religious calendars in the Indian trade 1994-2001. Jain notes the constraint is looser for secular subjects, for the upmarket multi-sheet calendars, and for wedding and greeting cards, "where the demand for novelty often outweighs considerations of expense, allowing for a greater degree of creative risk taking."

item.claim: Sullivan offers two questions to be asked before committing, both designed to reject work that is merely competent. The first, from Alex Bogusky: if you are about to spend money on a campaign and cannot imagine anybody writing or talking about it, rethink it. The second is a stated process rather than a question — write the press release for the idea before making it, picturing the newspaper story that will exist after it runs. He reports the origin: an agency principal tired of hearing teams open with what happens in the commercial, on the grounds that the press covers news and news is what the agency is trying to make. Sullivan sets the bar for that test explicitly at general news rather than trade press. He states the underlying reframe as the biggest thing in the chapter and attributes it: stop trying to come up with advertising ideas and work instead on coming up with ideas worth advertising.

item.claim: The source's clearest failure condition, and the one that separates his position from ordinary virality advice: content can be enormously transmitted and produce no benefit whatever for whoever paid for it, because what spreads is the content and not the sponsor. His two cases are chosen to make the point unmissable. A stunt at the 2004 Olympics carried an online casino's name and was discussed worldwide; the discussion was about Olympic security, the disrupted Chinese divers and the perpetrator's trial, and the casino dropped out because it was irrelevant to every version of the story. Evian's "Roller Babies" reached more than 50 million views and was declared the most viewed online advertisement in history; the same year Evian lost market share and sales fell almost 25 percent. He names the diagnosis directly: people focus so much on getting people to talk that they ignore what people are talking about.

mechanism.text: Retelling keeps what the story needs and drops what it does not. A sponsor attached to a story but not required by it is an extraneous detail, so it is either forgotten or omitted because including it does not make the story better.

scope.conditions: content produced or sponsored by an organisation that wants to benefit from its spread

caveats.text: Both cases are recounted with third-party outcome figures and neither is a controlled test. The Evian sales decline is reported from an Adweek piece and is not attributed by anyone to the campaign; a year of falling sales has many possible causes, and the source's placement of the two facts side by side implies more than the evidence carries.
The claim that the casino was irrelevant is inferred from what commentators discussed, not from any measurement of brand recall.

The underlying research is Berger's own but is cited only in the Notes as a Wharton working paper by Ezgi Akpinar and Jonah Berger titled 'Valuable Virality' (2012). Its design is not described anywhere in the text, so the reader is given the conclusion without the study.

The source's own definition of viral in the Introduction — raised likelihood of a pairwise pass-on, not long chains — makes this failure mode structurally predictable rather than surprising, but the book does not connect the footnote to this chapter.

item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a segmentation whose axis is not spending power but VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost. Her five: the rich as benefit maximizers, oriented to "money for value", willing to pay more for more, described as "anywhere in the world consumers who just happen to be in India"; the consuming class as cost-benefit optimizers, oriented to "value for money", balancing the two continuously, "very hard to seduce with imagery-oriented brand benefits"; the climbers as cash-constrained benefit maximizers with a fixed price point who shop for the maximum available within it; the aspirants, new and therefore occasional consumers; and the destitute. She claims the model is generic — "this value orientation-based consumer class model is a generic Indian model that works for all businesses" — and demonstrates it across office automation, hospital services, cellphones, education, chemicals and farm equipment.

mechanism.text: Two buyers with the same budget can want opposite things from it: one to spend it all on the most benefit obtainable, another to spend as little of it as will do. Since the offer that wins differs between them while the affordability data does not distinguish them, a segmentation on spending power will place them together and mis-specify the offer for at least one.

scope.conditions: Presented as a generic Indian model applicable across consumer and industrial categories, on NCAER's consumer-classes framework as the underlying population data.

caveats.text: the claim that the model 'works for all businesses' is a strong universal, supported by a series of illustrative applications the author asserts rather than by any validation. No case is given where it failed, and no test is offered

item.claim: Sullivan proposes systematically inverting the accepted executional norms of the category — put the logo where it never goes, make the small thing big, subordinate the headline to the copy — and reports Steve Dunn's observation that he is constantly surprised how often it works. Borrowing from Winsor and Bogusky, he names the target: doing something perfectly wrong, which he spells Rong. He states the degree condition explicitly and it is the substance of the claim: designing something wrong is easy, a little wrong is no good and a lot wrong is worse, and what works is the idea in direct opposition to all prevailing wisdom. He pairs it with a positive signal for the maker's own hesitation: if you catch yourself wondering whether they will even let you do this, you should definitely do it, because the forces you sense assembling against the idea may be a measure of the commotion it would cause. He is emphatic that this is not difference for its own sake, quoting Bernbach that provocation must stem from the product — standing a man on his head to get attention is wrong, doing it to show the product keeps things from falling out of his pockets is right.

mechanism.text: Convention is what the audience expects, so an execution in direct opposition is unpredicted and therefore noticed; partial deviation is still read inside the convention and so buys nothing. Sullivan connects this to talkability — people make remarks about what is remarkable — which is why the degree condition matters rather than being pedantry.

scope.conditions: the source frames this as work for makers who have already learned the conventions — Picasso learned to draw a realistic head first — and says explicitly it comes after the earlier chapters

caveats.text: the source's most detailed example is a food campaign built on filming the product rotting, and he concedes extraordinary advertising is often polarising and that the reader need not like it; the claim it succeeded rests on it being talked about worldwide, not on a sales figure

the 'will they even let us' signal is a heuristic that cannot distinguish an idea meeting resistance because it is strong from one meeting resistance because it is bad; the source does not address this
the whole chapter's examples are Cannes and One Show winners, a selected sample of survivors of exactly this strategy; inversions that failed are not shown
