source_terms: Other coined names are meaningless... They can be protected, and long-continued advertising may give them a meaning. When this is accomplished they become very valuable. But the great majority of them never attain that status.

Other coined names signify ingredients which anyone may use... They invite substitution. They are naturally classified with other products which have like ingredients, so the price must remain in that class.
On a patented product it must be remembered that the right to a name expires with the patent. Names like Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit, etc., have become common property.
Another serious fault in coined names is frivolity. In seeking uniqueness one gets something trivial. And that is a fatal handicap in a serious product.
When a product must be called by a common name, the best auxiliary name is a man's name. It is much better than a coined name, for it shows that some man is proud of his creation.
item.claim: The source distinguishes four distinct name failures, each with its own mechanism. A meaningless coined name is exclusive and protectable and long-continued advertising may eventually give it a meaning at which point it becomes very valuable — but the great majority never attain that status, so its display is doubtful. An ingredient name may dominate a market if the price is reasonable but invites substitution and forces the product into the price class of everything sharing the ingredient. A patented product's name right expires with the patent, which the source calls a very serious point that often makes a patent an undesirable protection. And a frivolous name, arrived at while seeking uniqueness, is a fatal handicap in a serious product because it almost prohibits respect. Where a product must be called by a common name, the best auxiliary is a man's name, better than a coined one because it shows that some man is proud of his creation.

mechanism.text: A name's exclusivity and its descriptive power trade against each other. Exclusivity protects demand but must be paid for in advertising to acquire meaning; description sells for free but is available to competitors, so the demand created is shared and the price class is set by the shared attribute.

scope.conditions: naming a new product, including products under patent and products with an unavoidable common name

caveats.text: The classification is the valuable content and it is a taxonomy without evidence: which names fell into which class is asserted, and no rate is given for the central quantitative claim that the great majority of meaningless coined names never acquire meaning.

Toasted Corn Flakes and Malted Milk appear here as they do in chapter 12 (sk_sa8_0023). `repeated_within_source` is recorded. The chapter also admits an untested counterfactual: "It is interesting to speculate on how much more profitable a coined name might have been."
The trademark and patent reasoning is 1923 American law as the author understood it. It is recorded as the source's claim about its period and is NOT relied on as legal fact.
The frivolity claim is the same respect argument used against eccentric pictures in chapter 9 (sk_sa8_0007), applied to naming, and it is equally unevidenced in both places.

item.label: the_measurable_branches_and_what_measurement_costs
item.description: The source's account of where in advertising a result can actually be attributed, why, what a practitioner may therefore conclude there, and what the measurement costs. It spans direct mail, business advertising by inquiry, the split run for choosing a promise, brand preference against recall for television, and the two constraints he states on all of it — that tests are serial, and that a measurable response is not the same as the outcome wanted.

whole_system_claim.text: Attributability, not format, is what makes a branch of advertising testable, and every testable branch in the book is testable for the same reason: the response returns to the advertiser rather than passing through a distribution channel that mixes it with everything else. Where that holds, the source will accept a finding over a judgement. But he also states three costs, in three different chapters, and they belong together: tests are serial, so experience must ration what gets tested; the response that is measurable may select a worse customer than the one wanted; and the two questions with the longest horizons — a campaign's long-run contribution and what price to charge — cannot be answered by research at all. The framework is therefore not "measure everything" but "know which branch you are in, and know what the measurement is substituting for."
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states each piece and never assembles them. He states the attributability argument in the direct mail chapter and again, in the same shape, for business inquiry. He states the serial limit twice — one variable at a time in direct mail, two headlines at a time in the split run — without connecting the two statements. He states the response-quality trade-off once, in the direct mail chapter, and the two unanswerable questions once, in the research chapter. The claim that these five statements constitute one framework, and that its conclusion is a qualified rather than an unqualified endorsement of measurement, is ours.

dependencies.nature: the serial limit bounds what the testable branch can actually test
the split run inherits the same serial limit, two headlines at a time

tradeoffs.nature: The response that makes a branch measurable is also a response that can be raised by devices which select customers who do not stay. Measurability and the wanted outcome pull apart on the same lever.

tradeoffs.nature: A measure that predicts purchase is preferred to one that does not, and neither can answer which campaign contributes most over years — which the source says still requires judgement.

conflicts.nature: Experience decides which variables are worth testing, and testing is what produces experience. The source states both halves and does not notice the circle.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Every member is a claim the source makes plainly. The assembly is entirely OURS, and it is the assembly that carries the value: the source's own presentation splits the endorsement of measurement from its three costs across three chapters, so a reader who takes any chapter alone gets a stronger position than the book as a whole supports. Retrieving the endorsement without the constraints would misrepresent him.

source_terms: minor changes kill great ideas
the load-bearing beam
protect the pyramid
base your defense on strategy
item.claim: Sullivan holds that the serious damage to work is not a single rejection but an accumulation of small changes, and that less experienced clients are particularly good at asking for the removal of the load-bearing beam — the one element holding the whole idea up. His stated response is triage rather than resistance: let the body copy be changed, let the colours be changed, and protect the idea; if you get out with the big idea intact, count it a success. He states the stopping condition too — if enough changes have destroyed the original idea, kill it yourself. His defence tactics are correspondingly specific. Base the defence on strategy, not on the creativity of the execution, because strategy is the thing the client helped author; be able to track step by step how you arrived at the work. Do not attempt to solve the problem in the meeting — write down the concerns, play them back, and take it away. Never show work you do not want bought, because clients gravitate to the safer second-rate option. And do not pre-kill your best work on the client's behalf. He frames the underlying posture as a humility rule: enter every discussion believing there is a fifty percent chance you are wrong, which he argues makes the argument more persuasive because it does not feel forced.

mechanism.text: Two mechanisms. On damage: an idea has load-bearing elements whose removal is not proportional to their size, so change count is a poor proxy for harm and battles must be chosen by what each change is holding up. On defence: the client's grounds for judgement are commercial rather than aesthetic — Sullivan notes marketing directors may spend as little as five percent of their time on advertising and that judging advertising is not what got them the job — so an argument pitched on strategy is one they can actually evaluate.

scope.conditions: client review and revision of presented work; the source's frame throughout is a client-service business in which the client has bought the right to their opinion

caveats.text: the source states plainly that advertising is a service industry and clients have paid for the right to their opinion, which bounds the whole chapter — it is not a licence to override the client
the fifty-percent-wrong rule is offered as a persuasion posture and simultaneously as a sincere belief; the source says to really believe it, which is a demanding and unfalsifiable instruction
the claim that clients gravitate to second-rate work is drawn from the source's own experience of presenting filler; no counting is offered

the closing advice of the chapter runs against the rest of it — he reports two senior practitioners arguing you should not make a career of protecting work, and concedes they may be right; the chapter does not resolve this

source_stated_problems: minor changes kill great ideas, very slowly and with incredible pain
less experienced clients are particularly good at asking you to take out 'the load-bearing beam'
the client will approve the work they feel safer with, less scared by, and that is always the second-rate work
'Oh, the client will never buy this' — and then you killed it yourself
source_stated_remedies: protect the pyramid; if you get out of there with the big idea intact, consider yourself a genius
base your defense on strategy; think like a creative person, but talk like an accountant
do not try to solve the problem in the meeting; write down their issues, play them back, and take it away
never show a client work you don't want them to buy
go as far as you can; let the client bring you back
if one too many client changes have hurt your original idea, pull the trigger
